sounds.name: Bright Pop Riff
sounds.ref: In the style of Yazoo — "Don’t Go"
sounds.blurb: Punchy, bright riff sound with a hard front edge on every note.
sounds.how: Sawtooth and pulse are switched on together on Oscillator A, which is something most synths cannot do, and Oscillator B adds a second, slightly detuned saw. The filter starts half closed and a fast envelope snaps it open at the start of each note. RETRIG makes sure every key press gets that snap, even in a fast run.

steps.title: Saw and pulse together
steps.why:
Oscillator A gets two waveforms at once, which most synths cannot do, and Oscillator B is set up as a second saw to widen it. Together they give a bright, full riff tone with plenty of harmonics for the filter to work on.
- Osc A sawtooth and pulse on: the saw is the buzz, the pulse adds a hollow body underneath. Each wave has its own switch, so both play and are added together.
- PULSE WIDTH 5 (50 %): a square wave, the roundest and most hollow the pulse gets. Moving it towards 0 or 10 would make it thinner and more nasal.
- OCTAVE 2 on both: the middle of the four octave settings (0 lowest, 3 highest), a normal riff register.
- Osc B sawtooth only, FREQUENCY +0.1 st: a plain saw tuned a hair sharp, so the two beat gently. B stays silent until the next step turns it up in the mixer.
- Listen for: switch Osc A pulse off and on while holding a note; the tone goes thinner and buzzier without it.

steps.title: Both oscillators in the mixer
steps.why:
The mixer sets how loud each source is going into the filter. Here Oscillator B comes in under A, and the slight detune from the last step becomes audible.
- OSC A 8: Oscillator A leads and sets the character.
- OSC B 7: just under A, so the detuned saw widens the sound without taking over. Lower it and the riff gets narrower and more focused; raise it and the beating gets stronger.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise, the riff should be clean.
- Listen for: hold a note and you hear a slow, gentle beating as the two oscillators drift in and out of phase. Turn OSC B to 0 and back to hear the width come and go.

steps.title: Half-close the filter
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs. This step sets the tone each note falls back to once the envelope snap (next step) has passed.
- CUTOFF 4.2 (about 364 Hz): half closed, so most of the buzz is gone and the note is warm and round. Higher is brighter but gives the snap less distance to travel, so it punches less.
- RESONANCE 3: a small boost at the cutoff point. It gives the opening snap a slightly nasal edge that helps it cut through a mix. Turn it up and the snap turns squelchy.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 6: the cutoff follows the keys a little more than half way. High notes of the riff open up to match the low ones rather than going dull.
- Listen for: the riff is now duller than before. That is the resting tone; the next step adds the bite back on each note.

steps.title: Snap it open with the envelope
steps.why:
The filter envelope is an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release): it pushes the cutoff up each time you play and lets it fall back. This is the snap at the front of every note.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 6: how far the envelope lifts the cutoff above 364 Hz. More gives a brighter, harder hit; less and the front edge softens.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): the filter opens instantly, so the brightness lands exactly on the beat.
- DECAY 4.6 (120 ms): how fast it closes again, about a tenth of a second. Shorter is more percussive; longer turns the snap into a “wow”.
- SUSTAIN 2.5, RELEASE 3.5 (54 ms): held notes settle back to a fairly dark tone, and the brightness dies quickly after you let go.
- Listen for: a bright “dat” at the start of each note, then the tone rounding off. Sweep DECAY while the riff plays to hear the punch tighten and loosen.

steps.title: Tight volume shape
steps.why:
The loudness envelope, also an ADSR, shapes the volume of each note. For a riff you want an instant start and a clean stop.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): full level at once, so the volume hit lines up with the filter snap.
- DECAY 5 (170 ms) to SUSTAIN 7: after the first hit the level drops a little, which adds a touch more punch to the front of each note.
- RELEASE 3.5 (54 ms): notes stop about a twentieth of a second after you let go, so fast notes do not smear into each other.
- Listen for: the gaps between notes in a quick run should be clean. Raise RELEASE to 6 and the notes start to blur together.

steps.title: Retrigger every note
steps.why:
The MODE section decides how key presses fire the envelopes. In NORMAL, a note played while another is still held changes pitch but does not restart the envelopes, so legato notes lose their snap.
- Retrigger on (RETRIG): every key press restarts both envelopes, so each note in a fast, overlapping run gets its own attack and filter snap.
- Listen for: play a run where each key goes down before the last one comes up. With RETRIG on every note snaps; switch it off and only the first note of the run does, the rest just change pitch.

context.oscA.pulse: On together with the saw. Switch it off and the riff gets thinner and buzzier.
context.oscB.freq: A tiny detune against Oscillator A. This is where the width comes from.
context.filter.cutoff: The resting tone between snaps. Raise it and the riff gets brighter but less punchy, because the envelope has less distance to travel.
context.filter.env: The size of the snap at the front of each note.
context.fenv.decay: The length of the snap. Shorter is more percussive; longer turns it into a "wow".
context.mode.retrig: Makes sure every note in a fast run gets its own attack.

tweaks.hear: From a tight click to a slower "wow" on each note.
The pulse narrows and the riff takes on a nasal, reedy edge.
An octave underneath makes the riff sound bigger and more like a bass-and-lead in one.
The snap becomes a squelch.

sounds.name: Bouncy Pulse Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of early Depeche Mode and Yazoo bass lines
sounds.blurb: Short, rubbery bass that bounces along under a pop song.
sounds.how: A narrow-ish pulse wave gives a woody, slightly nasal bass tone, and a saw an octave below adds weight. The filter envelope has no sustain, so every note opens and then closes completely: that is the bounce. The volume envelope is kept a little longer than the filter so the note has a soft tail.

steps.title: Pulse on top, saw underneath
steps.why:
Two oscillators split the job: a pulse wave gives the bass its character and a saw an octave lower gives it weight. Oscillator B is silent until the mixer step brings it in.
- Osc A pulse on, sawtooth off: a pulse wave on its own sounds woody and hollow rather than buzzy.
- PULSE WIDTH 3.6 (37 %): a bit narrower than a square (5). That thins the pulse slightly and adds a nasal edge; towards 2 it gets thin and buzzy, at 5 it is round and hollow.
- OCTAVE osc A 1: one below the default, a bass register. Octaves run 0 (lowest) to 3.
- Osc B sawtooth, OCTAVE 0, FREQUENCY 0: a saw a further octave down, in tune, for the low weight under the pulse.
- Listen for: sweep PULSE WIDTH slowly on a held note to hear the tone go from hollow to nasal.

steps.title: Mix
steps.why:
The mixer sets how loud each oscillator is going into the filter. The pulse leads and the low saw sits underneath as support.
- OSC A 8: the pulse carries the character of the bass.
- OSC B 6: the octave-down saw adds weight without muddying it. Turn it down for a lighter, more plucked bass; up for more low end.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: turn OSC B down to 0 and back on a low note. The note loses its bottom octave and sounds thin without it.

steps.title: Filter nearly shut
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass, keeping lows and cutting highs. It starts nearly shut, so each note will open from a dark, thumping tone.
- CUTOFF 2.8 (about 138 Hz): very dark. Most of the pulse’s edge is gone until the envelope opens it.
- RESONANCE 1.5: only a small boost at the cutoff. More resonance would thin the low end, so it is kept low to leave the bass full.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5: the cutoff follows the keys half way, so higher notes of the line are not much duller than low ones.
- Listen for: held notes now sound muffled and round. That is the closed state the bounce will start from.

steps.title: Open and shut on every note
steps.why:
The filter envelope is an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release) that lifts the cutoff on each note. With no sustain, the filter opens and then closes fully every time: that is the bounce.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 5.5: how bright the top of each bounce gets. More is a brighter, harder pop; less is softer and darker.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): the filter opens instantly on the beat.
- DECAY 4.2 (85 ms): the length of the bounce. Shorter is clickier, longer gives a slower “wow”.
- SUSTAIN 0: the filter always closes back to 138 Hz, however long you hold the key.
- RELEASE 3 (34 ms): short, so nothing lingers after you let go.
- Listen for: a rubbery “boing” at the start of each note. Sweep DECAY while the line plays to hear the bounce stretch and shrink.

steps.title: Volume a little longer than the filter
steps.why:
The loudness envelope, also an ADSR, shapes volume. It is set a little longer than the filter so the note carries on quietly after the filter has closed.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): the note starts at once, lined up with the filter pop.
- DECAY 5.5 (270 ms) to SUSTAIN 4: the level falls to under half over about a quarter of a second, longer than the 85 ms filter decay. That gives a rounded tail instead of a dead stop.
- RELEASE 3 (34 ms): notes end almost as soon as you let go, keeping the line tight.
- Listen for: hold a note and hear the dark tail after the bounce. Set SUSTAIN to 10 and the tail stays loud, which makes the bass heavier but less bouncy.

context.oscA.pw: Sets how woody or nasal the bass is. 5 is hollow and round; towards 2 it gets thin and buzzy.
context.fenv.decay: The length of the bounce.
context.fenv.sustain: At zero so the filter always closes fully.
context.filter.env: How bright the top of each bounce gets.
context.mix.oscB: The low saw. Turn it down for a lighter, more "plucked" bass.

tweaks.hear: Hollow, to woody, to thin and nasal. Every position is a usable bass.
Very short is a tight tick; longer gives a lazier, dubby bounce.

tweaks.try: Set to 5 and flip OSC A PW to DIR
tweaks.hear: The LFO moves the pulse width, so the tone shifts slightly from note to note.

sounds.name: Tearing Sync Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of The Prodigy — early-90s rave sync leads
sounds.blurb: Aggressive lead whose tone rips downwards through each note.
sounds.how: With SYNC on, Oscillator A is forced to restart every time Oscillator B finishes a cycle. B now fixes the pitch you hear. Pushing A’s frequency up no longer changes the note; it crams more of A’s wave into each of B’s cycles, which adds harsh, vocal overtones. Sending the filter envelope to A’s frequency through the modulation matrix sweeps those overtones on every note.

steps.title: Listen to Oscillator A only
steps.why:
The mixer sets what reaches the filter. For a sync lead the sound you hear is Oscillator A alone; Oscillator B will do its work silently as the sync master.
- OSC A 8: the synced oscillator is the sound.
- OSC B 0: kept out of the mixer. Mixed in, it would add a plain steady tone that softens the tearing effect.
- Osc A sawtooth on, pulse off: a saw has every harmonic, which gives sync the most to work with.
- Listen for: at this point it is a plain bright saw. The next step makes it tear.

steps.title: Sync A to B
steps.why:
Hard sync forces Oscillator A to restart every time Oscillator B finishes a cycle. On the Pro-1 A is the one that gets reset, the reverse of most synths, so B sets the pitch and A’s tuning changes the tone.
- Sync on: A is locked to B. The note you hear now comes from B.
- OCTAVE osc A 3, FREQUENCY +2.1 st: A is tuned well above B, so it crams more of its wave into each of B’s cycles. That gives harsh, vocal overtones.
- Osc B OCTAVE 2, FREQUENCY 0, sawtooth on: B sets the note at the normal octave.
- Osc B keyboard on, low frequency NORMAL: B follows the keys at audio rate, so the lead plays in tune.
- Listen for: turn osc A FREQUENCY by hand on a held note. The pitch stays put and only the tone shifts, with a nasal, ripping character.

steps.title: Route the filter envelope to A’s pitch
steps.why:
The modulation section routes three sources to five destinations. Each source has an AMOUNT and a ROUTE switch to the DIRECT bus (always on) or the WHEEL bus (only as you push the mod wheel).
- AMOUNT FIL ENV 7.5: sends a large amount of the filter envelope into the modulation. More gives a wider, more dramatic rip.
- FIL ENV route DIRECT: always on, no mod wheel needed.
- To OSC A FREQ DIR: A’s pitch listens to the DIRECT bus. With sync on, the envelope now sweeps A’s tone, not the note.
- Listen for: each note starts with A pushed high and falls back, tearing down through the overtones. Switch Sync off to hear it as a plain pitch drop instead.

steps.title: Shape the sweep
steps.why:
The filter envelope is an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release). There is no separate modulation envelope on the Pro-1, so this one is shaping the sync sweep. The filter itself is opened up so it does not hide the effect.
- ATTACK 0, DECAY 6.2 (510 ms): the sweep starts instantly and falls over half a second. DECAY is the speed of the rip.
- SUSTAIN 3, RELEASE 4 (87 ms): held notes settle with some brightness left in the sync tone.
- CUTOFF 7.5 (3.6 kHz), RESONANCE 1: the low-pass filter is wide open, so all the sync overtones come through.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 1.5, KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5: only a slight filter movement on each note, and the cutoff follows the keys half way.
- Listen for: sweep DECAY while playing. Short is a quick “zap”; long is a slow scream.

steps.title: Lead-style volume and glide
steps.why:
The loudness envelope shapes volume, and glide makes the pitch slide between notes. Together they set how the lead phrases.
- ATTACK 0, DECAY 5 (170 ms), SUSTAIN 8: an instant start and a nearly full held level, so long notes keep singing.
- RELEASE 4 (87 ms): a short tail after you let go.
- RATE 2.5 (190 ms): how long a slide takes. Higher settings make slower, more obvious swoops.
- Glide mode AUTO: only slides when you press a new key while still holding the last one (legato). Detached notes jump straight to pitch.
- Listen for: play two notes overlapping and hear the slide; lift between them and there is none.

context.oscA.sync: The heart of the sound. Switch it off and you just hear an oscillator falling in pitch.
context.oscA.freq: With sync on this is a tone control. Turn it by hand to hear the overtones shift.
context.mod.envAmt: How far the envelope pushes Oscillator A. More means a wider, more dramatic rip.
context.fenv.decay: The speed of the rip.
context.mix.oscB: Kept at zero: Oscillator B is only the sync master here.
context.mod.toAFreq: Connects the DIRECT bus (carrying the filter envelope) to Oscillator A’s pitch.

tweaks.try: Sweep by hand from −5 to 5 while holding a note
tweaks.hear: The same rip, played manually. This is how the effect was performed live.

tweaks.try: Flip to WHEEL and set OSC A FREQ to WH
tweaks.hear: The sweep only happens as you push the mod wheel, so you can bring it in on chosen notes.
A fast "pyew" at the start of each note instead of a long tear.
The plain saw underneath adds body and steadies the pitch.

sounds.name: PWM Solo Strings
sounds.ref: In the style of Howard Jones — early-80s synth-pop string lines
sounds.blurb: Smooth, shimmering line that sounds like more than two oscillators.
sounds.how: When the width of a pulse wave is moved slowly back and forth, its harmonics shift all the time, and the ear hears that as several detuned oscillators playing together. Here the LFO moves the pulse width of both oscillators through the modulation matrix. Slow attacks on both envelopes take away the hard front edge, which is what makes it read as strings.

steps.title: Two pulse waves
steps.why:
Two pulse waves are the raw material for PWM (pulse-width modulation), which the next step adds. Starting both at square width leaves room for the width to swing either way.
- Pulse on for both, other waves off: pulse waves only, hollow and reedy.
- PULSE WIDTH 5 (50 %) on both: square waves, the centre of the swing. Starting off-centre would let the pulse collapse to almost nothing at one end.
- OCTAVE 2 on both: the same, normal register.
- FREQUENCY osc B +0.2 st: a slight detune against A, for gentle beating.
- OSC A 7, OSC B 7: equal levels in the mixer, so both pulses count.
- Listen for: a hollow, slightly beating organ-like tone. It is still static; the movement comes next.

steps.title: Let the LFO move both pulse widths
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) is a slow wave used to move other settings. Here it moves the pulse width of both oscillators through the modulation section, which the ear hears as several detuned oscillators.
- LFO triangle only: a smooth up-and-down, right for PWM.
- FREQUENCY lfo 4.2 (0.96 Hz): a little under one cycle a second. Slower sounds like an ensemble; faster starts to sound like vibrato.
- AMOUNT LFO 6, route DIRECT: how far the width swings, always on. Too much and the pulse gets so thin at each end that the sound seems to drop out.
- To OSC A PW and To OSC B PW both DIR: both pulse widths listen to the DIRECT bus.
- Listen for: the tone starts to shimmer and swirl straight away. Set AMOUNT LFO to 0 and back to hear it go flat.

steps.title: Mellow filter, gentle movement
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass. Here it takes the fizz off the top, and a small, slow envelope makes each note brighten slightly after it starts, like a bow digging in.
- CUTOFF 6 (1.3 kHz), RESONANCE 1: mellow and smooth, with no peak.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 6: higher notes open the filter a little more, so the top of the line stays clear.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 2: only a small lift from the envelope.
- ATTACK 5 (110 ms), DECAY 6 (420 ms): the brightening swells in over a tenth of a second rather than snapping.
- SUSTAIN 7, RELEASE 5 (220 ms): held notes keep most of that brightness.
- Listen for: less edge than before, and a slight swell of brightness just after each note starts.

steps.title: Fade in, fade out
steps.why:
The loudness envelope shapes volume. Slow attacks take away the hard front edge, which is what makes the line read as strings rather than an organ.
- ATTACK 5.5 (170 ms): each note fades in, removing the click.
- DECAY 6 (420 ms) to SUSTAIN 9: held notes stay almost at full level.
- RELEASE 5.2 (270 ms): about a quarter of a second of tail, so notes overlap a little.
- Listen for: play a slow line and hear each note swell in and hang briefly into the next. Set ATTACK to 0 and it turns into an organ.

context.mod.lfoAmt: How far the pulse width swings. Too much and the pulse gets so thin at each end of the swing that the sound seems to drop out.
context.lfo.rate: The speed of the shimmer. Under 1 Hz sounds like an ensemble; faster sounds like vibrato.
context.oscA.pw: The centre of the swing. Keep it near 5 so the pulse never collapses at either end.
context.aenv.attack: The slow fade-in is what makes this strings rather than an organ.
context.mod.toAPw: Connects the DIRECT bus (carrying the LFO) to Oscillator A’s pulse width.

tweaks.hear: At 0 the sound is a static, organ-like square. At 6 it comes alive.
The shimmer becomes a nervous warble.
An octave on top adds a violin-like sheen.
With no fade-in it turns into a synth organ.

sounds.name: Mod-Wheel Growl Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of 80s electro-funk bass
sounds.blurb: Solid resonant bass that snarls when you push the mod wheel.
sounds.how: Oscillator B is wired to the filter cutoff through the WHEEL bus. Because B is running at audio rate, it shakes the filter fifty or more times a second. You do not hear that as wobble but as a rough, growling set of extra overtones. With the mod wheel down the patch is a clean bass; push the wheel and the growl comes in as far as you like.

steps.title: Two saws, low
steps.why:
Two saws in the bass register give a solid starting tone. Oscillator B is also heard here, but its main job later is to shake the filter at audio rate.
- Sawtooth on for both, other waves off: two bright saws.
- OCTAVE 1 on both, FREQUENCY osc B 0: both a bass octave down, in tune.
- Osc B keyboard on, low frequency NORMAL: B follows the keys at audio rate, so the growl it adds later keeps the same character on every note.
- Sync off: the oscillators run freely.
- OSC A 8, OSC B 4: A leads and B adds a little thickness.
- Listen for: a plain, bright saw bass. The filter step darkens it.

steps.title: Resonant bass filter
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass. Low cutoff with a good amount of resonance gives a solid bass, and the resonant peak is what Oscillator B will shake.
- CUTOFF 3.4 (209 Hz): dark, bass-weight tone.
- RESONANCE 5.5: a clear peak at the cutoff. The growl comes from this peak being moved; at 0 the effect is much milder.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 4.5: the filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), opens the cutoff on each note.
- DECAY 5.2 (210 ms), SUSTAIN 3: after an instant attack (ATTACK 0) it falls back over about 200 ms, for a resonant pluck.
- RELEASE 3.5 (54 ms), KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5: short tail; cutoff follows the keys half way.
- Listen for: a round bass with a squelchy “bow” at the start of each note.

steps.title: Put Oscillator B on the wheel bus
steps.why:
The modulation section sends sources to destinations over two buses: DIRECT (always on) and WHEEL (only as you push the mod wheel). Here Oscillator B goes to the filter cutoff on the WHEEL bus.
- AMOUNT OSC B 7.5: the most growl the wheel can bring in. B runs at audio rate, so it moves the cutoff fifty or more times a second. That is heard as rough extra overtones, not as a wobble.
- OSC B route WHEEL: B only reaches its destinations as the wheel comes up.
- To FILTER WH: the cutoff listens to the WHEEL bus. Down (DIR) would listen to the DIRECT bus, which is empty here.
- Listen for: nothing changes yet, because the mod wheel is down.

steps.title: Volume
steps.why:
The loudness envelope gives a plain bass shape. With it set, the patch is ready: play, and push the mod wheel beside the keyboard.
- ATTACK 0, DECAY 5 (170 ms), SUSTAIN 8: an instant start, then a nearly full held level so long notes keep their weight.
- RELEASE 3 (34 ms): notes stop cleanly.
- Listen for: with the wheel down, a clean resonant bass. Push the wheel slowly and a snarl comes in as far as you take it. Try OCTAVE osc B at 0 or 2 for different kinds of roughness.

context.mod.oscBAmt: The most growl the wheel can bring in.
context.mod.oscBRoute: WHEEL means Oscillator B only reaches the filter as you push the mod wheel.
context.mod.toFilter: Up (WH) listens to the WHEEL bus. Down (DIR) would listen to the DIRECT bus, which is empty in this patch.
context.filter.res: The growl is the resonant peak being shaken. With resonance at 0 the effect is much milder.
context.oscB.kbd: On, so the modulator moves with the note and the growl has the same character across the keyboard.
context.oscB.octave: The pitch of the modulator relative to the note. Each octave gives a different kind of roughness.

tweaks.hear: Lower gives a slower, purring roughness; higher gives a brighter, metallic rasp.
The modulator is no longer in tune with the note, so the growl turns clangy and bell-like.

tweaks.try: Flip to DIRECT, and FILTER to DIR
tweaks.hear: The growl is on all the time at full amount, with no wheel needed.

tweaks.try: Switch saw off and triangle on
tweaks.hear: A smoother modulator gives a rounder, less fizzy growl.

sounds.name: Slowing Wobble
sounds.ref: In the style of 80s sci-fi soundtracks and arcade effects
sounds.blurb: A filter wobble that starts fast on each note and winds down.
sounds.how: The LFO sweeps the filter to make a wobble. One patch cable then sends the filter envelope into the LFO CV jack, so the envelope controls the LFO’s speed. At the start of a note the envelope is high and the wobble is fast; as the envelope decays the wobble slows down. An envelope controlling the speed of another modulator is a basic modular-synth idea.

steps.title: A bright, low oscillator
steps.why:
A bright, low oscillator gives the filter plenty to chew on, so the wobble later is easy to hear.
- Osc A sawtooth and pulse on: both waves added together, full of harmonics.
- PULSE WIDTH 5 (50 %): the pulse is a square, hollow under the saw.
- OCTAVE osc A 1: one octave down from the default, in the low register.
- Sync off: A runs freely.
- OSC A 8, OSC B 0: only Oscillator A is heard.
- Listen for: a thick, buzzy tone. It is static for now.

steps.title: LFO sweeps the filter
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) is a slow wave. Sent through the modulation section to the filter cutoff, it sweeps the brightness up and down to make a wobble.
- LFO triangle only, FREQUENCY 5 (1.55 Hz): a smooth sweep about one and a half times a second. This is the speed the wobble ends up at later.
- AMOUNT LFO 6.5, To FILTER DIR: how deep the wobble is, sent on the DIRECT bus (always on) to the cutoff.
- CUTOFF 4.5 (448 Hz): the centre the LFO swings around, fairly dark.
- RESONANCE 5: a peak at the cutoff, so it sounds like “wow-wow” rather than a volume change.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 1, KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5: the filter envelope barely touches the cutoff; the cutoff follows the keys half way.
- Listen for: a steady, even wobble on a held note.

steps.title: Patch FILTER ENV into LFO CV
steps.why:
One patch cable sends the filter envelope into the LFO CV jack (control voltage for LFO speed). The envelope now controls how fast the LFO runs: an envelope controlling another modulator, a basic modular-synth idea.
- Cable FILTER ENV → LFO CV: the envelope voltage is added to the FREQUENCY knob. High envelope means a fast wobble.
- Filter ATTACK 0 (2 ms): the envelope jumps to its peak at once, so every note starts with the LFO running about eight times faster.
- DECAY 7.5 (1.6 s), SUSTAIN 0: the envelope falls slowly to nothing, so the wobble winds down over about a second and a half to the knob speed.
- RELEASE 5 (220 ms): a short fall after you let go.
- Listen for: each note starts with a fast flutter that slows down. Change DECAY to make the slow-down quicker or longer.

steps.title: Hold the volume
steps.why:
The loudness envelope holds the volume up so you can hear the whole slow-down.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): the note starts at once.
- DECAY 6 (420 ms) to SUSTAIN 9: held notes stay almost at full level for as long as you hold them, well past the 1.6 s wind-down.
- RELEASE 5 (220 ms): a brief tail after you let go.
- Listen for: hold a key for two seconds. The wobble starts fast and settles to a steady 1.5 Hz. Set SUSTAIN to 0 and the note fades before the slow-down finishes.

context.lfo.rate: The speed the wobble ends up at once the envelope has died away.
context.fenv.decay: How long the slow-down takes.
context.mod.lfoAmt: How deep the wobble is.
context.filter.env: Kept low. The envelope’s main job here is to control the LFO through the cable, not to open the filter.
context.filter.res: Makes the wobble sound more like "wow-wow" than a volume change.

tweaks.hear: A quick flutter at the start of the note that settles almost at once.
The reverse effect: the wobble speeds up as you hold the note.

tweaks.try: Switch triangle off and pulse on
tweaks.hear: The filter jumps between two positions, like a stuttering gate.

sounds.name: Repeat Pulse Line
sounds.ref: In the style of Italo disco and early electro pulse lines
sounds.blurb: Hold one key and get a stream of sixteenth-note blips.
sounds.how: REPEAT makes the LFO re-fire both envelopes again and again for as long as a key is held. With short envelopes and no sustain, each firing is a separate blip, so one finger produces a driving pulse line. The LFO frequency is the tempo. Change the held note and the pulses follow.

steps.title: Narrow pulse plus saw
steps.why:
A thin pulse gives the line its bite and a detuned saw at the same octave thickens it, so each blip later has both edge and body.
- Osc A pulse on, sawtooth off: pulse only.
- PULSE WIDTH 2.5 (27 %): well narrower than a square (5), so the pulse is thin and nasal. Towards 5 it gets rounder and hollower.
- OCTAVE osc A 1, Sync off: a low register, running freely.
- Osc B saw, OCTAVE 1, FREQ +0.1 st: a saw at the same octave, a hair sharp, so the pair beat gently.
- OSC A 7.5, OSC B 6: the mixer levels. The pulse leads; the saw fills in underneath.
- Listen for: a buzzy, slightly nasal tone with a slow swirl from the detune.

steps.title: Blip envelopes
steps.why:
Both envelopes are ADSRs (attack, decay, sustain, release). Here both get an instant attack, a short decay and no sustain, so each firing will be one short blip.
- CUTOFF 3.2 (182 Hz), RESONANCE 3.5: a dark low-pass filter with a slight peak, so the opening has some bite.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 5.5, KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5: each blip opens the filter well up; the cutoff follows the keys half way.
- Filter DECAY 3.8 (59 ms), SUSTAIN 0: after an instant attack, a bright flash lasting about 60 ms, then fully closed. RELEASE is a short 34 ms.
- Loudness DECAY 4.4 (100 ms), SUSTAIN 0: after an instant attack, each blip lasts about a tenth of a second, then silence even with the key held. RELEASE is 34 ms.
- Listen for: one short “bip” per key press, closing down as it fades because the filter decay is shorter than the volume decay.

steps.title: Switch REPEAT on
steps.why:
REPEAT makes the LFO (low-frequency oscillator, also the Pro-1’s clock) re-fire both envelopes for as long as a key is held. With the short envelopes from the last step, one held key becomes a stream of blips.
- Repeat on: the LFO acts as a gate generator.
- Drone off: the gate follows your key, so the stream stops when you let go.
- FREQUENCY lfo 7.8 (8.14 Hz): the tempo. About eight pulses a second is sixteenth notes at around 120 bpm. Turn it up for faster, down for slower.
- Listen for: hold one key and hear a driving pulse line. Change the held note and the pulses follow. If you lengthen loudness DECAY past the gap between pulses, they run together.

context.mode.repeat: The LFO re-fires the envelopes while a key is held.
context.lfo.rate: This is the tempo of the pulses.
context.aenv.decay: Length of each blip. Keep it shorter than the gap between pulses or they run together.
context.fenv.decay: How long the bright part of each blip lasts.
context.aenv.sustain: At zero, so the sound is silent between pulses.

tweaks.hear: The pulse rate changes from eighth notes up to a fast trill.
The pulses go from muted ticks to bright stabs: the classic build.

tweaks.try: Set to 5 and flip OSC A PW to DIR
tweaks.hear: The same LFO that fires the notes also moves the pulse width, so the tone changes within each blip.
The note now sounds all the time, with the pulses riding on top of it.

sounds.name: Radiophonic Drone
sounds.ref: In the style of BBC Radiophonic Workshop atmospheres
sounds.blurb: A self-playing siren that rises, falls and shifts in tone without a key held.
sounds.how: DRONE holds the gate open, so the synth sounds on its own. Oscillator B is dropped into LO FREQ and taken off the keyboard, which turns it into a very slow second LFO. Both B and the main LFO feed the DIRECT bus, and that one bus goes to Oscillator A’s pitch and to the filter, so pitch and tone drift together in a pattern that takes a long time to repeat. A cable from KYBD CV to LFO CV makes higher notes wobble faster.

steps.title: Hold the gate open
steps.why:
DRONE holds the gate open, so the synth sounds with no key held. The envelopes rise to their sustain levels and stay there, which makes the SUSTAIN knobs the level and brightness of the drone.
- Drone on, Repeat off: a steady, held gate. Keys now only choose the pitch.
- Loudness ATTACK 6 (260 ms): the drone fades in over about a quarter of a second rather than clicking on.
- Loudness SUSTAIN 8: how loud the drone is held.
- Filter SUSTAIN 5: where the filter envelope sits while the gate is held (the filter envelope amount is still 0 here).
- Listen for: the default saw starts sounding on its own. Switch Drone off to stop it.

steps.title: One low saw
steps.why:
One low saw is the sound. Oscillator B is about to become a modulator, so it is kept out of the mixer.
- Osc A sawtooth on, pulse off: bright and buzzy, full of harmonics for the resonant filter to pick out later.
- OCTAVE osc A 1: one below the default, a low drone register (octaves run 0 to 3).
- Sync off: A runs freely.
- OSC A 8, OSC B 0: only Oscillator A is heard.
- Listen for: the drone drops an octave and stays steady. It will not move until the next steps add modulation.

steps.title: Turn Oscillator B into a slow LFO
steps.why:
LO FREQ drops Oscillator B far below hearing, turning it into a second LFO (low-frequency oscillator) with three shapes. The Pro-1 lets you do this, at the cost of losing B as a sound.
- Osc B low frequency LO FREQ: B now moves slowly instead of making a tone.
- Osc B keyboard off: B ignores the keys, so the slow sweep does not change speed with the note.
- Triangle only: a smooth rise and fall.
- OCTAVE osc B 0, FREQUENCY −4: in LO FREQ these set speed. Low octave and FREQUENCY well to the left gives two to three seconds per cycle.
- Listen for: nothing yet. B is silent in the mixer and not routed anywhere.

steps.title: Feed both modulators into the DIRECT bus
steps.why:
The modulation section sends three sources over two buses: DIRECT (always on) and WHEEL (only as you push the mod wheel). Both slow sources go on the DIRECT bus, and pitch and filter both listen to it.
- AMOUNT OSC B 5, route DIRECT: the slow sweep, bending pitch and moving the filter by a good amount.
- AMOUNT LFO 4, LFO FREQUENCY 2 (0.26 Hz): the triangle LFO, also routed DIRECT, adds a smaller movement on top, about one cycle every four seconds.
- To OSC A FREQ DIR and To FILTER DIR: both destinations get the same mix of the two sources.
- Listen for: the drone starts rising and falling like a siren, in a pattern that takes a long time to repeat because the two speeds do not line up.

steps.title: Resonant filter
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass. With resonance up it picks out a moving band of the saw, and because the cutoff is on the DIRECT bus that band drifts on its own.
- CUTOFF 5 (632 Hz): the centre the modulation moves around, mid-dark.
- RESONANCE 6: a strong peak at the cutoff. The drifting peak sounds like a second, vocal voice over the drone. Lower it and the drift is heard only as brightness.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 0: the filter envelope does nothing here; the modulation bus moves the cutoff.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 3: higher notes open the filter a little.
- Listen for: a whistling, vowel-like band sweeping through the tone along with the pitch.

steps.title: Patch KYBD CV into LFO CV
steps.why:
A patch cable sends the keyboard pitch voltage into the LFO’s speed input. CV means control voltage: a voltage that sets another control.
- Cable KYBD CV → LFO CV: the keyboard voltage is added to the LFO FREQUENCY knob. Higher notes send a higher voltage, so the LFO runs faster; lower notes slow it down. Only the main LFO is affected: Oscillator B’s slow sweep has its keyboard switch off and keeps its own speed.
- Listen for: play keys an octave or two apart. On high notes the smaller movement quickens; on low ones it lazes.

context.mode.drone: Keeps the sound going with no key held. Switch it off to stop the drone.
context.oscB.lo: Drops Oscillator B below hearing so it works as an LFO.
context.oscB.freq: In LO FREQ this is Oscillator B’s speed. Further left is slower.
context.oscB.kbd: Off, so the slow sweep does not change speed with the note.
context.mod.oscBAmt: How far the slow sweep bends the pitch and moves the filter.
context.mod.lfoAmt: The smaller movement layered on the slow sweep.
context.mod.toFilter: Listens to the same DIRECT bus as OSC A FREQ, so tone and pitch move together.

tweaks.hear: The slow siren speeds up until it becomes a flutter.

tweaks.try: Switch triangle off and saw on
tweaks.hear: The pitch now ramps up and drops: an alarm rather than a siren.

tweaks.try: Switch SYNC on and bring OSC B back to NORMAL with KYBD on
tweaks.hear: A different lesson, but worth hearing: the bus now sweeps a synced oscillator and the drone turns vocal.
The filter starts to whistle on its own and the drone gains a second, sliding pitch.

sounds.name: Tight Square Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Depeche Mode — "Just Can’t Get Enough"
sounds.blurb: Bright, hollow lead with a short, clean note shape for fast hook lines.
sounds.how: Two pulse waves and no sawtooth. Oscillator A is a square wave, and Oscillator B is a narrower pulse one octave higher, which adds a bright edge on top of the hollow square. The filter is mostly open, and a small, quick envelope puts a slight click on the front of each note. Short decay and release times on the volume envelope keep fast notes apart.

steps.title: Two pulse waves, an octave apart
steps.why:
Two pulse waves and no saw: a square for the hollow body and a narrower pulse an octave up for edge. This is the core of a clean, bright pop lead.
- Osc A pulse, PULSE WIDTH 5 (50 %): a square wave with the saw off, hollow like a clarinet. Move it away from 5 and the lead gets thinner and more nasal.
- OCTAVE osc A 2, Sync off: normal lead register, running freely.
- Osc B pulse only, PULSE WIDTH 2.5 (27 %): a narrow pulse, so B adds edge rather than body.
- OCTAVE osc B 3, FREQUENCY +0.1 st: an octave higher, a hair sharp, so the pair drift slowly against each other.
- Osc B low frequency NORMAL, keyboard on: B plays at audio rate and follows the keys.
- Listen for: a hollow square. B is still at 0 in the mixer; the next step brings it in.

steps.title: Square in front, octave behind
steps.why:
The mixer sets how loud each oscillator is going into the filter. The square carries the note; the octave-up pulse sits behind it.
- OSC A 8: the square leads.
- OSC B 5: enough to brighten the top edge. Past about 7 it starts to sound like two notes an octave apart rather than one bright one.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: bring OSC B up slowly from 0 on a held note and stop when the top brightens but before you hear a second pitch.

steps.title: Filter mostly open
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass: it keeps lows and cuts highs. A lead like this wants its brightness, so the cutoff stays high.
- CUTOFF 6.6 (1.9 kHz): most of the pulse waves’ brightness gets through. Lower it for a rounder, flute-like lead.
- RESONANCE 1.5: only a slight peak, keeping the tone clean.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 7: more than half tracking, so the top notes of the hook stay as bright as the bottom ones.
- Listen for: very little change from before, just the harshest fizz taken off.

steps.title: A small click on the front
steps.why:
The filter envelope is an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release) that lifts the cutoff on each note. A small, quick one puts a slight click on the front of every note.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 3: the size of the click. More and the front becomes an obvious pluck.
- ATTACK 0, DECAY 4 (71 ms): instant, then gone in about 70 ms.
- SUSTAIN 2, RELEASE 3 (34 ms): held notes sit just above the resting cutoff; the tail is short.
- Listen for: the first instant of each note is slightly brighter, which makes the start sound harder. Set ENVELOPE AMOUNT to 0 and compare.

steps.title: Short, even volume shape
steps.why:
The loudness envelope shapes volume. Short times keep the notes of a fast hook apart.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): notes start at once.
- DECAY 4.8 (140 ms) to SUSTAIN 6: a small drop after the start, adding a little punch.
- RELEASE 3 (34 ms): notes stop almost as soon as the key comes up.
- Listen for: a small gap of silence between the notes of the riff. Raise RELEASE and they start to blur.

steps.title: Retrigger every note
steps.why:
The MODE section decides how key presses fire the envelopes. In NORMAL, a new key pressed while another is held does not restart them, so overlapping notes lose their click.
- Retrigger on (RETRIG): every key press restarts both envelopes, so a fast line played with overlapping fingers still gets a click on every note.
- Listen for: play the hook legato. With RETRIG on every note has its front edge; switch it off and the overlapped notes slide in soft.

context.oscA.pw: At 5 this is a square wave, the hollow centre of the sound. Move it away from 5 and the lead gets thinner and more nasal.
context.oscB.pw: A narrow pulse, so Oscillator B adds edge rather than body.
context.oscB.octave: One octave above Oscillator A. Set it to 2 and the lead loses its bright top.
context.mix.oscB: How much of the upper octave you hear. Past about 7 it starts to sound like two notes.
context.filter.cutoff: High, so most of the pulse waves’ brightness gets through. Lower it for a rounder, flute-like lead.
context.filter.env: The size of the click at the front of each note.
context.aenv.release: Short, so notes stop almost as soon as the key is released.
context.mode.retrig: Gives every note its own attack, even when keys overlap.

tweaks.hear: The hollow square thins out into a reedy, nasal tone.
At 0 the lead is plain and hollow. At 5 the upper octave adds a bright edge.

tweaks.try: Flip LFO ROUTE to WHEEL, set LFO AMOUNT to 2, LFO FREQUENCY to 7 and OSC A FREQ to WH, then push the mod wheel
tweaks.hear: Vibrato on Oscillator A that you bring in with the wheel. With the wheel down the sound is unchanged.
The click at the front stretches into a slower "wow".

sounds.name: Octave-Jump Sequencer Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of New Order — "Temptation"
sounds.blurb: Steady sixteenth-note bass that jumps up an octave on some steps.
sounds.how: Two saws at the same low octave, slightly detuned, through a half-closed filter with a short envelope. The important setting is KEYBOARD AMOUNT on the filter: it is turned up so that the notes an octave higher open the filter further and jump out of the pattern. On the hardware you would record a line like this into the sequencer; here the riff player under the keyboard plays it.

steps.title: Two saws at the same octave
steps.why:
Two saws at the same low octave, slightly detuned, make a bass wider than one oscillator can.
- Osc A saw, OCTAVE 1: a bright saw in the bass register (octaves run 0 to 3), in tune, with the pulse off.
- Sync off: the oscillators run freely.
- Osc B saw, OCTAVE 1, FREQ +0.2 st: the same octave, tuned slightly sharp so the two beat against each other. At 0 the bass is narrower and its tone changes note to note as the saws line up differently.
- Osc B low frequency NORMAL, keyboard on: B plays at audio rate and follows the keys.
- Listen for: B is still at 0 in the mixer, so this is one saw an octave down. The width comes next.

steps.title: Both up in the mixer
steps.why:
The mixer sets how loud each oscillator is going into the filter. Nearly equal levels give the strongest beating between the two saws.
- OSC A 8, OSC B 7: both saws almost level. Lower OSC B for a narrower, more focused bass.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: hold a low note and hear the slow swirl as the two saws drift in and out of phase.

steps.title: Half-closed filter that follows the keys
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass. The important setting here is keyboard tracking: it makes the octave-up steps of the line open the filter further and jump out.
- CUTOFF 3.8 (276 Hz): low enough to take the fizz off. This is the resting tone of each step; open it during a long run to build the line up.
- RESONANCE 2.5: a small peak, giving the low steps a little bite.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 8: a note one octave higher opens the filter most of an octave further. At 0 the high steps would sound duller than the low ones.
- Listen for: play a note and the one an octave above. The high one is clearly brighter.

steps.title: A short pluck on each step
steps.why:
The filter envelope is an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release) that lifts the cutoff at the start of each note. A short one turns a run of equal notes into a rhythm.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 4.5: how bright the front of each step gets.
- ATTACK 0, DECAY 4.3 (93 ms): instant, then closed in about 90 ms. Longer decay gives a slower, rounder pluck.
- SUSTAIN 1.5: held notes fall back close to the resting cutoff.
- RELEASE 3 (34 ms): short, so nothing lingers.
- Listen for: each step starts bright and closes quickly. Sweep DECAY while the riff plays to hear the groove tighten and loosen.

steps.title: Short notes, no overlap
steps.why:
The loudness envelope shapes volume. A very short release keeps each sixteenth note separate.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): each step hits at once.
- DECAY 5 (170 ms) to SUSTAIN 6: a small drop after the start, adding punch.
- RELEASE 2.8 (28 ms): each note stops before the next one starts.
- Listen for: clean gaps between the steps. Raise RELEASE to 5 and the sixteenth notes blur into a drone.

context.oscB.freq: A small detune against Oscillator A. At 0 the bass is narrower and its tone changes from note to note as the two saws line up differently.
context.filter.cutoff: The resting tone of each step. Open it during a long run to build the line up.
context.filter.kbd: High, so the octave-up steps are clearly brighter than the low ones. At 0 they would sound duller instead.
context.filter.env: How bright the front of each step gets.
context.fenv.decay: The length of the bright part of each step.
context.aenv.release: Keeps the steps separate. Longer settings blur the sixteenth notes together.

tweaks.hear: At 0 the octave-up notes sink into the pattern. At 8 they jump out.

tweaks.try: Open slowly from 3 to 6 while the riff loops
tweaks.hear: The line goes from muted to bright and buzzy, the usual way to build a sequence over time.
Every step now carries its own octave, so the line sounds lighter and busier.
Shorter gives a dry tick on each step; longer lets the steps run into each other.

sounds.name: Hard Gated Sync Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Front 242 — "Headhunter"
sounds.blurb: Hard, short sequencer bass with a rasping start and an abrupt stop.
sounds.how: Oscillator A is hard-synced to a low Oscillator B, and the filter envelope pushes A’s frequency up at the start of each note, so every note begins with a quick rasp of overtones. The hard edges come from a cable: GATE is patched into CUTOFF CV, so the filter is thrown open for exactly as long as the key is down and shuts the moment it is released. The note has a square filter shape instead of a fading one.

steps.title: Sync Oscillator A to a low Oscillator B
steps.why:
Hard sync forces Oscillator A to restart every time Oscillator B completes a cycle. On the Pro-1 A is the one reset, so B sets the pitch and A’s tuning becomes a tone control.
- Sync on: A is locked to B.
- Osc A saw, OCTAVE 2, FREQ +2.8 st: A sits an octave and a bit above B. Synced, that offset is heard as a hard, vocal tone, not a second pitch. Higher gives a thinner, more nasal bass.
- Osc B saw, OCTAVE 1, FREQUENCY 0: B sets the pitch in the bass register.
- Osc B low frequency NORMAL, keyboard on: B plays at audio rate and follows the keys.
- Listen for: turn osc A FREQUENCY on a held note; the tone shifts but the note does not.

steps.title: Add Oscillator B for weight
steps.why:
The mixer sets what reaches the filter. A synced oscillator can be thin in the low end, so B’s plain saw is brought in underneath.
- OSC A 8: the synced oscillator carries the rasp.
- OSC B 5.5: the plain low saw puts the fundamental back. Lower it and the bass gets thinner and harder.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: turn OSC B down and up to hear the weight come and go under the rasp.

steps.title: A quick sync sweep on every note
steps.why:
The modulation section routes the filter envelope to A’s pitch on the DIRECT bus (always on). With sync on, that sweeps A’s tone at the start of each note: the “zap”. There is no separate modulation envelope, so the filter envelope, an ADSR, does this job.
- FIL ENV 5.5 DIRECT, To OSC A FREQ DIR: pushes A up by about seven semitones at the start of each note.
- Filter ATTACK 0, DECAY 4 (71 ms): the push is instant and falls back in well under a tenth of a second. Longer DECAY gives a longer zap.
- SUSTAIN 0, RELEASE 3 (34 ms): after the zap, A sits back at its own tuning.
- Listen for: a short rasping “zap” at the front of each note. Switch Sync off to hear it as a plain pitch blip instead.

steps.title: Turn the cutoff right down
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass. Its cutoff goes right down on purpose: a cable in the next step supplies the opening.
- CUTOFF 1.6 (about 60 Hz): for now the bass is only a dull thump.
- RESONANCE 5.5: a hard, nasal peak once the filter opens. Lower it for a plainer, rounder bass.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 2.5: a small filter movement on each note, timed by the same short envelope as the zap.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5: the cutoff follows the keys half way.
- Listen for: the bass goes almost dark, with only a little brightness on the attack.

steps.title: Patch GATE into CUTOFF CV
steps.why:
A patch cable from GATE to CUTOFF CV (control voltage) throws the filter open for exactly as long as the key is down, and shuts it the moment you let go.
- Cable GATE → CUTOFF CV: the gate voltage lifts the cutoff by a fixed five octaves, from about 60 Hz to about 2 kHz at middle C. There is no depth control on the jack, so the CUTOFF knob sets where those five octaves start. The note now has a square filter shape, on or off, instead of a fading one.
- Listen for: how abruptly each note ends. Nudge CUTOFF up and the open position gets brighter.

steps.title: Short volume shape
steps.why:
The loudness envelope matches the filter slamming shut, so the note stops dead.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): notes start at once.
- DECAY 5 (170 ms) to SUSTAIN 7: a slight drop after the zap, then a steady level.
- RELEASE 2.2 (16 ms): very short. The volume and the filter close together.
- Listen for: hard, gated notes with clean silence between them. Raise RELEASE and you hear a dark tail after the filter has shut.

context.oscA.sync: Oscillator A restarts with every cycle of Oscillator B. Switch it off and the rasp turns into a plain falling pitch.
context.oscA.freq: With SYNC on this is a tone control. Higher settings give a thinner, more nasal bass.
context.mod.envAmt: How far the envelope pushes Oscillator A at the start of the note: the size of the "zap".
context.fenv.decay: How long the "zap" lasts. It also times the small filter envelope movement.
context.filter.cutoff: Very low, because the GATE cable adds five octaves whenever a key is down. This knob sets how bright the open position is.
context.filter.res: A hard, nasal peak at the cutoff. Lower it for a plainer, rounder bass.
context.mix.oscB: The plain low saw under the synced oscillator.
context.aenv.release: Very short, to match the filter slamming shut.

tweaks.try: Move between 0.8 and 3 while the riff loops
tweaks.hear: The open position of the gated filter moves from dull to bright. The five-octave jump stays the same size.

tweaks.try: Raise OSC B AMOUNT to 5 (its ROUTE is already DIRECT)
tweaks.hear: Oscillator B joins the filter envelope on the DIRECT bus and shakes Oscillator A’s frequency at audio rate. The tone gets rougher and more distorted.
The "zap" becomes a slower tearing sweep that lasts the whole note.
The vowel-like tone of the synced oscillator shifts while the pitch stays where it is.

sounds.name: Dark Eighth-Note Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of John Carpenter — "Escape from New York" main title
sounds.blurb: Low, steady eighth notes whose tone slowly opens and closes by itself.
sounds.how: A pulse wave and a saw an octave below it play even eighth notes through a dark filter. The notes themselves hardly change, so the interest comes from a very slow triangle LFO routed to the cutoff: over about four seconds the whole line gets brighter and then duller again. A small filter envelope gives each note just enough of a front edge to be heard as a pulse.

steps.title: Pulse on top, saw an octave below
steps.why:
A pulse on top and a saw an octave below give a low bass with both pitch definition and weight.
- Osc A pulse, PULSE WIDTH 4 (41 %): with the saw off, slightly narrower than a square (5), giving a slightly nasal, reedy colour.
- OCTAVE osc A 1, FREQUENCY 0, Sync off: bass register, in tune, running freely.
- Osc B sawtooth only, OCTAVE 0: an octave below A, for weight. FREQUENCY +0.1 st tunes it a touch sharp.
- Osc B low frequency NORMAL, keyboard on: B plays at audio rate and follows the keys.
- Listen for: B is still silent in the mixer. Sweep PULSE WIDTH on a held note to hear the reedy colour change.

steps.title: Mix
steps.why:
The mixer sets how loud each oscillator is going into the filter. Close to equal, with the pulse slightly ahead.
- OSC A 7: the pulse gives the note its pitch.
- OSC B 6: the low saw gives it weight. Turn it down for a lighter bass.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: the bass fills out an octave below.

steps.title: Dark filter, small envelope
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass. It is set dark, and its ADSR envelope (attack, decay, sustain, release) is kept small: it only puts a soft front on each note.
- CUTOFF 3.2 (182 Hz): dark. This is also the centre the slow LFO will sweep around.
- RESONANCE 3: a little peak, so the slow sweep is easier to hear later.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 2.5: a small lift on each note.
- ATTACK 0, DECAY 4.8 (140 ms), SUSTAIN 2: a soft front edge on each eighth note, not a pluck.
- RELEASE 3.2 (41 ms), KEYBOARD AMOUNT 4: short tail; slight key tracking.
- Listen for: low, round notes with just enough edge to hear each one as a pulse.

steps.title: Slow LFO
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) is a slow wave used to move other settings. It is set very slow here, to drift the tone over several bars.
- LFO triangle only: a smooth rise and fall.
- FREQUENCY lfo 1.8 (0.23 Hz): one cycle takes a little over four seconds. It is not tied to the tempo, so the sweep lands differently on every bar.
- Listen for: nothing changes yet, because the LFO is not routed anywhere.

steps.title: Route the LFO to the filter
steps.why:
The modulation section sends the LFO over the DIRECT bus (always on, no mod wheel needed) to the filter cutoff.
- AMOUNT LFO 5.5: the cutoff drifts about an octave and a half either side of the knob.
- LFO route DIRECT: always on.
- To FILTER DIR: the cutoff listens to the DIRECT bus.
- Listen for: let the riff loop a few times and hear the whole line brighten and darken on its own. Lower CUTOFF and the dark half of the cycle almost disappears.

steps.title: Even volume shape
steps.why:
The loudness envelope shapes volume. An even shape keeps the eighth notes clearly separate without clipping them.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): each note starts at once.
- DECAY 5.5 (270 ms) to SUSTAIN 6: a gentle drop to a steady level.
- RELEASE 3.2 (41 ms): short, so the notes stay apart.
- Listen for: steady, evenly spaced eighth notes, with the slow brightening and darkening riding on top.

context.oscA.pw: Slightly narrower than square, which gives the bass a slightly nasal, reedy colour.
context.oscB.octave: An octave below Oscillator A, for weight.
context.filter.cutoff: The centre of the slow sweep. Lower it and the dark half of the cycle almost disappears.
context.filter.res: A little resonance makes the slow sweep easier to hear.
context.lfo.rate: The speed of the slow brightening and darkening. It is not tied to the tempo, so the sweep falls differently on every bar.
context.mod.lfoAmt: How far the cutoff drifts either side of the knob.
context.mod.toFilter: Connects the DIRECT bus (carrying the LFO) to the cutoff.
context.filter.env: Small, so each note has a soft front edge and the LFO does most of the tone movement.

tweaks.hear: At 0 the line is static. At 5.5 it slowly opens and closes.
The sweep speeds up to a little under one cycle a second and starts to sound like a deliberate wobble.

tweaks.try: Flip LFO ROUTE to WHEEL and FILTER to WH, then move the mod wheel
tweaks.hear: The wheel now sets how deep the slow sweep is, so you can bring it in during a long passage.
The sweep becomes a clear moving peak, more like a slow "wah".

sounds.name: Pitch-Drop Blip
sounds.ref: In the style of Soft Cell — "Tainted Love"
sounds.blurb: A very short, high blip whose pitch falls as it sounds.
sounds.how: The filter envelope is sent to Oscillator A’s pitch through the modulation matrix. Each note starts almost an octave sharp and falls to the played pitch in about 40 milliseconds, which is too fast to hear as a slide; the ear hears a percussive "bip" instead. The filter is left open with its own envelope amount at 0, so the envelope is only bending pitch. The volume envelope is just as short.

steps.title: One high square wave
steps.why:
One high square wave is the whole sound. A square has a clear, hollow pitch, which suits a short blip.
- Osc A pulse, PULSE WIDTH 5 (50 %): with the saw off, a square wave. Away from 5 it would get thinner and more nasal.
- OCTAVE osc A 3, FREQUENCY 0: the highest octave setting (they run 0 to 3), in tune. This sets the register of the blip.
- Sync off: A runs freely.
- OSC A 8, OSC B 0, NOISE/EXT 0: only Oscillator A reaches the filter.
- Listen for: a plain, high, organ-like tone that holds as long as the key does.

steps.title: Send the filter envelope to pitch
steps.why:
The modulation section sends sources to destinations over two buses: DIRECT (always on) and WHEEL (only as you push the mod wheel). Here the filter envelope goes to A’s pitch. The Pro-1 has no separate pitch envelope, so the filter envelope does the job.
- AMOUNT FIL ENV 7: at the top of the envelope, Oscillator A is pushed up about 12 semitones. The scale is uneven: 5 is about 6 semitones, 10 is two octaves.
- FIL ENV route DIRECT: always on.
- To OSC A FREQ DIR: A’s pitch listens to the DIRECT bus.
- Listen for: hold a key. With the default envelope you hear a slow downward swoop that settles part way down while the key is held.

steps.title: Make the drop very fast
steps.why:
The filter envelope is an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release). Its settings now shape the pitch drop, and making it very fast turns a swoop into a percussive blip.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): the pitch starts at the top immediately.
- DECAY 3.4 (42 ms): the drop takes about 40 ms, too quick to hear as a slide. Longer gives an audible “pyoo”.
- SUSTAIN 0: the pitch always comes to rest on the played note.
- RELEASE 3 (34 ms): short, so letting go does not bend anything.
- Listen for: each note now starts with a “bip” rather than a swoop. Sweep DECAY from 3 to 6 to hear it turn from click to “pyoo”.

steps.title: Keep the filter out of it
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass. It is kept out of the way, because the filter envelope is busy bending pitch and should not change the tone as well.
- CUTOFF 8 (5.0 kHz): wide open, so the square’s brightness comes through.
- RESONANCE 0: no peak.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 0: the envelope does not reach the filter at all.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5: the cutoff follows the keys half way, which makes little difference this high.
- Listen for: the blip stays the same bright tone throughout; only its pitch moves.

steps.title: Blip-length volume
steps.why:
The loudness envelope sets the length of the blip. With no sustain, however long you hold the key you only get a short blip.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): instant start, lined up with the pitch drop.
- DECAY 4 (71 ms): the blip lasts about 70 ms. Longer makes a ringing “pew”.
- SUSTAIN 0: the sound always dies away.
- RELEASE 3.2 (41 ms): a short tail if you let go early.
- Listen for: a short, high “bip” on every key. Play a quick pattern and it sounds like a percussion part.

context.mod.envAmt: How far above the played note each blip starts. The scale is not even: 5 is about 6 semitones, 7 about 12, 10 is two octaves.
context.mod.toAFreq: Connects the DIRECT bus (carrying the filter envelope) to Oscillator A’s pitch.
context.fenv.decay: The speed of the pitch drop. Short is a click-like "bip"; longer is an audible "pyoo".
context.fenv.sustain: At 0, so the pitch always comes to rest on the played note.
context.filter.env: At 0. The filter envelope is being used as a pitch envelope here.
context.aenv.decay: The length of the blip.

tweaks.hear: From a dry click, through a "bip", to a falling "pyoo" like an arcade laser.
A small drop sounds like a plucked note; a large one sounds like a drum-machine tom or zap.
The blip gets a short ringing tail at the played pitch.

tweaks.try: Raise to 7 and lower CUTOFF to 6
tweaks.hear: The filter rings briefly as the falling pitch passes through it, which adds a "chirp".

sounds.name: Resonant Slide Line
sounds.ref: In the style of Josh Wink — "Higher State of Consciousness"
sounds.blurb: Squelchy one-oscillator line where some notes slide into the next and others do not.
sounds.how: Lines like this are normally made on a Roland TB-303; this is the Pro-1’s version. One saw goes through a filter with high resonance and a short envelope, so every new note gets a squelch. Glide is set to AUTO, which only slides when a new key is pressed while the last one is still down. In the riff some notes overlap and some do not: the overlapping ones slide and share one envelope, and the separate ones jump and get a fresh squelch.

steps.title: One saw
steps.why:
One saw leaves room for the filter to be the main feature. Lines like this are usually made on a Roland TB-303; this is the Pro-1’s version.
- Osc A sawtooth on, pulse off: every harmonic, so the resonant filter has plenty to pick out.
- OCTAVE osc A 1, FREQUENCY 0: a bass octave (octaves run 0 to 3), in tune.
- Sync off: A runs freely.
- OSC A 8, OSC B 0, NOISE/EXT 0: only Oscillator A reaches the filter.
- Listen for: a plain, bright, low saw.

steps.title: Low cutoff, high resonance
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass. Low cutoff and very high resonance mean any movement of the cutoff is heard as a sharp, vocal peak sweeping through the saw.
- CUTOFF 3 (159 Hz): where each squelch will end up. Sweeping this slowly by hand over a long time is the main performance move in this style.
- RESONANCE 8.3: just short of the point, around 9.2, where the filter starts to whistle by itself. Lower it and the squelch gets milder.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 4: the cutoff follows the keys a little, so high notes do not go dull.
- Listen for: turn CUTOFF slowly by hand on a held note and hear the peak sing through the harmonics.

steps.title: Short envelope for the squelch
steps.why:
The filter envelope is an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release) that lifts the cutoff on each note and drops it again. With the resonance high, that sweep is heard as a squelch.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 5: lifts the cutoff by about four octaves. This is the height of the squelch.
- ATTACK 0, DECAY 4.8 (140 ms): up instantly, then down in roughly 150 ms. DECAY is the length of the squelch.
- SUSTAIN 1, RELEASE 3 (34 ms): held notes fall back almost to the resting cutoff.
- Listen for: a “wow” on each separately played note. Sweep DECAY while the riff plays to stretch it.

steps.title: Plain volume shape
steps.why:
The loudness envelope gives a plain shape, and the trigger mode is left so slid notes will not restart the envelopes.
- ATTACK 0, DECAY 5 (170 ms), SUSTAIN 8: instant start, nearly full held level.
- RELEASE 2.6 (23 ms): very short, so separate notes stay separate.
- Retrigger off (NORMAL): a note played while another is still held changes pitch but does not restart either envelope. That is what lets slid notes skip the squelch.
- Listen for: play two notes overlapping. The second changes pitch without a new “wow”. Switch RETRIG on and every note squelches.

steps.title: AUTO glide
steps.why:
Glide makes the pitch slide between notes. AUTO is the Pro-1’s name for legato (fingered) glide: it only slides when a new key is pressed while the last one is still down.
- RATE 2.6 (200 ms): how long a slide takes. Higher makes slower, more obvious swoops.
- Glide mode AUTO: only overlapping notes slide. In NORMAL every note would slide.
- Listen for: in the riff, where two notes overlap the pitch slides and there is no new squelch; where they do not, the pitch jumps and the filter fires again. That mix of slides and fresh hits is the groove of the style.

context.filter.res: High, so the envelope sweep is heard as a squelch. Above about 9.2 the filter starts to whistle by itself.
context.filter.cutoff: Where each squelch ends up. Sweeping this slowly by hand over a long time is the main performance move in this style.
context.filter.env: The height of the squelch.
context.fenv.decay: The length of the squelch.
context.glide.mode: AUTO: only overlapping (legato) notes slide. In NORMAL every note would slide.
context.mode.retrig: At NORMAL, so slid notes share the envelope of the note before. Switch to RETRIG and slid notes squelch too.

tweaks.try: Sweep slowly between 2 and 6 while the riff loops
tweaks.hear: The line goes from a muffled bubble to a bright scream and back.
Every note now slides, and the contrast between slid and jumped notes is lost.
Short is a tight "blip"; long lets the squelch cover the whole note.

tweaks.try: Switch saw off and pulse on
tweaks.hear: The square wave gives a hollower, more rubbery version of the same line.

sounds.name: Detuned Reese Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Renegade — "Terrorist"
sounds.blurb: Dark, sustained bass that slowly churns as two detuned saws beat against each other.
sounds.how: Two saws at the same octave are detuned by about a third of a semitone. Their harmonics drift in and out of step, so some cancel and then return, and this is heard as a slow phasing movement. A low filter removes the bright buzz and leaves the movement in the low-mids. A very slow LFO on the cutoff adds a second, slower movement on top.

steps.title: Two saws, deliberately out of tune
steps.why:
Two saws at the same octave, deliberately out of tune, are the whole trick. Their harmonics drift in and out of step, so some cancel and return, which is heard as a slow churning.
- Sawtooth on for both, other waves off: two bright saws.
- OCTAVE 1 on both, FREQUENCY osc A 0: a bass octave (octaves run 0 to 3).
- FREQUENCY osc B 0.2 (+0.3 st): about 30 cents sharp. This one knob sets the speed of the churning: closer to 0 is slower, further away is faster and more out of tune.
- Sync off, Osc B NORMAL, keyboard on: both run freely at audio rate and follow the keys.
- Listen for: B is still at 0 in the mixer, so the churn comes in at the next step.

steps.title: Equal levels
steps.why:
The mixer sets how loud each oscillator is going into the filter. The cancelling between the saws is deepest when both are equally loud.
- OSC A 8, OSC B 8: equal levels. Pull OSC B down and the movement gets shallower.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: hold a low note and hear the tone churn about once a second, hollowing out and filling back in.

steps.title: Low, plain filter
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass. A low, plain setting removes the bright buzz and leaves the movement in the low-mids.
- CUTOFF 3.8 (276 Hz): keeps only the dark part of the sound. Open it and the bass becomes a buzzing, hoover-like tone.
- RESONANCE 1.5: hardly any peak.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 0: no filter envelope, so the tone does not pluck.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 3: higher notes open the filter a little.
- Listen for: a dark, rolling bass where the churning is now the main feature.

steps.title: Sustained volume shape
steps.why:
The loudness envelope is an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release). A sustained shape lets long notes hold steady and join up.
- ATTACK 2.5 (15 ms): slightly softened, taking the click off the front.
- DECAY 5 (170 ms), SUSTAIN 10: full level for as long as the key is held.
- RELEASE 4.5 (140 ms): a medium tail, so notes join rather than stop dead.
- Listen for: long notes staying at one level with the churning carrying on underneath.

steps.title: A very slow drift on the cutoff
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) is a slow wave. Sent through the modulation section on the DIRECT bus (always on) to the filter, it adds a second, slower movement on top of the beating.
- LFO triangle, FREQUENCY 2.4 (0.33 Hz): a smooth cycle about every three seconds.
- AMOUNT LFO 3, route DIRECT: a small amount, moving the cutoff less than half an octave.
- To FILTER DIR: the cutoff listens to the DIRECT bus.
- Listen for: a slow brightening and darkening on held notes, so the bass never sits still. Set AMOUNT LFO to 0 to compare.

steps.title: A little glide
steps.why:
Glide makes the pitch slide between notes. A short slide makes the pitch changes lean into each other.
- RATE 2 (120 ms): a quick slide, just over a tenth of a second.
- Glide mode NORMAL: slides between every pair of notes, overlapping or not.
- Listen for: a small swoop into each new note of the line. Turn RATE up for an obvious slide, or to 0 to hear the notes jump.

context.oscB.freq: The detune. This one knob sets the speed of the churning: closer to 0 is slower, further away is faster and more out of tune.
context.mix.oscB: Equal to Oscillator A so the cancelling is as deep as possible.
context.filter.cutoff: Low, to keep only the dark part of the sound. Open it and the bass becomes a buzzing, hoover-like tone.
context.mod.lfoAmt: A small, slow cutoff drift on top of the beating.
context.lfo.rate: The speed of that drift.
context.aenv.sustain: Full, so held notes stay at one level.

tweaks.hear: The churn goes from a slow sweep to a fast, seasick wobble.
The bright buzz of the saws comes back and the bass gets much more aggressive.

tweaks.try: Turn down to 0, then back to 8
tweaks.hear: With one saw the movement stops completely. It only exists between the two oscillators.
A sub-octave version: heavier, with the same beat.

sounds.name: FM Metal Clank
sounds.ref: In the style of Depeche Mode — "Construction Time Again" metal percussion
sounds.blurb: Short, clanging hit with the out-of-tune overtones of struck metal.
sounds.how: Oscillator B is taken off the keyboard, set to a fixed pitch that has nothing to do with the keys, and kept out of the mixer. Through the modulation matrix it shakes Oscillator A’s pitch hundreds of times a second. That is too fast to hear as vibrato; it adds a dense set of extra overtones that do not line up with the note, which is the character of struck metal. Short envelopes turn it into a hit. Because Oscillator B stays at one pitch, every key gives a different clank.

steps.title: Listen to Oscillator A only
steps.why:
The mixer sets what reaches the filter. Oscillator B is going to be a modulator, not a sound source, so it stays out of the mixer.
- OSC A 8: the only oscillator you hear.
- OSC B 0: B will only be heard through what it does to A.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: a plain saw for now, the default Oscillator A.

steps.title: Square wave carrier, fixed modulator
steps.why:
Oscillator A is the carrier, the tone you hear. Oscillator B is set up as the modulator: fixed at one pitch so it has no simple relation to the notes you play.
- Osc A pulse, PW 5 (50 %), OCTAVE 3: a high square wave in tune (octaves run 0 to 3), saw off.
- Sync off: A runs freely.
- Osc B triangle only: the smoothest modulator shape, giving the most bell-like result.
- OCTAVE osc B 1, FREQUENCY 4.1 (+5.7 st): the modulator’s pitch. Low settings pack the extra overtones close for a dense clang; higher ones spread them for a thinner, glassier hit.
- Osc B keyboard off, NORMAL: B stays at one audio-rate pitch whatever you play.
- Listen for: a high square. B is silent, so nothing else changes yet.

steps.title: Route Oscillator B to Oscillator A’s pitch
steps.why:
This is FM (frequency modulation): B shakes A’s pitch hundreds of times a second through the modulation section’s DIRECT bus (always on). That is too fast to hear as vibrato; it adds dense overtones that do not line up with the note, the character of struck metal.
- AMOUNT OSC B 9: A is swung about 19 semitones either side of its pitch. Low amounts give a bell; high amounts give noisy clang.
- OSC B route DIRECT: always on.
- To OSC A FREQ DIR: A’s pitch listens to the DIRECT bus.
- Listen for: the clean square turns into a harsh clang. Play different keys: because B stays put, each key gives a different clank. Nudge osc B FREQUENCY as a tone control.

steps.title: Bright start, quick fade in tone
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass with an ADSR envelope (attack, decay, sustain, release). A short envelope from a fairly high cutoff makes the hit start with all its overtones and dull quickly, as a struck object does.
- CUTOFF 6.2 (1.4 kHz), RESONANCE 2: a mid-bright resting tone with a slight peak.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 4: opens the filter well above that on each hit.
- ATTACK 0, DECAY 4.4 (100 ms), SUSTAIN 0: bright for about a tenth of a second, then closed back down.
- RELEASE 4.2 (110 ms), KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5: a short fall after you let go; half key tracking.
- Listen for: a bright “clang” at the front of each note that quickly turns duller.

steps.title: Hit-shaped volume
steps.why:
The loudness envelope turns the clang into a hit. With no sustain, the sound always dies away however long you hold the key.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): instant, like a strike.
- DECAY 4.8 (140 ms), SUSTAIN 0: the length of the hit. Longer DECAY makes a ringing bell.
- RELEASE 4.6 (150 ms): a little longer than the decay, so a short tap on the key still rings for a moment.
- Listen for: short metallic hits. Play a pattern across several keys and each one clanks differently.

context.mix.oscB: At 0. Oscillator B is only heard through what it does to Oscillator A.
context.oscB.kbd: Off, so the modulator stays at one pitch. The relation between the two oscillators changes with every key, and so does the clank.
context.oscB.freq: Tunes the modulator. Small moves change which overtones appear, so treat it as a tone control.
context.oscB.octave: The rough pitch of the modulator. Low settings pack the extra overtones close together for a dense clang; higher settings spread them out and the hit sounds thinner and glassier.
context.oscB.tri: The triangle is the smoothest modulator shape and gives the most bell-like result.
context.mod.oscBAmt: How far Oscillator A is swung. Low amounts give a bell; high amounts give noise-like clang.
context.mod.toAFreq: Connects the DIRECT bus (carrying Oscillator B) to Oscillator A’s pitch.
context.aenv.decay: The length of the hit.

tweaks.hear: From a slightly sour bell, through struck pipe, to a burst of pitched noise.

tweaks.try: Sweep from −5 to 5 while tapping one key
tweaks.hear: The overtones rearrange themselves at every position. Some positions sound almost in tune, most do not.
The modulator now follows the keys, so every note has the same tone and the sound becomes a playable bell.
The clank becomes a long ringing gong.

sounds.name: Electronic Tom
sounds.ref: In the style of Simmons SDS-V toms — 80s pop drum fills
sounds.blurb: Falling "doooh" tom with a short burst of noise at the front.
sounds.how: Oscillator B is used as the drum because it has a triangle wave, which is close to the plain tone of a drum shell; Oscillator A only has saw and pulse. The filter envelope is routed to Oscillator B’s pitch, so each hit starts about eight semitones high and falls. A little noise goes through the filter, and the same envelope closes the filter fast, so the noise is only heard as a "tch" at the start of the hit.

steps.title: Oscillator B’s triangle as the drum
steps.why:
Oscillator B is used as the drum because it has a triangle wave, which is close to the plain tone of a drum shell. Oscillator A has only saw and pulse, so it is muted.
- OSC A 0, OSC B 9: the mixer levels. Only B reaches the filter.
- Osc B triangle only: saw and pulse off, leaving a soft, plain tone with very few overtones.
- OCTAVE osc B 1, FREQUENCY 0: a low, tom-like register (octaves run 0 to 3), in tune.
- Osc B NORMAL, keyboard on: B plays at audio rate and follows the keys, so different keys give different tom pitches.
- Listen for: a soft, round tone like a flute played low.

steps.title: Envelope to Oscillator B’s pitch
steps.why:
The modulation section sends sources to destinations over two buses: DIRECT (always on) and WHEEL (mod wheel only). Here the filter envelope goes to B’s pitch, so each hit starts high and falls.
- AMOUNT FIL ENV 6: the envelope pushes B up about eight semitones at the start of each hit. About 6 sounds like a tom; higher is a disco “pew”.
- FIL ENV route DIRECT: always on.
- To OSC B FREQ DIR: B’s pitch listens to the DIRECT bus.
- Listen for: each note starts high and swoops down, settling above the played pitch while you hold it.

steps.title: Set the speed of the fall
steps.why:
The filter envelope is an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release). It now sets the speed of the pitch fall, and later how fast the filter shuts on the noise.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): the pitch starts at the top immediately.
- DECAY 5 (170 ms): the fall takes about a sixth of a second.
- SUSTAIN 0: the pitch always ends on the played note.
- RELEASE 4.6 (150 ms): nearly as long as the decay, so the pitch keeps falling after a short tap on the key.
- Listen for: “doooh” rather than “dip”. Shorten DECAY and it turns into a clicky blip.

steps.title: Add a little noise
steps.why:
White noise is added to the mixer. It stands in for the stick hitting the drum head.
- NOISE/EXT 4: a moderate level of hiss. Too much and the tom turns into a snare.
- Listen for: for now the hiss runs all through the note. The next step shuts it off after the start.

steps.title: Let the filter hide the noise after the start
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass. A low cutoff with a large envelope amount means it opens wide at the start of each hit and closes a moment later, so the noise is only a “tch” at the front.
- CUTOFF 4 (317 Hz): low enough to hide the noise once the envelope has fallen, while letting the triangle through.
- RESONANCE 1: no real peak.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 6: the filter opens wide on each hit, letting the noise through for a moment.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 3: higher toms open the filter a little more.
- Listen for: a short “tch” at the front, then just the falling tone.

steps.title: Drum-shaped volume
steps.why:
The loudness envelope gives the drum its shape: an instant hit that dies away, with no sustain.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): instant, like a stick strike.
- DECAY 5.4 (250 ms), SUSTAIN 0: the drum fades over about a quarter of a second, however long you hold the key. Longer DECAY gives a bigger, boomier tom.
- RELEASE 5 (220 ms): long enough for the drum to ring after a short tap.
- Listen for: play a fill down three or four keys and hear a run of falling toms.

context.oscB.tri: The triangle is the nearest shape on this synth to the plain tone of a drum shell.
context.mix.oscA: At 0. Oscillator A has no triangle, so it is not used.
context.mod.envAmt: The size of the pitch drop. About 6 sounds like a tom; higher sounds like a disco "pew".
context.mod.toBFreq: Connects the DIRECT bus (carrying the filter envelope) to Oscillator B’s pitch.
context.fenv.decay: One envelope does two jobs here: the speed of the pitch fall and how fast the filter shuts on the noise.
