context.mix.noise: The "tch" of the stick. Too much and the tom turns into a snare.
context.filter.env: Opens the filter at the start of the hit so the noise gets through for a moment.
context.aenv.decay: The length of the drum.

tweaks.hear: A small drop is a tuned, natural-sounding tom. A large drop is the exaggerated "pew" of disco drum pads.

tweaks.try: Raise to 8 and set CUTOFF to 6
tweaks.hear: The noise takes over and the hit becomes a synthetic snare.
The fall is too quick to follow and the tom becomes a tight, knocking sound.
An octave lower: a floor tom, or a kick drum if you also shorten the amplifier DECAY.

sounds.name: Filtered Noise Riser
sounds.ref: In the style of 90s trance build-ups
sounds.blurb: A rush of noise that climbs from a low rumble to a bright hiss over about three seconds.
sounds.how: No oscillators at all: only the noise generator goes into the filter. Noise has no pitch of its own, but a resonant filter gives it one, because the resonance boosts a narrow band at the cutoff. A filter envelope with a three-second attack then drags that band upwards by nearly seven octaves. Hold one key for the length of the build.

steps.title: Noise only
steps.why:
No oscillators at all: only the noise generator goes into the filter. Noise has no pitch of its own, which makes it the raw material for a riser.
- OSC A 0, OSC B 0: both oscillators out of the mixer.
- NOISE/EXT 9: white noise near full level. It is the only sound source in this patch.
- Listen for: plain hiss, sounding much the same on every key.

steps.title: Low, resonant filter
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass. A resonant filter gives noise a pitch of sorts, because the resonance boosts a narrow band at the cutoff.
- CUTOFF 2.4 (105 Hz): the rise starts down here, as a low rumble.
- RESONANCE 7: a strong peak, giving the rumble a windy, half-pitched tone. At 0 the riser would be a plain “shhh” getting brighter.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 0: the cutoff ignores the keys, so every key gives the same riser.
- Listen for: the hiss turns into a low rumble with a whistling band in it. Turn CUTOFF by hand to hear the band move.

steps.title: A three-second rise
steps.why:
The filter envelope is an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release). A very long attack drags the resonant band upwards while you hold the key.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 8.5: how far the rise goes, nearly seven octaves from the rumble to the top of the hearing range.
- ATTACK 9 (2.9 s): the length of the rise. Match it to the build: 10 is about six and a half seconds.
- SUSTAIN 10: the filter stays open at the top once it arrives, instead of falling back. DECAY 5 (170 ms) therefore does nothing here.
- RELEASE 3 (34 ms): the filter shuts quickly when you let go.
- Listen for: hold one key for three seconds and hear the whistle climb to a bright hiss.

steps.title: Fade in, stop sharply
steps.why:
The loudness envelope fades the noise in and gives a sharp stop at the end of the build.
- ATTACK 6.5 (380 ms): a slowish fade-in hides the start of the noise.
- DECAY 5 (170 ms), SUSTAIN 10: full level for as long as the key is held.
- RELEASE 2.5 (21 ms): a clean cut when you let go, which is where the track would come back in.
- Listen for: a smooth swell into the rise, then silence the instant you lift your finger.

context.mix.noise: The only sound source in this patch.
context.filter.cutoff: Where the rise starts from.
context.filter.res: Gives the noise a whistling, pitched band. At 0 the riser is a plain "shhh" getting brighter.
context.filter.env: How far the rise goes: 8.5 is nearly seven octaves.
context.fenv.attack: The length of the rise. Match it to the length of the build: 9 is about three seconds, 10 about six and a half.
context.fenv.sustain: At 10, so the filter stays open at the top instead of falling back.
context.filter.kbd: At 0, so the riser is the same whichever key you hold.
context.aenv.release: Short, for a sharp stop at the end of the build.

tweaks.hear: The band narrows into a rising whistle riding on the noise.
A one-second sweep for a short fill, or a six-second one for a long build.

tweaks.try: Set to 6, switch LFO triangle off and pulse on, FREQUENCY to 7.8, and flip FILTER to DIR
tweaks.hear: The square LFO jumps the cutoff up and down eight times a second, so the riser is chopped into a rhythm.
A pitched saw joins the noise and is opened by the same sweep.

sounds.name: Two-Tone Siren
sounds.ref: In the style of Altern-8 — early-90s hardcore rave sirens
sounds.blurb: A siren that flips between two pitches a few times a second.
sounds.how: The LFO is set to its pulse shape, which has only two values: high and low. Routed to the pitch of both oscillators, it makes them jump between two notes instead of wobbling smoothly. The LFO amount sets how far apart the two notes are and the LFO frequency sets how fast they alternate. Hold one key and the synth does the rest.

steps.title: A bright, high tone
steps.why:
A bright, high tone with some body underneath gives the siren something that cuts through a mix.
- Osc A saw + pulse, PULSE WIDTH 5 (50 %): both waves added together, buzzy with a hollow square under it.
- OCTAVE osc A 3, FREQUENCY 0: the highest octave setting (they run 0 to 3), in tune.
- Osc B saw, OCTAVE 2, FREQUENCY 0: a saw one octave lower, for body.
- Sync off, Osc B NORMAL, keyboard on: both run freely at audio rate and follow the keys.
- OSC A 8, OSC B 6, NOISE/EXT 0: the mixer levels. A leads, B supports.
- Listen for: a bright, steady, piercing tone.

steps.title: Pulse-shaped LFO
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) is a slow wave used to move other settings. Its pulse shape has only two values, high and low, which is what will make the pitch jump rather than sweep.
- LFO triangle off, sawtooth off, pulse on: the two-value shape. With the triangle on as well, the pitch would slide between the jumps.
- FREQUENCY lfo 6.2 (3.15 Hz): about three flips a second. This is how fast the two tones alternate.
- Listen for: nothing changes yet, because the LFO is not routed anywhere.

steps.title: Route it to both oscillators’ pitch
steps.why:
The modulation section sends sources over the DIRECT bus (always on) or the WHEEL bus (mod wheel only). Here the LFO goes DIRECT to the pitch of both oscillators, so they jump together.
- AMOUNT LFO 3.2: each oscillator is pushed about two and a half semitones up, then the same distance down, so the two tones are roughly a fourth apart. 5 would make them an octave apart.
- LFO route DIRECT: always on.
- To OSC A FREQ DIR and To OSC B FREQ DIR: both pitches listen to the DIRECT bus, keeping the octave between them.
- Listen for: hold one key and the synth flips between two notes, with the played key between them.

steps.title: Open filter with a little edge
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass. A siren should cut through, so it stays open.
- CUTOFF 7.2 (2.9 kHz): open, letting the brightness through. Lower it and the siren gets muffled and distant.
- RESONANCE 3: a small peak, adding a nasal, horn-like colour.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 0: no filter movement per note.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5: the cutoff follows the keys half way.
- Listen for: slightly more honk in the tone.

steps.title: On while held
steps.why:
The loudness envelope is an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release). Full sustain keeps the siren running for as long as the key is down.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): on at once.
- DECAY 5 (170 ms), SUSTAIN 10: no drop in level while held.
- RELEASE 4 (87 ms): a short fade when you let go.
- Listen for: a steady, even two-tone siren. Try LFO FREQUENCY faster for a panicky alarm, or AMOUNT LFO higher for wider jumps.

context.lfo.pulse: The two-value LFO shape. It is the reason the pitch jumps rather than sweeps.
context.lfo.tri: Off. With the triangle on as well, the pitch would slide between the jumps.
context.lfo.rate: How fast the two tones alternate.
context.mod.lfoAmt: The distance between the two tones. 3.2 is about a fourth; 5 is an octave.
context.mod.toAFreq: Connects the DIRECT bus (carrying the LFO) to Oscillator A’s pitch.
context.mod.toBFreq: The same bus to Oscillator B, so both oscillators jump together.
context.filter.cutoff: Open, so the siren is bright.

tweaks.hear: The gap between the two tones grows from about a tone to an octave.
From a slow emergency-vehicle siren to a fast trill, and finally a rough buzz.

tweaks.try: Switch pulse off and triangle on
tweaks.hear: The pitch now sweeps smoothly up and down: an air-raid siren instead of a two-tone one.

tweaks.try: Set OSC B FREQ to OFF
tweaks.hear: Oscillator B holds the played note while Oscillator A jumps around it, so you hear a drone with a siren on top.

sounds.name: LFO-Clocked Filter Pulses
sounds.ref: In the style of The Who — "Baba O’Riley"
sounds.blurb: Hold one note and the filter pulses in sixteenths on top of it, like a sequencer running under a drone.
sounds.how: A cable from LFO OUT to GATE/CLK lets the pulse-wave LFO fire the filter envelope again and again at its own rate. In this app that jack only reaches the filter envelope, so the volume envelope is not affected: it opens when you press the key and stays open. The result is a steady held note with a row of bright filter pulses on top. Compare it with REPEAT mode, which re-fires both envelopes and leaves silence between the pulses.

steps.title: Saw below, pulse above
steps.why:
A saw below and a narrow pulse above give the filter a lot of overtones to open up, so each filter pulse later will be bright and obvious.
- Osc A saw, OCTAVE 1, FREQUENCY 0: a low saw (octaves run 0 to 3).
- Sync off: A runs freely.
- Osc B pulse only, PULSE WIDTH 3 (31 %): narrower than a square, thin and nasal.
- OCTAVE osc B 2, FREQUENCY +0.1 st: an octave above A, a hair sharp.
- Osc B NORMAL, keyboard on: B plays at audio rate and follows the keys.
- OSC A 8, OSC B 6, NOISE/EXT 0: the mixer levels.
- Listen for: a full, buzzy tone with a reedy top.

steps.title: A dull held note
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass. It is set low with some resonance, and a large envelope amount is dialled in for the pulses to come.
- CUTOFF 3.4 (209 Hz): the tone of the held note underneath the pulses.
- RESONANCE 4: a clear peak, so each pulse will have a vocal edge.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 6: the brightness of each pulse. For now it opens the filter once at the start of each note.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5: the cutoff follows the keys half way.
- Listen for: a bright opening at the start of each note. Once the next step sets the envelope’s sustain to 0, the held note settles to a dull hum.

steps.title: Short filter envelope
steps.why:
The filter envelope is an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release). A short one gives a single bright pulse each time it fires. So far it fires once per key press.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): the pulse starts instantly.
- DECAY 4 (71 ms): each pulse lasts about 70 ms. A pulse can never be longer than half an LFO cycle once the cable is in.
- SUSTAIN 0: between pulses the filter falls back to the dull held tone.
- RELEASE 2.5 (21 ms): very short.
- Listen for: one short bright “blip” at the start, then a dark, steady hum.

steps.title: Keep the volume open
steps.why:
The loudness envelope keeps the volume open, so anything rhythmic you hear next comes from the filter alone.
- ATTACK 3 (23 ms): slightly soft, taking the click off the front.
- DECAY 5 (170 ms), SUSTAIN 8: the note holds steady while the key is down.
- RELEASE 4 (87 ms): a short fade after you let go.
- Listen for: a steady held note. REPEAT stays off: it would chop the volume as well, which is a different sound.

steps.title: Pulse LFO at the tempo
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) is set to its pulse shape at the tempo. The pulse is high for half of each cycle and low for the other half: a clean on/off gate.
- LFO triangle off, sawtooth off, pulse on: the gate shape.
- FREQUENCY lfo 7.8 (8.00 Hz): about sixteenth notes at 120 bpm. 6.6 is about eighth notes. The LFO runs freely, so the pulses are not locked to the riff player; set the rate by ear.
- Listen for: nothing yet. The LFO is not connected to anything.

steps.title: Patch LFO OUT into GATE/CLK
steps.why:
A cable from LFO OUT to GATE/CLK lets the pulse LFO fire the filter envelope again and again. In this app that jack only reaches the filter envelope, so the volume stays open.
- Cable LFO OUT → GATE/CLK: every time the LFO goes high it fires the filter envelope; every time it goes low it releases it. There is no depth to set, because a gate is either on or off. The size of each pulse is ENVELOPE AMOUNT; the speed is LFO FREQUENCY.
- Listen for: hold a key and the note stays on while the filter pulses on top of it, like a sequencer under a drone. Compare with REPEAT mode, which re-fires both envelopes and leaves silence between pulses.

context.lfo.rate: The speed of the pulses. 6.6 is about eighth notes at 120 bpm, 7.8 about sixteenths.
context.lfo.pulse: The pulse shape gives a clean on/off gate. It is high for half of each cycle.
context.filter.env: The brightness of each pulse.
context.fenv.decay: The length of each pulse. The envelope is released as soon as the LFO goes low, so a pulse can never last longer than half an LFO cycle.
context.fenv.sustain: At 0, so the filter falls back to the dull held tone between pulses.
context.filter.cutoff: The tone of the held note underneath the pulses.
context.aenv.sustain: High, so the note holds steady and only the filter moves.
context.mode.repeat: Off. REPEAT would chop the volume as well, which is a different sound.

tweaks.hear: The pulses change from eighth notes to sixteenths and faster, while the held note is unaffected.
The pulses grow from faint ticks to wide "wow"s that fill their half of each LFO cycle.
Now the LFO chops the volume envelope too, so the held note disappears between pulses. Switch it off again to compare.
Each pulse becomes a sharp, liquid "pip".

sounds.name: Liquid Resonance Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of 90s techno and electro "liquid" bass lines
sounds.blurb: Bass where each note starts with a wet, whistling "pew" and settles into a clean round tone.
sounds.how: On most synths resonance is a fixed setting. The Pro-1 has a RESO CV jack, so resonance can move during a note. Here the filter envelope is patched into it: at the start of each note the resonance is pushed right up to the point of whistling, and it falls back as the envelope decays. The same envelope is also sweeping the cutoff downwards, so the whistle slides down into the note and then disappears.

steps.title: Saw and square, low
steps.why:
A saw and a square, low and slightly detuned, make a full, ordinary bass tone to start from.
- Osc A saw, OCTAVE 1, FREQUENCY 0: a low saw (octaves run 0 to 3), bright and buzzy.
- Sync off: A runs freely.
- Osc B pulse only, PULSE WIDTH 5 (50 %): a square wave, hollow and round.
- OCTAVE osc B 1, FREQUENCY +0.1 st: the same octave, a hair sharp, for a slight beating.
- Osc B NORMAL, keyboard on: B plays at audio rate and follows the keys.
- OSC A 8, OSC B 5, NOISE/EXT 0: the saw leads, the square fills in.
- Listen for: a thick, buzzy low tone.

steps.title: Low filter with almost no resonance
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass. It is set low with almost no resonance, because a cable later will add resonance on top of this knob.
- CUTOFF 3 (159 Hz): where the sweep comes to rest.
- RESONANCE 1.5: the resting resonance. Remember it: the cable adds to it, so raising this knob makes the filter whistle for longer at the start of each note.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 5: the depth of the cutoff sweep on each note.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5: the cutoff follows the keys half way.
- Listen for: a dark bass with a plain, non-resonant brightening at the start of each note.

steps.title: A pluck-length filter envelope
steps.why:
The filter envelope is an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release). A pluck-length shape gives a normal plucked bass for now.
- ATTACK 2.5 (15 ms): very slightly softened, so the resonance will swell in rather than click once the cable is in.
- DECAY 5.2 (210 ms): the cutoff falls in about 200 ms. Later this also sets how long the resonance stays high.
- SUSTAIN 0: both cutoff and, later, resonance return to their knob settings on a held note. Raise it and the note stays resonant.
- RELEASE 3.5 (54 ms): short.
- Listen for: a plain pluck with no whistle.

steps.title: Patch FILTER ENV into RESO CV
steps.why:
On most synths resonance is a fixed setting. The Pro-1 has a RESO CV jack (control voltage for resonance), so resonance can move during a note.
- Cable FILTER ENV → RESO CV: the filter envelope now pushes resonance up as well as cutoff. The jack has a fixed depth: a full envelope adds the whole range of the RESONANCE knob. At the top of the envelope the filter is on the edge of whistling. As the envelope falls, the resonance drains away while the cutoff sweeps down, so the whistle slides down into the note and disappears.
- Listen for: a wet “pew” at the front of each note that was not there a moment ago. Pull the cable out to compare.

steps.title: Bass volume shape
steps.why:
The loudness envelope gives a bass shape: hit hard, hold, stop clean.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): instant start, lined up with the “pew”.
- DECAY 5 (170 ms), SUSTAIN 7: a slight drop after the start, then a steady level.
- RELEASE 3 (34 ms): notes stop cleanly.
- Listen for: each note starting wet and settling into a clean, round tone. Sweep filter DECAY while the line plays to make the whistle longer or shorter.

context.filter.res: The resting resonance. The cable adds the envelope on top of this, so raising the knob makes the filter whistle for longer at the start of each note.
context.fenv.decay: One envelope now controls two things: how long the cutoff sweep lasts and how long the resonance stays high.
context.fenv.attack: Slightly softened, so the resonance swells in over about 15 ms instead of clicking.
context.fenv.sustain: At 0, so both cutoff and resonance return to their knob settings on a held note. Raise it and the note stays resonant.
context.filter.env: The depth of the cutoff sweep. The depth of the resonance sweep is fixed by the jack.
context.filter.cutoff: Where the sweep comes to rest.

tweaks.hear: Short gives a quick "pip"; long gives a slow, whistling slide down into each note.
The resonance no longer drains away fully, so held notes keep a ringing, nasal peak.
Knob plus cable now go past the whistling point for longer, and the start of each note squeals.
The cutoff no longer moves, so you hear the resonance change by itself: a ringing peak that fades at a fixed pitch.

sounds.name: Whistling Filter Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of 70s sci-fi soundtrack whistle leads
sounds.blurb: A pure whistle played by the filter alone, with vibrato that speeds up as each note swells.
sounds.how: All three mixer levels are at 0, so no oscillator is heard. With RESONANCE at 10 the filter feeds back on itself and produces a sine-like whistle at its cutoff frequency. KEYBOARD AMOUNT at 10 makes the cutoff follow the keys exactly, so the whistle plays in tune and CUTOFF becomes the tuning knob. The LFO adds vibrato by moving the cutoff, and a cable from AMP ENV to LFO CV makes that vibrato start slow, speed up as the note swells, and slow down again as it fades.

steps.title: Turn everything in the mixer off
steps.why:
All three mixer levels go to 0, so no oscillator or noise feeds the filter. The filter will make the sound on its own.
- OSC A 0, OSC B 0, NOISE/EXT 0: nothing reaches the filter.
- Listen for: silence on every key. That is expected.

steps.title: Make the filter whistle
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass. With resonance at the top it feeds back on itself and produces a sine-like whistle at the cutoff frequency.
- RESONANCE 10: the filter oscillates by itself. Below about 9.2 the whistle dies away and the patch is silent.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 10: the cutoff follows the keys exactly, one octave per octave, so the whistle plays in tune. Any lower and the intervals shrink.
- CUTOFF 4.7 (525 Hz): now the tuning knob. It puts the whistle an octave above the played key; one panel unit is almost exactly an octave, so adjust by ear.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 0: any amount would bend the whistle’s pitch at the start of each note.
- Listen for: a pure, flute-like whistle that plays in tune.

steps.title: Slow swell and fade
steps.why:
The loudness envelope is an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release). A slow swell and fade makes the whistle breathe in and out like a voice.
- ATTACK 6.3 (330 ms): the note fades in over a third of a second. Through a cable later, this also sets how long the vibrato takes to get up to speed.
- DECAY 5 (170 ms), SUSTAIN 10: full level while held.
- RELEASE 5.8 (480 ms): about half a second of fade after you let go.
- VOLUME 9.5: the whistle is quieter than an oscillator, so the main output goes up. Turn it back to 7 before bringing any oscillator up in the mixer.
- Listen for: each note swelling in and fading out.

steps.title: Vibrato from the LFO
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) adds vibrato. The filter is the oscillator here, so vibrato means moving the cutoff through the modulation section’s DIRECT bus (always on).
- LFO triangle only: a smooth up-and-down.
- FREQUENCY lfo 3.2 (0.53 Hz): about one cycle every two seconds. This is the slowest the vibrato will get.
- AMOUNT LFO 1.3, route DIRECT: a very small amount, about a semitone either way.
- To FILTER DIR: the cutoff listens to the DIRECT bus.
- Listen for: for now it sounds more like slow drifting than vibrato.

steps.title: Patch AMP ENV into LFO CV
steps.why:
A cable from AMP ENV to LFO CV (control voltage for LFO speed) makes the vibrato follow the loudness of each note.
- Cable AMP ENV → LFO CV: the jack has a fixed depth of three octaves of LFO speed. At full volume the LFO runs eight times faster than the knob, about 4 Hz, a normal vibrato. As the note swells in, the vibrato speeds up with it; as it fades, it slows down.
- Listen for: hold a note. The pitch drifts at first, then settles into a steady vibrato once the note reaches full volume, then slows as you let go.

steps.title: Glide between notes
steps.why:
Glide makes the pitch slide between notes. It works on the keyboard voltage, and the filter is following that voltage, so the whistle slides just as an oscillator would.
- RATE 3 (270 ms): about a quarter of a second per slide. Higher makes slower, more theremin-like swoops.
- Glide mode NORMAL: slides between every pair of notes.
- Listen for: each new note swooping up or down from the last one.

context.filter.res: At 10 the filter oscillates by itself. Below about 9.2 the whistle dies away and the patch is silent.
context.filter.kbd: At 10 the cutoff follows the keys exactly, so the whistle plays in tune. Any lower and the intervals shrink.
context.filter.cutoff: The tuning knob for this sound. Small moves are large pitch changes: one panel unit is almost exactly an octave.
context.out.volume: Turned up because the whistle is quieter than an oscillator. Turn it back to 7 before you bring any oscillator up in the mixer.
context.filter.env: At 0. Any amount would bend the pitch of the whistle at the start of each note.
context.mix.oscA: At 0: the filter is the only thing making sound.
context.mod.lfoAmt: The depth of the vibrato, about a semitone either way.
context.lfo.rate: The slowest the vibrato gets. The AMP ENV cable multiplies this by up to eight.
context.aenv.attack: Sets how long the note takes to swell, and through the cable, how long the vibrato takes to get up to speed.

tweaks.try: Move very slightly either side of 4.73
tweaks.hear: The whole instrument goes sharp or flat. This is how you tune it to other instruments.

tweaks.try: Bring up to 4 and turn VOLUME down to 7
tweaks.hear: A saw an octave below appears underneath, and the whistle becomes a sharp resonant peak on top of it.
The note takes over a second to swell, and you can clearly hear the vibrato winding up with it.
The vibrato widens to several semitones, more like a theremin played with a shaky hand.

sounds.name: Triangle Kick Drum
sounds.ref: In the style of Vince Clarke and early Depeche Mode synth kick drums
sounds.blurb: Short, round kick drum: a low thud with a very fast downward pitch bend at the front.
sounds.how: Early synth-pop producers such as Vince Clarke often built each drum on a monosynth and recorded it to tape, instead of using a drum machine. This kick is Oscillator B’s triangle wave, taken off the keyboard so every key gives the same drum. The filter envelope is routed to Oscillator B’s pitch, so each hit starts at about 135 Hz and falls to about 55 Hz within a few hundredths of a second. That is too fast to hear as a slide; the ear hears a thud. Analogue drum machines of the time made their kicks the same way: a plain low tone with a quick pitch drop.

steps.title: Oscillator B only
steps.why:
The mixer sets what reaches the filter. Oscillator A has no triangle wave, so it is muted and Oscillator B is brought up full.
- OSC A 0: not used.
- OSC B 10: Oscillator B is the drum.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: for the moment you hear Oscillator B’s default saw, following the keys.

steps.title: Triangle at a fixed low pitch
steps.why:
The triangle has very few overtones, the plainest shape on the synth and the closest to a drum skin. Taking B off the keyboard parks it at one low pitch, so every key gives the same drum.
- Osc B triangle only: saw and pulse off, leaving a soft, round tone with no buzz.
- OCTAVE osc B 0: the lowest octave setting (they run 0 to 3).
- FREQUENCY osc B −2 (−2.8 st): tunes the drum down to about 55 Hz. This is the tuning knob for the kick.
- Osc B low frequency NORMAL, keyboard off: audio rate, but ignoring the keys.
- Listen for: every key now gives the same low hum.

steps.title: Bend the pitch with the filter envelope
steps.why:
The modulation section sends sources over the DIRECT bus (always on) or the WHEEL bus (mod wheel only). Here the filter envelope goes to B’s pitch, so each hit starts high and falls.
- AMOUNT FIL ENV 8: at the top of the envelope B is pushed up about 15 semitones, to roughly 135 Hz.
- FIL ENV route DIRECT: always on.
- To OSC B FREQ DIR: B’s pitch listens to the DIRECT bus.
- Listen for: with the default envelope, a slow downward swoop on each key press that settles part way down while held.

steps.title: Make the fall very fast
steps.why:
The filter envelope is an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release). Making it very fast turns the swoop into a thud.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): the pitch starts at the top at once.
- DECAY 4.2 (85 ms): most of the fall happens in the first third of that, too fast to hear as a slide.
- SUSTAIN 0: the pitch always lands on the low note.
- RELEASE 4.2 (110 ms): close to DECAY, so a short tap and a held key sound alike.
- Listen for: a thud instead of a swoop. Lengthen DECAY and it turns into a disco-style “boom-pew”.

steps.title: Low, plain filter
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass. A low, plain setting rounds the triangle off, and the same envelope opens it briefly for a click.
- CUTOFF 3.4 (209 Hz), RESONANCE 0: rounds the tone further, with no peak.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 3.5: opens the filter by nearly three octaves for an instant, letting a small click through at the front. At 0 the kick is all thud.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 0: the tone is the same on every key.
- Listen for: a small click at the start of each hit.

steps.title: Drum-shaped volume
steps.why:
The loudness envelope gives the kick its length. With no sustain, the drum always dies away.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): instant, like a beater hitting a skin.
- DECAY 5.4 (250 ms), SUSTAIN 0: about a quarter of a second. Shorter is a tight, clicky kick; longer is a boomy one.
- RELEASE 4.6 (150 ms): a short tail if you let go early.
- Listen for: in the pattern, a click, a thud and a short low tail on every hit.

context.oscB.tri: The triangle is the plainest shape on the synth, and the closest to the tone of a drum skin.
context.oscB.kbd: Off, so the drum has the same pitch on every key.
context.oscB.freq: The tuning of the drum. −2 is about 55 Hz.
context.mix.oscA: At 0. Oscillator A has no triangle, so it is not used.
context.mod.envAmt: How far above its resting pitch each hit starts. 8 is about 15 semitones.
context.mod.toBFreq: Connects the DIRECT bus (carrying the filter envelope) to Oscillator B’s pitch.
context.fenv.decay: The speed of the pitch fall, and of the click, because the same envelope opens the filter.
context.filter.env: The size of the click at the front. At 0 the kick is all thud.
context.aenv.decay: The length of the drum.

tweaks.hear: A small bend gives a soft, deep kick. At 10 the hit starts two octaves up and sounds more like a disco tom.
Short gives a hard click and a dead thud. Long turns the bend into an audible "peow".
The drum is tuned from a very low boom up to a small, tight kick.
A long, booming tail of about two thirds of a second, as on a drum-machine kick with its decay turned up.

sounds.name: Two-Envelope Noise Snare
sounds.ref: In the style of Kraftwerk and early Depeche Mode synth snares
sounds.blurb: Bright crack of noise over a short tuned body that drops in pitch.
sounds.how: A snare has two parts: the shell of the drum, which gives a short tone, and the wires under it, which give noise. Oscillator B’s triangle is the shell, fixed at about 185 Hz, and the filter envelope bends its pitch down at the start of the hit. That leaves the filter with no envelope of its own, so a cable brings in the amplifier envelope to do the job. AMP ENV into CUTOFF CV opens the filter wide at the start and closes it as the hit fades, so the noise starts bright and gets duller as it dies away.

steps.title: Noise and Oscillator B
steps.why:
A snare has two parts: the shell, which gives a short tone, and the wires under it, which give noise. The mixer sets both.
- OSC A 0: not used.
- OSC B 6: the shell of the drum, under the noise.
- NOISE/EXT 9: the snare wires, most of the sound.
- Listen for: loud hiss with Oscillator B’s default saw underneath.

steps.title: Triangle body at a fixed pitch
steps.why:
Oscillator B’s triangle becomes the drum shell, fixed at one pitch so every key gives the same drum.
- Osc B triangle only: saw and pulse off, leaving a plain, round tone.
- OCTAVE osc B 1, FREQUENCY 4.3 (+6 st): together these give about 185 Hz. With the keyboard off they are the only pitch controls.
- Osc B low frequency NORMAL, keyboard off: audio rate, ignoring the keys.
- Listen for: the tone under the hiss is now softer and the same on every key.

steps.title: A quick pitch drop on the body
steps.why:
The modulation section sends the filter envelope over the DIRECT bus (always on) to B’s pitch, for a quick drop at the start of the hit. The filter envelope is an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release).
- FIL ENV 5 DIRECT, To OSC B FREQ DIR: the shell starts six semitones sharp.
- Filter ATTACK 0, DECAY 3.6 (50 ms): the pitch falls straight back in about 50 ms.
- SUSTAIN 0, RELEASE 3.6 (60 ms): the pitch always lands on 185 Hz.
- Listen for: a “tock” in place of a steady “boop” under the noise.

steps.title: Filter low, its own envelope amount at 0
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass. Its envelope is busy bending pitch, and 50 ms is too short for the noise, so its own envelope amount stays at 0.
- CUTOFF 5.4 (834 Hz): parked low. Later this is where a cable sweep starts from and where the cutoff ends up as the hit dies.
- RESONANCE 2: a slight peak.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 0: the filter envelope does not touch the cutoff.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5: lower keys start from a lower cutoff; the riff uses a key an octave down for duller in-between hits.
- Listen for: the snare is now a dull thump with a little hiss.

steps.title: Patch AMP ENV into CUTOFF CV
steps.why:
A cable brings in the amplifier envelope to open the filter, since the filter envelope is busy on pitch.
- Cable AMP ENV → CUTOFF CV: CV means control voltage. The loudness envelope now opens the filter as well as the volume. The jack has a fixed depth of five octaves for a full envelope, so the CUTOFF knob sets where those five octaves start. From 830 Hz the top of the sweep is above the hearing range, and as the loudness falls, the cutoff falls with it.
- Listen for: the noise is bright again. The loudness envelope still holds at full while a key is down, so the darkening comes with the next step.

steps.title: Snare-length volume
steps.why:
The loudness envelope gives the snare its length, and through the cable it also sets how fast the noise darkens.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): instant crack.
- DECAY 5 (170 ms), SUSTAIN 0: the hit fades over about a sixth of a second, and the cutoff falls with it. Longer DECAY gives a longer, splashier snare.
- RELEASE 4.5 (140 ms): a short tail after a quick tap.
- Listen for: a bright crack that darkens as it dies. Mute OSC B to hear how much the tuned body adds.

context.mix.noise: The snare wires. This is most of the sound.
context.mix.oscB: The shell of the drum under the noise.
context.oscB.freq: Tunes the shell. With KYBD off, this and OCTAVE are the only pitch controls.
context.oscB.kbd: Off, so every key gives the same drum pitch.
context.mod.envAmt: The size of the pitch drop on the shell: 5 is six semitones.
context.fenv.decay: The speed of the pitch drop. It has no effect on the filter here, because ENVELOPE AMOUNT is at 0.
context.filter.env: At 0. The cable from AMP ENV sweeps the filter in its place.
context.filter.cutoff: Where the cable’s five-octave sweep starts from, and where the cutoff ends up as the hit dies.
context.filter.kbd: At 5, lower keys start the sweep from a lower cutoff. The riff uses a key an octave down for the duller in-between hits.
context.aenv.decay: The length of the snare and, through the cable, how fast the noise darkens.

tweaks.hear: Less noise gives a tom-like knock. Full noise gives a loose, hissy snare.
The whole sweep moves down or up: a dull, fat snare at the low end, a thin, bright one at the top.
A tight, clipped snare. The darkening speeds up too, because the same envelope drives the cable.
The shell is tuned from a deep 130 Hz up to a higher, ringing 200 Hz.

sounds.name: Filter-Whistle Hi-Hat
sounds.ref: In the style of early-80s electro and synth-pop hi-hats made on a synth
sounds.blurb: Thin, metallic "tss": a short tap is a closed hat, a held key is an open hat.
sounds.how: A hi-hat needs only the very top of the spectrum, and the Pro-1 has a low-pass filter, which removes the top and keeps the bottom. Two tricks get round that. First, RESONANCE at 10: on this kind of filter, high resonance turns down everything below the cutoff and makes the filter whistle at the cutoff, here about 10 kHz. Second, a cable from the MIXER jack to CUTOFF CV lets the noise shake that whistle at audio rate, which smears it from one thin tone into a band of hiss between roughly 5 and 15 kHz. The volume envelope has a short spike and a low sustain level, so a tap gives a closed hat and a held key gives an open one.

steps.title: Noise only
steps.why:
Only the noise generator goes into the filter. Noise has every frequency in it, which is where a hi-hat starts, but it needs shaping.
- OSC A 0, OSC B 0: both oscillators out of the mixer.
- NOISE/EXT 5: white noise at half level. Later, through a cable, this knob also sets how far the noise shakes the cutoff: low gives a thin, whistling hat, high a broad, noisy one.
- Listen for: plain hiss, with far too much low end for a hi-hat.

steps.title: Make the filter whistle at 10 kHz
steps.why:
A hi-hat needs only the very top of the spectrum, and the Pro-1’s filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass, which removes the top. The trick is full resonance: on this kind of filter it turns down everything below the cutoff and makes the filter whistle at the cutoff.
- CUTOFF 9 (10 kHz): the centre of the hat’s tone.
- RESONANCE 10: the filter oscillates by itself at 10 kHz, and the noise below drops well back. Lower it and the low end returns, turning the hat into a “tsh”.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 0: the filter envelope is not used.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5: higher keys give a slightly brighter hat, half an octave of cutoff per octave of keys.
- Listen for: a very high whistle with some hiss round it.

steps.title: Patch MIXER into CUTOFF CV
steps.why:
A cable from the MIXER jack (the raw mixer output, before the filter) to CUTOFF CV (control voltage for cutoff) lets the noise shake the whistle at audio rate.
- Cable MIXER → CUTOFF CV: the noise moves the cutoff thousands of times a second, smearing the whistle from one thin tone into a band of bright hiss, roughly 5 to 15 kHz. The jack has a fixed depth of five octaves for a full-scale signal and no knob of its own, so NOISE is the depth control. At 5 it swings the cutoff about an octave either way.
- Listen for: the single whistle turning into a metallic “tss”. Move NOISE to hear the band get narrower or wider.

steps.title: A spike, then a low sustain
steps.why:
The loudness envelope is an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release). A short spike and a low sustain let one patch play both closed and open hats.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): instant.
- DECAY 3.2 (35 ms): the “t” of the hat, the length of a closed hat.
- SUSTAIN 2.5: after the spike the level sits at a quarter while the key is down. That is the open hat.
- RELEASE 3 (34 ms): shuts it quickly when you let go, like choking the cymbal.
- VOLUME 10: the whistle is much quieter than an oscillator. Turn it back to 7 before moving to a sound that uses the oscillators.
- Listen for: tap a key for a closed hat; hold one for an open hat that is choked when you release.

context.mix.noise: Two jobs: it is the sound going into the filter and, through the cable, how far the cutoff is shaken. Low settings give a thin, whistling hat; high settings a broad, noisy one.
context.filter.res: At 10 the filter whistles and everything below the cutoff is turned down. Lower it towards 0 and the low end of the noise comes back, so the hat turns into a "tsh".
context.filter.cutoff: The centre of the hat’s tone: 9 is about 10 kHz.
context.filter.kbd: At 5, so a higher key gives a slightly brighter hat: half an octave of cutoff for each octave of keys.
context.filter.env: At 0. The filter envelope is not used.
context.aenv.decay: The length of the closed hat.
context.aenv.sustain: The level of the open hat while a key is held.
context.out.volume: At 10 because the whistle is quiet. Turn it back to 7 before you move on to a sound that uses the oscillators.

tweaks.hear: At 2 you hear the bare whistle with a little hiss. At 8 the whistle has gone and the hat is a broad "tsss".
The band drops to about 5 kHz and the hat sounds more like a shaker.
Closed hats only: holding a key no longer gives an open hat.
Open hats ring on for about a fifth of a second after the key is released, in place of being choked.

sounds.name: REPEAT Handclap
sounds.ref: In the style of the Roland TR-808 handclap
sounds.blurb: Three or four quick spikes of noise and a short tail, like several people clapping not quite together.
sounds.how: A drum-machine clap is filtered noise fired several times in quick succession and then left to die away. REPEAT mode does the firing: while a key is held, the LFO re-triggers both envelopes at its own rate, and with the LFO at its maximum of 30 Hz that is one spike every 33 ms. The filter sits in the middle of its range with some resonance, so most of the noise falls between roughly 1 and 5 kHz and it is not a full hiss. When the key is released, the sound dies away over the longer RELEASE time, which does the job of the reverb tail on a drum-machine clap. How long you hold the key sets how many spikes you get.

steps.title: Noise only, full up
steps.why:
A drum-machine clap is filtered noise fired several times in quick succession, then left to die away. The source is noise only.
- OSC A 0, OSC B 0: both oscillators out of the mixer.
- NOISE/EXT 10: noise at full level.
- VOLUME 10: a band of filtered noise is quieter than an oscillator, so the main output goes up. Turn it back to 7 before moving on to a sound that uses the oscillators.
- Listen for: plain, full hiss on every key.

steps.title: A band of noise, not a hiss
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass. It sits mid-range with some resonance, so the noise becomes a band where the smack of a clap sits, rather than a full hiss.
- CUTOFF 6.4 (1.7 kHz): the tone of the clap. The filter envelope will push it higher at the front of each spike, so most of the noise ends up between roughly 1 and 5 kHz. Lower is a duller, bigger pair of hands; higher is thin and snappy.
- RESONANCE 4: narrows the band a little. At 0 more low rumble gets through and the clap is more of a “pshh”.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 3: a small lift at the front of each spike.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 0: every key gives the same clap.
- Listen for: the hiss thins into a mid-range “shh”.

steps.title: Very short spikes over a bed of noise
steps.why:
Both envelopes are ADSRs (attack, decay, sustain, release). Very short decays make each firing a spike, and the loudness falls to a bed of noise rather than silence.
- Filter DECAY 3 (29 ms), SUSTAIN 0: with an instant attack and a 34 ms release, a quick brightening at the front of each spike.
- Loudness ATTACK 0, DECAY 3 (29 ms): each spike lasts about 30 ms.
- Loudness SUSTAIN 4: the bed of noise under the spikes, and the level the tail starts from.
- Loudness RELEASE 4.8 (190 ms): the tail after the key is released, standing in for the reverb on a drum-machine clap.
- Listen for: hold a key and get one spike, then steady noise.

steps.title: Let the LFO fire the spikes
steps.why:
REPEAT makes the LFO (low-frequency oscillator, also the Pro-1’s clock) re-fire both envelopes while a key is held. That turns one burst of noise into several.
- Repeat on: the LFO re-triggers both envelopes.
- Drone off: the gate follows the key, so the spikes stop when you let go.
- FREQUENCY lfo 10 (30 Hz): the LFO at maximum, one spike every 33 ms. At 9 it is 60 ms and the clap turns into a flam.
- Listen for: hold a key for about a tenth of a second and get three or four spikes, then the tail. How long you hold sets how many spikes. The LFO runs freely, so no two claps are quite the same.

context.mode.repeat: The LFO re-fires both envelopes while a key is held. This is what turns one burst of noise into several.
context.lfo.rate: The gap between spikes. At 10 it is 33 ms. At 9 it is 60 ms, and the clap turns into a flam.
context.aenv.decay: The length of each spike.
context.aenv.sustain: The bed of noise under the spikes, and the level the tail starts from.
context.aenv.release: The tail after the key is released: about 190 ms.
context.filter.cutoff: The tone of the clap. Lower is a duller, bigger pair of hands; higher is thin and snappy.
context.filter.res: Narrows the noise into a band. At 0 more low rumble gets through and the clap is more of a "pshh".
context.out.volume: At 10 because filtered noise is quiet. Turn it back to 7 before you move on to a sound that uses the oscillators.

tweaks.hear: The spikes are now 80 ms apart: a ragged burst of applause in place of one clap.
From a dull, thudding clap to a thin, snappy one.
A noisy tail of about half a second, as if the clap had a lot of reverb on it.
The bed of noise and the tail both go, and the clap becomes a dry, stuttering rattle.

sounds.name: Two-Pulse Cowbell
sounds.ref: In the style of the Roland TR-808 cowbell
sounds.blurb: Hollow, clanky "tonk" made from two square waves that are deliberately not quite in tune.
sounds.how: The 808 cowbell is two square waves a little under a fifth apart, about 540 and 800 Hz, through a band-pass filter. The Pro-1 can do the same with its two oscillators: both on pulse at width 5, with Oscillator B tuned 6.8 semitones above Oscillator A. That is not a clean fifth, so the two tones beat against each other and the result sounds like struck metal, not like a chord. Resonance gives the low-pass filter a peak around 2.5 kHz, which is as close as it gets to a band-pass. The volume drops fast to a low sustain and then rings out on the release.

steps.title: Two square waves, not quite a fifth apart
steps.why:
A drum-machine cowbell is two square waves a little under a fifth apart. The two oscillators do the same here, deliberately out of tune so they beat like struck metal rather than a chord.
- Pulse only on both, PULSE WIDTH 5 (50 %): two square waves. Narrow A and the bell gets thinner and more tinny.
- OCTAVE 3 on both, FREQUENCY osc A 0: the highest octave setting, so middle C gives the pitch of the drum-machine original. Other keys give other sizes of bell.
- FREQUENCY osc B 4.9 (+6.8 st): just short of a fifth (5 on the knob). On middle C that is 523 Hz and about 775 Hz.
- Sync off, Osc B NORMAL, keyboard on: both run freely and follow the keys.
- Listen for: B is silent in the mixer until the next step.

steps.title: Equal levels
steps.why:
The mixer sets how loud each oscillator is going into the filter. Neither tone should lead.
- OSC A 7, OSC B 7: equal levels, so the two tones clash evenly.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: a sour two-note buzz. Nudge osc B FREQUENCY to 5 to hear it turn into a clean fifth, then back to 4.9 for the clank.

steps.title: A resonant peak for the clank
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass. Resonance gives it a peak, which is as close as it gets to the band-pass filter a drum machine would use. Its ADSR envelope (attack, decay, sustain, release) adds a tick.
- CUTOFF 7 (2.5 kHz): the position of the peak, following the keys at half rate (KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5).
- RESONANCE 5: boosts the overtones round 2.5 kHz. At 0 the bell is duller and fuller.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 3, DECAY 3.5 (45 ms): with instant ATTACK and SUSTAIN 0, a quick brightening of about 45 ms.
- RELEASE 3.5 (54 ms): short.
- Listen for: a harder “tick” at the front and a more metallic, clanky tone.

steps.title: Fast drop, then ring
steps.why:
The loudness envelope gives a loud knock followed by a quieter ring, which is how a struck bell behaves.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): instant knock.
- DECAY 3.8 (59 ms): the level falls fast, in about 60 ms.
- SUSTAIN 2.5: the ring after the knock sits at a quarter level.
- RELEASE 5 (220 ms): when you let go it rings out over about 220 ms. This is the length of the ring.
- Listen for: tap the keys rather than holding them. Each tap gives a hollow, clanky “tonk”.

context.oscB.freq: The interval between the two tones. 4.86 is just short of a fifth, which is where the clank comes from.
context.oscA.pw: At 5, a square wave. Narrow it and the bell gets thinner and more tinny.
context.oscA.octave: Both oscillators at 3, so middle C gives the pitch of the drum-machine original. Other keys give other sizes of bell.
context.filter.cutoff: The position of the resonant peak. It follows the keys at half rate.
context.filter.res: Turns the low-pass filter into something closer to a band-pass. At 0 the bell is duller and fuller.
context.aenv.sustain: The level of the ring after the first knock.
context.aenv.release: The length of the ring.

tweaks.hear: At exactly 5 the two tones make a clean fifth and the sound turns into a chord stab. Just below it the beating comes back, and it is a cowbell again.
A dry "tick-tock", closer to a woodblock.
The peak gets sharper and the bell more nasal.
A larger, lower bell.

sounds.name: Self-Oscillating Filter Clave
sounds.ref: In the style of Kraftwerk-style electronic percussion ticks
sounds.blurb: A dry, high "tock" with a tiny downward chirp, tuned from the keyboard.
sounds.how: There is no oscillator in this sound. With RESONANCE at 10 the filter oscillates by itself and gives a sine-like tone at its cutoff frequency all the time, whether or not a key is down. The amplifier envelope lets a slice of about 50 ms of that tone through on each key press, and a touch of filter envelope makes the pitch fall by about half an octave during the slice, which turns a "beep" into a "tock". KEYBOARD AMOUNT at 10 makes the cutoff follow the keys exactly, so the clave is tuned by which key you play.

steps.title: Turn everything in the mixer off
steps.why:
All three mixer levels go to 0. There is no oscillator in this sound; the filter will make it.
- OSC A 0, OSC B 0, NOISE/EXT 0: nothing feeds the filter.
- Listen for: silence. That is expected.

steps.title: The filter as the sound source
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass. With resonance at full it oscillates by itself and gives a sine-like tone at its cutoff, the only sound source in this patch.
- RESONANCE 10: the filter whistles on its own.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 10: the cutoff follows the keys exactly, so the clave can be played in tune.
- CUTOFF 6 (1.3 kHz): the tuning knob. The whistle sits at about 1.26 kHz on middle C and an octave higher for each octave up the keys; one panel unit is almost exactly an octave. The riff plays the C above middle C, about 2.5 kHz.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 0: no filter movement yet.
- Listen for: a steady, pure whistle while a key is held.

steps.title: Let a 50 ms slice through
steps.why:
The loudness envelope is an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release). It lets a short slice of the whistle through on each key press.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): instant.
- DECAY 3.6 (50 ms), SUSTAIN 0: each press lets through about 50 ms, then silence. This is the length of the hit.
- RELEASE 3.6 (60 ms): a short tail if you let go early.
- VOLUME 10: the whistle is much quieter than an oscillator. Turn it back to 7 before bringing any oscillator up.
- Listen for: a short “bip” on each key. The very first hit can be faint, because the filter needs a few hundredths of a second to start oscillating.

steps.title: A small downward chirp
steps.why:
The filter envelope, also an ADSR, adds a small chirp. Because the filter is the oscillator here, moving the cutoff moves the pitch: this is a pitch envelope.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 0.6: only a little, lifting the pitch about half an octave at the start of each hit. More and it becomes a laser “pew”.
- ATTACK 0, DECAY 2.5 (19 ms): the pitch falls back in under 20 ms, the speed of the chirp.
- SUSTAIN 0, RELEASE 2.5 (21 ms): the pitch always settles on the key’s note.
- Listen for: compare with the step before. The plain “bip” has become a woody, dry “tock”.

context.filter.res: At 10 the filter oscillates by itself. It is the only sound source in this patch.
context.filter.kbd: At 10 the cutoff follows the keys exactly, so the clave can be played in tune.
context.filter.cutoff: The tuning knob. One panel unit is almost exactly an octave.
context.filter.env: The size of the chirp at the front of each hit. Because the filter is the oscillator, this is a pitch envelope.
context.fenv.decay: The speed of the chirp.
context.aenv.decay: The length of the hit.
context.out.volume: At 10 because the whistle is quiet. Turn it back to 7 before you bring any oscillator up in the mixer.

tweaks.hear: The chirp grows to more than two octaves and the hit becomes a "pew", the zap of 70s electronic drums.
A pure ringing tone, like a struck glass on high keys or a tuned tom on low ones.
Two octaves down: a hollow knock, closer to a woodblock or a small tom.
The filter stops oscillating and the patch goes silent, because nothing else is feeding the filter.

sounds.name: Soft Pulse Pluck
sounds.ref: In the style of Yazoo — "Only You"
sounds.blurb: Gentle, rounded pluck for slow broken-chord patterns.
sounds.how: Vince Clarke used a Pro-One heavily on the first Yazoo album. This pluck is a narrowish pulse wave from Oscillator A with a triangle an octave above it from Oscillator B, which adds a soft, glassy top without any buzz. The filter starts low, and a medium-length envelope opens it on each note and lets it fall most of the way back, so every note starts clear and turns mellow. A slow LFO moves the pulse width a little, so repeated notes are never quite the same.

steps.title: Pulse below, triangle above
steps.why:
A narrowish pulse gives the pluck its reedy colour, and a triangle an octave above adds a soft, glassy top without any buzz.
- Osc A pulse only, PULSE WIDTH 3.4 (35 %): a little reedier than a square (5). Towards 2 it gets thin and nasal; at 5 it is hollow.
- OCTAVE osc A 2, FREQUENCY 0, Sync off: normal register, in tune, running freely.
- Osc B triangle only: almost no overtones, so it adds a clear upper octave with no fizz. The saw or pulse in its place would be much brighter.
- OCTAVE osc B 3, FREQUENCY +0.1 st: one octave higher, a hair sharp.
- Osc B NORMAL, keyboard on: audio rate, following the keys.
- Listen for: B is still silent in the mixer; the next step brings it in.

steps.title: Pulse in front
steps.why:
The mixer sets how loud each oscillator is going into the filter. The pulse carries the note and the triangle clears the top.
- OSC A 8: the pulse leads.
- OSC B 6: how much upper octave you hear. Bring it up until the top of the sound clears, and stop before the octave stands out by itself.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: a slightly brighter, glassier top on each note.

steps.title: Low filter that follows the keys
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass. It starts low, so every note will settle mellow after the envelope opens it.
- CUTOFF 4.4 (418 Hz): where each note settles. Lower is rounder and more muted.
- RESONANCE 2: a little peak, no squelch.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 7: higher notes open the filter more, so the top of a broken chord is not duller than the bottom.
- Listen for: a warm, muted tone.

steps.title: Open on each note, then fall most of the way back
steps.why:
The filter envelope is an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release) that opens the filter on each note and lets it fall most of the way back.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 4.2: lifts the cutoff about three and a half octaves. This is how bright the start of each note is.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): opens at once.
- DECAY 5.2 (210 ms): falls over about 200 ms, the length of the brightness.
- SUSTAIN 1.5: settles just above the resting cutoff.
- RELEASE 4.6 (150 ms): the tone closes gently after you let go.
- Listen for: a clear start that turns mellow, with no squelch.

steps.title: Plucked volume shape
steps.why:
The loudness envelope, also an ADSR, gives the pluck its shape: instant, then fading, with a short ring after the key comes up.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): instant.
- DECAY 6 (420 ms): the level falls over about 400 ms. This is the length of the pluck while a key is held.
- SUSTAIN 2.5: it settles at a quarter level.
- RELEASE 5 (220 ms): each note rings a little into the next.
- Listen for: play a slow broken chord and hear the notes overlap slightly.

steps.title: A slow drift on the pulse width
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) is a slow wave. Sent over the modulation section’s DIRECT bus (always on) to A’s pulse width, it gives PWM (pulse-width modulation): a slow shift in the tone.
- LFO triangle, FREQUENCY 3.5 (0.64 Hz): a smooth cycle about every one and a half seconds.
- AMOUNT LFO 3.5, route DIRECT: the width moves between about 29 % and 40 %.
- To OSC A PW DIR: A’s pulse width listens to the DIRECT bus.
- Listen for: repeated notes are never quite the same colour. Set AMOUNT LFO to 0 to hear them go static.

context.oscA.pw: The basic colour of the pluck. 5 is hollow; towards 2 it gets thin and nasal.
context.oscB.tri: A soft upper octave. The saw or pulse in its place would be much brighter.
context.mix.oscB: How much upper octave you hear.
context.filter.cutoff: Where each note settles. Lower is rounder and more muted.
context.filter.env: How bright the start of each note is.
context.fenv.decay: How long the brightness lasts.
context.aenv.decay: The length of the pluck while a key is held.
context.aenv.release: Lets each note ring into the next one.
context.mod.lfoAmt: How far the LFO moves the pulse width.

tweaks.hear: A square wave: hollower and rounder, more like a clarinet.
Short gives a tight, muted pluck; long gives a slower "bow" on each note.
Without the triangle the pluck is plainer and sits lower. With it, a clear upper octave appears.
Held notes no longer die away, and the pluck turns into a soft organ.

sounds.name: Gliding Twin-Saw Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of 2010s synthwave lead lines
sounds.blurb: Wide, bright lead with steady vibrato that slides between joined-up notes.
sounds.how: Synthwave takes its lead sounds from early-80s polysynths such as the Prophet-5, whose voice the Pro-1 shares. Two sawtooth waves at the same octave are detuned by about a fifth of a semitone, so they beat and sound wide. The filter is half open with a medium envelope, so each note starts bright and settles. A steady 5 Hz vibrato on both oscillators, and AUTO glide, which only slides between overlapping notes, make the line phrase like a singer or a guitarist.

steps.title: Two saws, slightly apart
steps.why:
Two saws at the same octave, detuned by a fifth of a semitone, beat against each other and sound wide. This is the basis of a big, bright lead.
- Sawtooth on for both, other waves off: two bright, buzzy saws.
- OCTAVE 2 on both, FREQUENCY osc A 0: a normal lead register (octaves run 0 to 3).
- FREQUENCY osc B 0.1 (+0.2 st): about a fifth of a semitone sharp. This is where the width comes from; further out beats faster and starts to sound out of tune.
- Sync off, Osc B NORMAL, keyboard on: both run freely and follow the keys.
- Listen for: B is silent in the mixer until the next step, so this is one plain saw for now.

steps.title: Both up in the mixer
steps.why:
The mixer sets how loud each oscillator is going into the filter. Nearly equal levels give the widest sound.
- OSC A 8, OSC B 7: both saws almost level. Pull OSC B down and the lead gets narrower and more focused.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: hold a note and hear the slow beating between the two saws.

steps.title: Half-open filter with a medium envelope
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass with an ADSR envelope (attack, decay, sustain, release). Half open with a medium envelope, each note starts bright and settles without going dull.
- CUTOFF 5.6 (957 Hz): the settled brightness of the lead.
- RESONANCE 2.5: a small peak for a little edge.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 3.5: lifts the cutoff nearly three octaves at the start of each separately played note.
- ATTACK 0, DECAY 5.6 (300 ms), SUSTAIN 4: bright at once, falling over about 300 ms to a moderate level.
- RELEASE 4.8 (190 ms), KEYBOARD AMOUNT 6: gentle close after you let go; high notes stay bright.
- Listen for: a bright start that settles into a warm, still-clear tone.

steps.title: Held volume with a soft edge
steps.why:
The loudness envelope, also an ADSR, holds long notes and gives phrases a short tail.
- ATTACK 1.5 (7 ms): a few milliseconds, just enough to take the click off.
- DECAY 5 (170 ms), SUSTAIN 8.5: held notes stay almost at full level.
- RELEASE 5 (220 ms): each phrase ends with a short tail rather than a hard stop.
- Listen for: long notes that sing evenly, and a slight ring when you lift off.

steps.title: Vibrato on both oscillators
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) adds vibrato through the modulation section’s DIRECT bus (always on). It goes to both oscillators so the saws stay the same distance apart.
- LFO triangle only, FREQUENCY 7 (5.07 Hz): a smooth wobble about five times a second, a singer’s vibrato speed.
- AMOUNT LFO 0.9, route DIRECT: small, about a fifth of a semitone either way. The scale is uneven: 2 is about a semitone.
- To OSC A FREQ DIR and To OSC B FREQ DIR: both pitches move together. On one only, the vibrato would sound like detune.
- Listen for: a steady shimmer on held notes. Set AMOUNT LFO to 0 and the lead sounds flat and static.

steps.title: AUTO glide
steps.why:
Glide makes the pitch slide between notes. AUTO is the Pro-1’s name for legato glide: it only slides when you press a key before releasing the last one.
- RATE 2.2 (150 ms): a quick slide. Higher is a slower, more obvious swoop.
- Glide mode AUTO: only overlapping notes slide.
- Retrigger off (NORMAL): overlapping notes do not restart the envelopes, so they share one.
- Listen for: in the riff, joined-up notes slide and stay settled; separate ones jump and get a fresh bright start. That is what makes the line phrase like a singer or guitarist.

context.oscB.freq: The detune between the saws. This is where the width comes from.
context.filter.cutoff: The settled brightness of the lead.
context.filter.env: How much brighter the start of each separately played note is.
context.mod.lfoAmt: The depth of the vibrato. The scale is not even: 0.9 is a fifth of a semitone, 2 is about a semitone.
context.lfo.rate: The speed of the vibrato.
context.mod.toBFreq: Sends the same vibrato to Oscillator B, so the two saws stay the same distance apart.

tweaks.try: Flip LFO ROUTE to WHEEL, set OSC A FREQ and OSC B FREQ to WH, and raise LFO AMOUNT to 2
tweaks.hear: No vibrato until you push the mod wheel, so you can add it to long notes only.
An octave on top: thinner and more piercing, and the beating is harder to hear.

tweaks.try: Sweep between 4.5 and 7 while the riff plays
tweaks.hear: From a rounded, distant lead to a bright, buzzing one.
The beating speeds up and the lead starts to sound out of tune.

sounds.name: Swelling Brass Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of early-80s Prophet-5 brass leads
sounds.blurb: Bold brass-like lead whose tone rises into each note instead of snapping open.
sounds.how: A brass player’s note starts dull and brightens over a few hundredths of a second as the air pressure builds. The filter envelope copies that: its ATTACK is slowed to about 40 ms, so the cutoff rises into each note. The tone is a sawtooth plus a pulse wave whose width is moved slowly by the LFO, which thickens the pair in the way a section of players thickens one line. The Pro-1 has the same oscillators, filter and envelopes as one voice of a Prophet-5, the synth that made this kind of brass sound common on early-80s records.

steps.title: Saw plus pulse
steps.why:
A saw plus a pulse at the same octave: the saw gives the buzz of brass and the pulse fills in underneath it.
- Osc A saw, OCTAVE 2, FREQUENCY 0: a bright saw in the lead register (octaves run 0 to 3).
- Sync off: A runs freely.
- Osc B pulse only, PULSE WIDTH 5 (50 %): a square wave, hollow and full.
- OCTAVE osc B 2, FREQUENCY +0.1 st: the same octave, a hair sharp, for gentle beating.
- Osc B NORMAL, keyboard on: audio rate, following the keys.
- Listen for: B is still silent in the mixer, so this is a single saw for now.

steps.title: Mix
steps.why:
The mixer sets how loud each oscillator is going into the filter. The saw leads slightly.
- OSC A 8: the saw’s buzz is the front of the sound.
- OSC B 7: the square fills in just underneath.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: a thicker, fuller tone with a slow beating between the two.

steps.title: Move Oscillator B’s pulse width
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) moves Oscillator B’s pulse width through the modulation section’s DIRECT bus (always on). This PWM (pulse-width modulation) thickens the pair, the way a section of players thickens one line.
- LFO triangle, FREQUENCY 5.2 (1.74 Hz): a smooth swing a little under twice a second.
- AMOUNT LFO 5, route DIRECT: the width swings about 11 % either side of square.
- To OSC B PW DIR: B’s pulse width listens to the DIRECT bus.
- Listen for: a slow thickening, as if a second player had joined in. Set AMOUNT LFO to 0 to compare.

steps.title: A filter that rises into the note
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass. A brass note starts dull and brightens as the air pressure builds; the filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), copies that.
- CUTOFF 3.8 (276 Hz), RESONANCE 1: a dull starting point for each note, no peak.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 5.5: at the top of the rise the filter opens about four and a half octaves.
- ATTACK 3.8 (43 ms): the key setting. The cutoff climbs to its peak instead of jumping. About 40 ms sounds like a trumpet; longer is a slow horn swell.
- DECAY 5.6 (300 ms), SUSTAIN 5.5: held notes stay fairly bright after the swell.
- RELEASE 4 (87 ms), KEYBOARD AMOUNT 6: short close; high notes stay bright.
- Listen for: “bwah” at the front of each note, where a zero attack would give “dat”.

steps.title: Firm volume shape
steps.why:
The loudness envelope gives a firm shape that lets the filter rise be heard.
- ATTACK 2.5 (15 ms): the volume is up before the filter has finished rising, so you hear the swell in tone, not in level.
- DECAY 5 (170 ms), SUSTAIN 9: held notes stay nearly at full level.
- RELEASE 4 (87 ms): a short tail.
- Listen for: a solid, even note with the brightness swelling in at the front.

steps.title: Retrigger every note
steps.why:
The MODE section decides how key presses fire the envelopes. The rising filter is the whole character of this sound, so every note needs it.
- Retrigger on (RETRIG): every key press restarts both envelopes, including notes played with overlapping fingers.
- Listen for: play a legato phrase. Every note gets its own “bwah”. Switch RETRIG off and the overlapped notes arrive already bright.

context.fenv.attack: The brass "bwah". Around 40 ms sounds like a trumpet; longer sounds like a slow horn swell.
context.filter.env: How far the filter opens at the top of the rise: 5.5 is about four and a half octaves.
context.fenv.sustain: How bright a held note stays after the first swell.
context.filter.cutoff: The dull starting point of each note.
context.mod.lfoAmt: How far the LFO moves Oscillator B’s pulse width.
context.mod.toBPw: Connects the DIRECT bus (carrying the LFO) to Oscillator B’s pulse width.
context.lfo.rate: The speed of the thickening movement.
context.mode.retrig: Gives every note its own filter rise.

tweaks.hear: At 0 it is a hard synth stab. At 3.8 it is brass. At 6 the rise takes a quarter of a second and sounds like a slow horn swell.
From a muted, flugelhorn-like tone to a bright, blaring one.
At 0 the tone is static. At 5 it slowly shifts and sounds thicker.
An octave underneath, like a trombone doubling the trumpet line.

sounds.name: Feedback-Driven Sequencer Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Skinny Puppy and late-80s industrial sequencer bass
sounds.blurb: Thick, overloaded sixteenth-note bass that sounds as if it is being pushed through a small amplifier.
sounds.how: Two kinds of overload make this bass heavy. First, both oscillators are turned up so far in the mixer that the filter input cannot take them cleanly, which flattens the tops of the waves. Then a cable takes AUDIO OUT back into the EXT input, so the sound goes round the filter and amplifier a second time. That feedback raises the level, fills out the low end and pushes the filter input further into overload. With a cable in EXT the noise generator is switched out, and the NOISE/EXT knob becomes the amount of feedback.

steps.title: Low saw, narrow pulse an octave above
steps.why:
A low saw gives the weight and a narrow pulse an octave above adds a hard, nasal upper edge.
- Osc A saw, OCTAVE 1, FREQUENCY 0: a bright saw in the bass register (octaves run 0 to 3).
- Sync off: A runs freely.
- Osc B pulse only, PULSE WIDTH 3 (31 %): narrower than a square, thin and nasal.
- OCTAVE osc B 2, FREQUENCY +0.1 st: an octave above A, a hair sharp.
- Osc B NORMAL, keyboard on: audio rate, following the keys.
- Listen for: B is still silent in the mixer; this is the low saw on its own.

steps.title: Run the mixer hot
steps.why:
The mixer is run hot: together the two oscillators are more than the filter input can take cleanly, which flattens the tops of the waves and thickens the tone.
- OSC A 9: high, to drive the filter input hard.
- OSC B 8: also high. The overload depends on the two levels added together.
- NOISE/EXT 0: nothing yet. With a cable later this knob changes job.
- Listen for: compare with both knobs at 5. That is cleaner and much smaller; this is thick and slightly crushed.

steps.title: Resonant filter with a short envelope
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass with an ADSR envelope (attack, decay, sustain, release). A resonant peak and a short envelope make it a hard sequencer bass.
- CUTOFF 5.2 (726 Hz): the settled tone of each note.
- RESONANCE 5: a hard peak. The feedback coming next works against it, so it is set higher than you might expect.
- ENV AMOUNT 5, DECAY 4.6 (120 ms): from an instant attack, each note opens four octaves and falls back in about 120 ms, a bright front edge.
- SUSTAIN 3.5, RELEASE 3 (34 ms): held notes stay moderately bright and close quickly. KEYBOARD AMOUNT 4 adds slight key tracking.
- Listen for: a hard, fairly clean sequencer bass.

steps.title: Patch AUDIO OUT into EXT
steps.why:
A cable takes AUDIO OUT back into the EXT input, so the sound goes round the filter and amplifier a second time. That feedback raises the level, fills out the low end and pushes the filter input further into overload.
- Cable AUDIO OUT → EXT: with a cable in EXT the noise generator is switched out.
- NOISE/EXT 7: now the feedback amount, not noise. The jack has no depth of its own. Higher gives more level, low end and overload.
- VOLUME 6: down from 7 to make up for the extra level. Put it back when you remove the cable.
- Listen for: the level jump and the low end fill out, with the ringing of the resonance held back a little.

steps.title: Short, hard volume shape
steps.why:
The loudness envelope gives a short, hard shape so the sixteenth notes are clipped.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): instant.
- DECAY 5 (170 ms), SUSTAIN 7: a small drop after the bright front, then a steady level.
- RELEASE 2.6 (23 ms): very short, so notes stop dead.
- Listen for: tight, overloaded sixteenths with clean gaps between them. Turn NOISE/EXT from 7 down to 0 while the line plays to hear the feedback leave.

context.mix.noise: With the cable in EXT this is the feedback amount, not the noise level. Higher settings give more level, more low end and more overload.
context.mix.oscA: High, to drive the filter input hard.
context.mix.oscB: Also high. The overload depends on the two levels added together.
context.oscB.octave: An octave above Oscillator A, so the bass has a hard upper edge as well as weight.
context.filter.cutoff: The settled tone of each note.
context.filter.res: A hard peak at the cutoff. Feedback works against this peak, so it is set higher than you would expect.
context.fenv.decay: The length of the bright front of each note.
context.out.volume: Turned down to 6 because feedback makes the patch louder. Put it back to 7 when you remove the cable.
context.aenv.release: Very short, so the notes are clipped.

tweaks.try: Move between 0 and 10 while the riff plays
tweaks.hear: At 0 there is no feedback, and the bass is quieter and a little brighter. Towards 10 it gets louder, heavier in the low end and more squashed.

tweaks.try: Raise to 8, then turn NOISE/EXT to 0 and back
tweaks.hear: With no feedback the filter rings sharply on every note. Bring the feedback back and the ringing is pulled down into the body of the sound.
Both oscillators at the same octave: heavier and rounder, with less of an edge.
From a muffled throb to a bright, tearing bass.

sounds.name: Triangle Sub Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of 90s hip-hop and R&B sub bass
sounds.blurb: Deep, smooth bass that is nearly a pure tone, with a soft knock at the start of each note.
sounds.how: Sub bass is close to a pure tone: a lot of low end and almost no buzz. The nearest shape the Pro-1 has is Oscillator B’s triangle, so that carries the sound. By itself it would vanish on small speakers, so a quiet square wave from Oscillator A at the same pitch adds a few overtones that mark the note. A low filter keeps those in check, and a very short filter envelope puts a soft knock on the front of each note. AUTO glide slides between overlapping notes.

steps.title: Triangle for the weight, square for the outline
steps.why:
Sub bass is close to a pure tone: lots of low end, almost no buzz. Oscillator B’s triangle carries it, and a square from Oscillator A at the same pitch will mark the note on small speakers.
- Osc B triangle, OCTAVE 1: in tune, the closest shape the Pro-1 has to a pure tone, in the bass register (octaves run 0 to 3).
- Osc B NORMAL, keyboard on: audio rate, following the keys.
- Osc A pulse, PW 5 (50 %), OCTAVE 1: a square at exactly the same pitch, so there is no beating.
- Sync off: A runs freely.
- Listen for: B is still silent in the mixer, so you hear the square on its own for now.

steps.title: Mostly triangle
steps.why:
The mixer sets how loud each oscillator is going into the filter. The triangle is nearly all of the sound.
- OSC B 10: the triangle full up, for weight.
- OSC A 3.5: only a little square, so the note can be heard on small speakers. At 0 the bass is felt more than heard.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: turn OSC A to 0 and back. It adds a slight edge that lets you follow the pitch.

steps.title: Low filter
steps.why:
The filter is a 24 dB per octave low-pass. Set low, it keeps the square’s overtones in check.
- CUTOFF 3.2 (182 Hz): only the first few overtones of the square get through.
- RESONANCE 0.5: almost no peak, keeping the low end smooth.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 4: higher notes open the filter a little.
- Listen for: the edge from the square gets softer and rounder.

steps.title: A soft knock at the front
steps.why:
The filter envelope is an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release). A very short one opens the filter for an instant and shuts it again: a soft knock.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 3: the size of the knock. More gives a clickier front.
- ATTACK 0, DECAY 3.8 (59 ms): open at once, shut again in about 60 ms. This is the length of the knock.
- SUSTAIN 0: held notes go back to the smooth low tone.
- RELEASE 3.5 (54 ms): short.
- Listen for: a muffled “b” on the front of each separately played note.

steps.title: Long, even volume
steps.why:
The loudness envelope, also an ADSR, keeps long notes even.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): instant, lined up with the knock.
- DECAY 6.5 (660 ms), SUSTAIN 8: a slow, slight drop to a high level, so held notes stay nearly level.
- RELEASE 4.2 (110 ms): about a tenth of a second, so notes do not click off.
- Listen for: long, steady notes that fill the low end.

steps.title: AUTO glide
steps.why:
Glide makes the pitch slide between notes. AUTO is the Pro-1’s name for legato glide: only overlapping notes slide.
- RATE 3 (270 ms): about a quarter of a second per slide.
- Glide mode AUTO: separate notes jump; overlapping ones slide.
- Retrigger off (NORMAL): a slid note does not restart the envelopes, so it has no new knock.
- Listen for: in the riff one note is held over into the next, and the pitch leans down into it.

context.oscB.tri: The triangle is the closest the Pro-1 gets to a pure tone. It is nearly all of this sound.
context.mix.oscA: A little square wave so the note can be heard on small speakers. At 0 the bass is felt more than heard.
context.filter.cutoff: Limits how much of the square’s edge gets through.
context.filter.env: The size of the knock at the front of each note.
context.fenv.decay: The length of the knock.
context.aenv.sustain: High, so long notes hold their level.

tweaks.hear: From a pure, deep hum to a hollow, more audible bass.
The knock becomes a definite click, which helps the bass cut through a busy track.
Long, lazy slides of about three quarters of a second between overlapping notes.
The triangle drops an octave below the square. On most speakers you will feel it more than hear it.

sounds.name: Dark Swelling Pad
sounds.ref: In the style of Phil Collins — "In the Air Tonight"
sounds.blurb: Slow, dark, sustained tone that fades in, brightens a little and hangs on after the key is released.
sounds.how: The slow, dark chords on that record were played on a Prophet-5. The Pro-1 has the same kind of voice but only one of them, so this is a single line of that pad: play it slowly, or record it several times to build chords. Two saws an octave apart go through a filter that is almost closed. Both envelopes have attacks of well over half a second, so each note fades in and brightens slightly after it starts, and a release of more than a second lets each note hang over into the next. A very slow LFO drifts the cutoff so that held notes do not sit still.

steps.title: Two saws an octave apart
steps.why:
Two sawtooth oscillators an octave apart are the raw material for a dark pad: plenty of harmonics for the filter to work on, and enough low end to give the line weight.
- Osc A sawtooth, OCTAVE 1: octaves run 0 to 3 here, and 1 is an octave below where the synth starts. This is the root and the weight of the pad. Pulse and SYNC stay off, FREQUENCY at 0.
- Osc B sawtooth, OCTAVE 2: an octave above A, to give the dark tone some definition. Triangle and pulse off; low frequency at NORMAL and keyboard on, so it plays as an ordinary second oscillator.
- Osc B FREQUENCY 0.1 (+0.1 semitone): a tenth of a semitone sharp. Too little to sound out of tune, enough to make the two saws drift slowly against each other.
- Listen for: only Oscillator A is in the mixer so far, so you hear one bright saw an octave down. Oscillator B joins in the next step.

steps.title: Lower octave in front
steps.why:
The mixer sets how much of each oscillator reaches the filter. The low saw carries the weight and the upper one adds definition.
- OSC A 8: the lower octave stays in front, so the pad has a solid bottom.
- OSC B 6.5: the upper saw a little behind. Turn it up and the pad gets brighter and more obviously two notes; turn it down and it goes plainer.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no white noise; this is a clean tone.
- Listen for: hold a note. With B a tenth of a semitone sharp the two saws beat slowly, a gentle swirl in the tone. Turn OSC B to 0 and back to hear it come and go.

steps.title: Nearly closed filter
steps.why:
The filter is where the pad gets dark. The Pro-1’s is a 24 dB per octave low-pass: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs steeply, so a low cutoff takes away most of the buzz of the saws.
- CUTOFF 4 (about 320 Hz): nearly closed. What is left is a dark hum. This is the first knob to reach for: higher is brighter and more present, lower is duller and further back.
- RESONANCE 1.5: a small boost at the cutoff point. It gives the hum a slight edge without making it squelchy.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5: half key tracking, as the synth starts. Higher notes open the filter a little so the top of the range does not go muffled.
- Listen for: sweep CUTOFF from 7 down to 4 while holding a note and hear the buzz drain out.

steps.title: Slow brightening
steps.why:
The filter envelope is an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release) that pushes the cutoff up each time a note starts. Here it is slow and small, so the tone opens a little after the note has begun.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 2.5: how far the envelope lifts the cutoff, about two octaves at the peak. More makes the swell brighter; less keeps it dark throughout.
- ATTACK 7.5 (860 ms): the cutoff takes nearly a second to reach its peak, so the brightening creeps in rather than hitting.
- DECAY 7 (1.0 s), SUSTAIN 6: it then eases back over about a second and settles most of the way up while the key is held.
- RELEASE 6.5 (920 ms): after you let go the tone closes slowly. You will hear this once the volume release is lengthened in the next step.
- Listen for: hold a key and hear the tone open over the first second, then dip slightly. Set ATTACK to 0 to compare: the brightness then jumps in at the front.

steps.title: Fade in, long fade out
steps.why:
