The loudness envelope shapes volume over time. A pad wants no front edge and a long tail, so notes blur into each other.
- ATTACK 7 (570 ms): each note fades in over about half a second. Shorter turns it into an organ; longer makes it hard to play in time.
- DECAY 5, SUSTAIN 10: with sustain at full, the decay has nothing to do; the note holds its full level while the key is down.
- RELEASE 6.8 (1.2 s): the note fades for over a second after you let go, covering the gap before the next one. The slow filter release from the last step is now heard as the tail darkening.
- Listen for: play slow notes one after another. Each is still fading as the next fades in, so the line sounds joined up.

steps.title: A slow drift on the cutoff
steps.why:
An LFO (low-frequency oscillator, a wave too slow to hear as a pitch) nudges the cutoff up and down so held notes do not sit still. On the Pro-1 you route it in the modulation section: a source gets an AMOUNT and a bus, and a destination switch picks that bus.
- LFO triangle on, saw and pulse off: a smooth up-and-down shape, with no jumps or ramps.
- LFO FREQUENCY 2.2 (0.29 Hz): one cycle about every three and a half seconds. Slow enough to feel like drift rather than wobble.
- AMOUNT LFO 2.5: the cutoff moves about a third of an octave either way. More gives an obvious sweep; less is barely there.
- LFO route DIRECT, To FILTER DIR: DIRECT is the always-on bus (WHEEL only works as you push the mod wheel), and the FILTER switch at DIR listens to it.
- Listen for: hold one note for ten seconds. The tone gets slightly brighter and darker in a slow cycle.

context.oscB.octave: An octave above Oscillator A. It gives the dark tone some definition.
context.filter.cutoff: Low, which is what makes the pad dark. This is the first knob to reach for.
context.filter.env: How far the tone opens after each note starts.
context.aenv.attack: The fade-in. Shorter settings make it an organ, not a pad.
context.aenv.release: The fade-out after the key is released. It covers the gap between notes.
context.mod.lfoAmt: How far the cutoff drifts.
context.lfo.rate: The speed of the drift.

tweaks.try: Open slowly to 5.5 over several notes
tweaks.hear: The pad comes forward and turns from a dark hum into a bright string-like tone.
At 3 notes start almost at once. At 8 they take over a second to arrive.
The drift grows to more than an octave each way and becomes a slow, obvious sweep.

tweaks.try: Switch Oscillator B’s saw off and its pulse on, then flip OSC B PW to DIR
tweaks.hear: The same slow LFO now also moves Oscillator B’s pulse width, which adds a gentle chorus-like motion to the upper octave.

sounds.name: Two-Octave Power-Down
sounds.ref: In the style of early-80s arcade and sci-fi power-down effects
sounds.blurb: Hold a key: a two-note tone starts two octaves high and sinks to rest while it darkens and fades.
sounds.how: The OSC CV jack bends both oscillators by the same amount at once, without using the modulation matrix. Here Oscillator B is tuned a fifth above Oscillator A, and a cable sends the filter envelope into OSC CV. Each note starts two octaves sharp and sinks to the played pitch over a few seconds, fast at first and then slower, with the fifth staying a fifth all the way down. The same envelope closes the filter as it goes, and the volume fades on a similar curve, so the sound winds down like a machine losing power.

steps.title: A fifth between the oscillators
steps.why:
A two-note tone, root and fifth, gives the power-down its machine-like, slightly hollow character, and keeps the interval clear as it falls.
- Osc A saw + pulse, PULSE WIDTH 5: both waveforms added together. The saw brings buzz and the square (a pulse at width 5) adds a hollow body. OCTAVE 2 and FREQUENCY 0 leave it at the usual pitch; SYNC off.
- Osc B sawtooth, FREQUENCY 5 (+7 st): seven semitones, a fifth above Oscillator A at the same octave. Triangle and pulse off.
- Osc B low frequency NORMAL, keyboard on: it stays an audio oscillator and follows the keys.
- Listen for: only Oscillator A is in the mixer so far, so you hear a single buzzy note. The fifth joins in the next step.

steps.title: Mix
steps.why:
The mixer balance decides whether you hear one coloured note or two separate ones. Here Oscillator A leads and the fifth sits a little behind it.
- OSC A 8: the root, in front.
- OSC B 6: the fifth, slightly lower so it reads as part of the tone. Raise it to make the interval more obvious.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: a bare, organ-like fifth with no movement yet. Turn OSC B to 0 and back up to hear the interval appear.

steps.title: Patch FILTER ENV into OSC CV
steps.why:
One cable makes the whole fall. The filter envelope is an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release) voltage, and patching it into OSC CV (the oscillators’ pitch control voltage input) bends both oscillators together, outside the modulation matrix.
- Cable FILTER ENV → OSC CV: the jack has a fixed depth of 24 semitones for a full envelope, so each note starts two octaves up. Both oscillators move by the same amount, so the fifth stays a fifth all the way down.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): the note starts at the top of the fall.
- DECAY 8.5 (3.9 s): the length of the fall, fast at first then slower. About an octave is gone in the first second; after three seconds it is within a couple of semitones.
- SUSTAIN 0: the fall ends on the played note. At 5 it would stay parked an octave sharp.
- RELEASE 6 (570 ms): if you let go early, the envelope keeps falling from where it was.
- Listen for: hold a key and hear the pitch dive, then slow as it settles.

steps.title: Let the same envelope close the filter
steps.why:
Now the same envelope also sweeps the filter, so the tone darkens as the pitch sinks, like a motor running down.
- CUTOFF 4 (about 320 Hz): where the tone comes to rest. The Pro-1’s 24 dB low-pass filter cuts the highs steeply above it, so the end of the fall is dull.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 4.5: about three and a half octaves of extra cutoff at the start, falling on the same 3.9 s curve as the pitch. More makes the top of the fall brighter.
- RESONANCE 3: a moderate peak at the cutoff that moves down with the sweep, giving it a slightly vocal edge.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5: half key tracking, so high notes come to rest a little brighter than low ones.
- Listen for: bright and buzzy at the top, closing to a dark hum as it settles.

steps.title: Fade as it falls
steps.why:
The loudness envelope fades the sound on a similar curve, so pitch, brightness and volume all wind down together.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): full volume from the first instant, at the top of the fall.
- DECAY 8.8 (5.1 s), SUSTAIN 0: the volume falls to silence over about five seconds even with the key held. By the time the pitch has arrived the sound has nearly gone. Shorten DECAY and it dies before it reaches the bottom.
- RELEASE 5 (220 ms): letting go early ends the note with a short fade rather than a click.
- Listen for: hold a key to the end. The sound sinks, darkens and trails away like a machine losing power.

context.fenv.decay: The length of the fall. Through the cable it times the pitch, and through ENVELOPE AMOUNT it times the filter.
context.fenv.sustain: At 0, so the pitch ends on the played note. Any other value leaves the sound parked sharp: 5 would be an octave up.
context.oscB.freq: The interval between the oscillators: 5 is a fifth.
context.filter.env: How much brighter the sound is at the top of the fall.
context.filter.cutoff: How dark the sound is when it comes to rest.
context.aenv.decay: How long the sound takes to fade.

tweaks.hear: The fall takes well under a second: a quick "pyoom", like a shot or a falling object in an arcade game.

tweaks.try: Raise to 8 and set the filter SUSTAIN to 10
tweaks.hear: The reverse: the pitch climbs two octaves in a little over a second and stays there. A power-up.
The fifth closes to a detuned unison, and the fall sounds like one thick voice.

tweaks.try: Set to 4, LFO FREQUENCY to 8.5, and flip OSC A FREQ to DIR
tweaks.hear: Oscillator A flutters about four semitones either way at 12 Hz while both fall, so the machine sounds unstable as it winds down.

sounds.name: One-Key Octave Bass Line
sounds.ref: In the style of 80s Hi-NRG octave bass lines
sounds.blurb: Hold one key and get a sixteenth-note bass line that jumps up an octave on every other note.
sounds.how: Two clocks run this patch. REPEAT lets the LFO fire both envelopes about eight times a second, which turns a held key into a row of short notes. Oscillator B is switched to LO FREQ and taken off the keyboard, so it is a second LFO; its pulse wave runs at half the speed of the first and is sent to Oscillator A’s pitch, where it pushes every other note up an octave. A Hi-NRG producer would have programmed this low-high pattern into a sequencer; here the synth makes it from one finger. The two clocks are not locked together, so they have to be tuned against each other by ear.

steps.title: A bright bass oscillator, tuned six semitones sharp
steps.why:
A bright bass tone for the pattern to play, tuned six semitones sharp on purpose. It sounds wrong for now: the pitch modulation in the last step swings six semitones either way, so its low position lands on the key and its high position an octave above.
- Osc A saw + pulse, PULSE WIDTH 4 (41 %): both waves added, the saw for buzz and a slightly narrow pulse for a reedy edge.
- OCTAVE 1: an octave below the starting pitch, in bass range.
- FREQUENCY 4.3 (+6 st): the deliberate offset. SYNC stays off.
- OSC A 8, OSC B 0, NOISE/EXT 0: only Oscillator A is heard. Oscillator B is about to become a modulator.
- Listen for: a buzzy bass note a tritone above the key you press.

steps.title: Blip envelopes
steps.why:
Short blip envelopes turn each note into a plucked sixteenth. Both ADSRs (attack, decay, sustain, release) have no sustain, so a note dies on its own.
- CUTOFF 4.4 (about 420 Hz), RESONANCE 3.5: a fairly dark resting point with a nasal peak, so the pluck has a squelchy edge.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 5.5: the filter envelope opens the cutoff a long way at the start of each blip. KEYBOARD AMOUNT stays at 5.
- Filter ATTACK 0, DECAY 78 ms, SUSTAIN 0: an instant snap open, closed again within a tenth of a second.
- Loudness ATTACK 0, DECAY 120 ms, SUSTAIN 0: the volume falls a little slower than the filter, so each blip closes down as it fades. Both RELEASE at 34 ms.
- VOLUME 8.5: short blips with gaps are quieter than a held note.
- Listen for: one short "dip" per key, however long you hold it.

steps.title: REPEAT at sixteenth-note speed
steps.why:
REPEAT turns a held key into a stream of notes. The LFO (low-frequency oscillator), which on the Pro-1 doubles as the clock, re-fires both envelopes on every cycle.
- Repeat on, Drone off: while you hold a key, each LFO cycle restarts the blip. DRONE would hold the gate open with no key held, which is not wanted here.
- LFO FREQUENCY 7.8 (8.19 Hz): about eight blips a second, sixteenth notes at about 123 bpm. This is the tempo knob for the whole pattern.
- Listen for: hold a key and get a row of identical blips, all at the same sharp pitch. Turn LFO FREQUENCY to speed it up or slow it down.

steps.title: Oscillator B as a half-speed square LFO
steps.why:
Oscillator B becomes a second clock. Switched to low frequency it runs far below hearing and works as a second LFO, here a square wave at half the speed of the first.
- Osc B pulse only, PULSE WIDTH 5: a square jumps between two values with nothing in between, so the pitch will jump between two notes rather than slide.
- Osc B LO FREQ, keyboard off: below hearing, and not following the keys, so the pattern runs at the same speed on every note.
- OCTAVE 1, FREQUENCY 0 (about 4.1 Hz): in LO FREQ each octave step halves or doubles the speed. At 1 you get low-high-low-high; at 0, two low then two high.
- Listen for: nothing changes yet. Oscillator B is out of the mixer and not routed anywhere.

steps.title: Send it to Oscillator A’s pitch
steps.why:
The modulation section sends Oscillator B’s square to Oscillator A’s pitch, and the one-key bass line appears.
- AMOUNT OSC B 5: six semitones either way, an octave from bottom to top. With the +6 offset from step 1, the low half lands on the key and the high half an octave up.
- OSC B route DIRECT: onto the always-on bus. WHEEL would bring it in only as you push the mod wheel.
- To OSC A FREQ DIR: Oscillator A’s pitch listens to the DIRECT bus.
- Listen for: low-high-low-high, one change per blip. If a jump lands mid-blip, nudge Oscillator B’s FREQUENCY a hair until the pattern holds still. The two clocks are not locked, so it drifts slowly, as it does on the hardware.

context.mode.repeat: The LFO re-fires both envelopes while a key is held. It is the note clock.
context.lfo.rate: The tempo of the blips.
context.oscB.lo: Drops Oscillator B below hearing so that it works as a second LFO.
context.oscB.kbd: Off, so the pattern runs at the same speed on every key.
context.oscB.freq: In LO FREQ this is the fine speed control for the octave jumps. Use it to line them up with the blips.
context.oscB.octave: In LO FREQ each step halves or doubles the speed. 1 gives low-high-low-high; 0 gives two low, two high.
context.oscB.pulse: A pulse wave has only two values, so the pitch jumps between two notes and does not slide.
context.mod.oscBAmt: The size of the jump. 5 swings six semitones either way, an octave in all.
context.oscA.freq: Six semitones sharp, to cancel the downward half of the swing so the low note is in tune with the key.
context.mix.oscB: At 0: Oscillator B is a modulator here and is not heard.

tweaks.hear: Oscillator B runs at a quarter of the blip rate, so the pattern becomes two low notes, then two high.

tweaks.try: Switch Oscillator B’s pulse off and its saw on, with OCTAVE at 0
tweaks.hear: The pitch climbs over four blips and drops back: a rising run in place of an octave jump. The ramp never stops moving, so each blip also bends upwards slightly.

tweaks.try: Lower to 3.8 and set Oscillator A FREQUENCY to 2.5
tweaks.hear: The jump shrinks from an octave to a fifth.
The tempo changes but Oscillator B does not follow, so the octave pattern breaks up into irregular jumps until you retune it.

sounds.name: Swooping Answer Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Talking Heads — "Burning Down the House"
sounds.blurb: Bright lead that whoops up two octaves into every detached note and sinks away as it fades.
sounds.how: The swoop comes from one cable, not from glide. AMP ENV is patched into OSC CV, so the volume envelope also bends the pitch of both oscillators, by a fixed two octaves at full level. The oscillators are set two octaves low to cancel that out. A held note therefore sits in tune, but it has to climb there during the attack and it sinks again during the release. Notes played legato share one envelope, so they join on without a swoop: you choose which notes swoop by how you finger them.

steps.title: Two oscillators, both two octaves low
steps.why:
Two oscillators for a bright lead, both parked two octaves low on purpose. The cable in step 4 adds 24 semitones back to both, so both need the same offset.
- Osc A sawtooth, OCTAVE 0: the bright, buzzy lead voice, two octaves below where a held note will end up. Pulse and SYNC off, FREQUENCY 0.
- Osc B pulse, PULSE WIDTH 4 (41 %): a slightly narrow pulse, reedier than a square, to fill in under the saw. Saw and triangle off.
- Osc B OCTAVE 0, FREQUENCY 0.1: the same low octave, a tenth of a semitone sharp so the pair beat gently. Low frequency at NORMAL and keyboard on.
- Listen for: the riff two octaves too low, a growly saw. Oscillator B is not in the mixer until the next step.

steps.title: Mix
steps.why:
The saw leads and the pulse fills in under it, giving the lead a thicker, slightly hollow body.
- OSC A 8: the saw in front for bite.
- OSC B 6: the pulse a little lower. More makes the lead hollower and reedier; less leaves a plain saw.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: the tone thickening, with slow beating between the two. Still two octaves low.

steps.title: Bright filter with a small snap
steps.why:
A bright filter with a small snap on the front of each note. The Pro-1’s filter is a 24 dB low-pass that keeps the lows and cuts the highs, and the filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), pushes it open as each note starts.
- CUTOFF 6.2 (about 1.4 kHz), RESONANCE 2.5: fairly open with a small peak, so the lead cuts through.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 6: a little more than half tracking. The filter follows the keys, not the OSC CV jack, so later it stays put while the pitch swoops up through it.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 2.5: opens the filter about two octaves further at the start. ATTACK 0, DECAY 270 ms and SUSTAIN 4 make it snap open and settle back; RELEASE 140 ms.
- Listen for: a brighter "t" at the front of each note, then the tone steadying.

steps.title: Patch AMP ENV into OSC CV
steps.why:
One cable makes the swoop. OSC CV is the oscillators’ pitch control voltage input, and patching the loudness envelope into it means volume and pitch rise and fall together.
- Cable AMP ENV → OSC CV: a fixed depth, no amount knob. A full envelope adds 24 semitones to both oscillators, which puts the notes back where the keys say.
- SUSTAIN 10: here it is a tuning control. Only at 10 does the cable add the full two octaves; lower and held notes go flat.
- ATTACK 5.2 (130 ms): each note fades in and climbs two octaves in that time, the first octave within 40 ms while it is still quiet. Longer makes a slower whoop.
- RELEASE 5.6 (390 ms): after you let go the pitch sinks as the note fades, an octave down by half volume. DECAY at 170 ms does nothing with SUSTAIN at 10.
- Listen for: each detached note whooping up into pitch and sinking away as it ends.

steps.title: Leave RETRIG off
steps.why:
How the envelopes restart decides which notes swoop. With RETRIG off, overlapping notes share one envelope.
- Retrigger off (NORMAL): a key pressed while another is still down changes pitch but does not restart the envelopes, so it arrives in tune with no swoop. Switch it on and every key press swoops.
- Glide RATE 0: no portamento. The swoop comes from the cable, and glide on top would blur it.
- Listen for: in the riff the second and third notes overlap. The third joins on cleanly while every detached note whoops.

context.oscA.octave: Two octaves lower than the pitch you hear on a held note. The cable supplies the missing 24 semitones.
context.oscB.octave: Also at 0. OSC CV moves both oscillators together, so both need the same offset.
context.aenv.attack: The length of the upward swoop. Through the cable this one knob times both the fade-in and the climb.
context.aenv.sustain: A tuning control in this patch. Only at 10 does the cable add the full 24 semitones; any lower and held notes go flat.
context.aenv.release: The length of the fall after the key is released.
context.filter.cutoff: Fixed while the pitch swoops, so the low start of each swoop is relatively bright and buzzy.
context.mode.retrig: Off, so overlapping notes do not swoop. Switch it on and every key press swoops, however you finger it.

tweaks.hear: At 3.5 the climb takes about 35 ms and is more of a chirp. At 7 it takes over half a second, and the note fades in as it rises like a siren starting up.
Each note reaches its pitch and then sags an octave, because the envelope settles at half level and the cable then adds only 12 semitones.
The fall after each note stretches to over a second and runs into the start of the next note.
Oscillator B sits a fifth above Oscillator A, and the pair swoop in parallel.

sounds.name: Sweet Wobbly Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Talking Heads — "This Must Be the Place (Naive Melody)"
sounds.blurb: Soft, rounded lead with a gentle, constant waver in its pitch.
sounds.how: Most of the tone is Oscillator B’s triangle, the softest shape on the panel, with a quieter square wave from Oscillator A to give it an outline. The filter takes off what little edge is left. The waver is the LFO moving the pitch of both oscillators by about a third of a semitone, four times a second: enough to sound slightly unsteady, like a toy instrument, without sounding out of tune. A short glide rounds off the joins between notes.

steps.title: Triangle and square
steps.why:
A soft pair of waves for a gentle lead: Oscillator B’s triangle, the softest shape on the panel, and a square from Oscillator A for an outline.
- Osc A pulse only, PULSE WIDTH 5: a square wave, hollow and slightly reedy. Saw and SYNC off; OCTAVE 2 and FREQUENCY 0 at the usual pitch.
- Osc B triangle only: very few overtones, close to a plain whistle. It will carry most of the sound. Saw and pulse off.
- Osc B OCTAVE 2, FREQUENCY +0.1 st: the same octave, a hair sharp so the pair move slightly. Low frequency at NORMAL and keyboard on.
- Listen for: only the square is in the mixer so far, a hollow, clarinet-like tone. The triangle comes in next.

steps.title: Mostly triangle
steps.why:
Mostly triangle, with the square underneath for shape.
- OSC B 9: the triangle nearly full, the body of the lead.
- OSC A 5: the square at about half. More makes the lead hollower and reedier; less makes it plainer.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: turn OSC A to 0 and back. By itself the triangle is close to a plain whistle; the square adds a hollow, reedy outline.

steps.title: Round off the top
steps.why:
The low-pass filter trims the edge of the square. The triangle has so few overtones that it is hardly touched.
- CUTOFF 5.8 (about 1.1 kHz), RESONANCE 1: a rounded top with almost no peak, so nothing sounds squelchy.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 7: more tracking than the starting 5, so high notes open the filter further and do not go dull.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 1.5: the filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), adds only a little brightness at the start of each note. ATTACK 0, DECAY 170 ms, SUSTAIN 5, RELEASE 87 ms.
- Listen for: the square’s buzz softening. Push CUTOFF up to 8 to hear what it is trimming.

steps.title: Soft start, short tail
steps.why:
The loudness envelope sets how notes start and stop. A soft lead wants no click on the front and a short tail.
- ATTACK 2.8 (19 ms): takes the click off the front without sounding slow.
- DECAY 170 ms, SUSTAIN 9: a very slight dip after the start, then held notes stay nearly full.
- RELEASE 4.6 (150 ms): each note tails off briefly instead of stopping dead, which joins the phrase together.
- Listen for: play short notes, then set ATTACK to 0 to compare. The front becomes a tick.

steps.title: A small, steady waver
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) adds the waver: a small, steady wobble in pitch that sounds slightly unsteady, like a toy instrument, without going out of tune.
- LFO triangle only: a smooth up-and-down, the usual shape for vibrato.
- LFO FREQUENCY 6.6 (4.00 Hz): four wobbles a second. Faster sounds nervous; slower sounds seasick.
- AMOUNT LFO 1.2: the knob is squared, so this is only about a third of a semitone each way. Small moves matter: 2 is already a full semitone.
- LFO route DIRECT, To OSC A and B FREQ DIR: both oscillators take the always-on bus. If only one did, the pair would beat against each other instead.
- Listen for: hold a note and hear the pitch gently rocking.

steps.title: A touch of glide
steps.why:
Glide, or portamento, slides the pitch from one note to the next. A short setting rounds off the joins.
- RATE 1.8 (97 ms): about a tenth of a second. You hear it as a softened join, not as a slide. At 0 the pitch jumps.
- Glide mode NORMAL: slides between every pair of notes. AUTO would slide only when notes overlap.
- Listen for: the riff’s leaps sounding slightly smoothed. Turn RATE to 5 to hear the slide clearly, then bring it back.

context.oscB.tri: The triangle carries the sound. It has very few overtones, which is why the lead is soft.
context.mix.oscA: The square wave. More of it makes the lead more hollow and reedy; less makes it plainer.
context.filter.cutoff: Trims the edge of the square wave. The triangle is hardly affected.
context.mod.lfoAmt: The depth of the waver. Small moves matter: 2 is already a full semitone each way.
context.lfo.rate: The speed of the waver.
context.mod.toBFreq: Both oscillators have to take the waver. If only one did, the pair would beat against each other instead.
context.glide.rate: Short, so it softens the joins without being heard as a slide.

tweaks.hear: At 0 the lead is steady and a little plain. At 1.2 it wavers. At 2.5 the swing is a semitone and a half each way and sounds seasick.

tweaks.try: Switch OSC B FREQ to OFF
tweaks.hear: Only Oscillator A wavers now, so the two oscillators drift in and out of tune with each other four times a second: a rougher, chorus-like wobble.
At about 1 Hz the waver turns into a slow sway, like a tape running unevenly.
The square wave takes over and the lead becomes hollow, more like a clarinet.

sounds.name: Dry Clavinet-Style Comp
sounds.ref: In the style of Talking Heads — "Remain in Light"
sounds.blurb: Thin, wiry, very short note for tight funk rhythm parts.
sounds.how: A clavinet is bright, thin and dead short, and all three can be had from the panel. Thin comes from narrow pulse waves: Oscillator A at about 18 % width, with a quieter one from Oscillator B an octave higher. Bright and percussive comes from a filter envelope that opens more than four octaves and is nearly shut again within 50 ms. Short comes from a volume envelope with no sustain at all, so a note is over in about a tenth of a second however long the key is held. The rhythm then comes entirely from where you place the notes.

steps.title: Two narrow pulses
steps.why:
Narrow pulse waves give a clavinet its thin, wiry tone, so both oscillators swap the saw for a pulse.
- Osc A pulse, PULSE WIDTH 1.6 (18 %): a narrow pulse, thin and wiry. Towards 5 it fills out and stops sounding like a clavinet. OCTAVE 2, FREQUENCY 0, SYNC off.
- Osc B pulse, PULSE WIDTH 2.8 (29 %): slightly wider, so a little fuller.
- Osc B OCTAVE 3: an octave above A for the bright, stringy top, a hair sharp. Low frequency at NORMAL, keyboard on.
- Listen for: hold a note and set Oscillator A’s PULSE WIDTH to 5 and back to hear how much body the narrow pulse gives away. Oscillator B is not in the mixer until the next step.

steps.title: Upper octave behind
steps.why:
The upper octave goes in behind, as brightness rather than a second note.
- OSC A 8: the main pulse.
- OSC B 4: half level. It adds a string-like brightness on top; much higher and you start to hear two notes an octave apart.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: the tone gaining a brighter, jangly top. Turn OSC B to 0 to hear it go plain.

steps.title: A very fast filter pluck
steps.why:
A very fast filter pluck gives the hard "tk" at the front of each note. The 24 dB low-pass filter sits low, and the filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), flicks it open and shut.
- CUTOFF 4.6 (about 480 Hz), RESONANCE 3.5: dark between plucks, with a peak that makes the snap slightly vocal.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 7: higher notes rest brighter, so the top of a part stays crisp.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 5.5: opens the filter 4.4 octaves at the start of the note.
- DECAY 3.7 (54 ms), SUSTAIN 0.5: with ATTACK 0 and RELEASE 21 ms, instant open, most of the way back within about 50 ms. A longer DECAY turns the "tk" into a "tow".
- Listen for: a hard click of brightness at the front of each note, then a duller body.

steps.title: No sustain on the volume
steps.why:
No sustain on the loudness envelope makes every note dead short whatever you do with the key. The rhythm now comes entirely from where you place the notes.
- ATTACK 0: full level at once, lined up with the filter snap.
- DECAY 4.4 (100 ms), SUSTAIN 0: the whole note is over in about a tenth of a second, even with the key held. DECAY, not the key, decides the length.
- RELEASE 2.4 (19 ms): no ring after the key comes up.
- VOLUME 8.5: raised because notes this short sound quieter. Turn it back to 7 if you lengthen them.
- Listen for: short, dry chops. Raise DECAY to 6 to hear the part get looser and lose its funk.

steps.title: Retrigger every note
steps.why:
Retrigger decides whether overlapping notes get a fresh start.
- Retrigger on (RETRIG): every key press restarts both envelopes. Fast rhythm parts are played with overlapping fingers, and in NORMAL an overlapped note would lose its pluck and, with SUSTAIN at 0, might barely sound.
- Listen for: play quick notes that overlap. Each one still clicks like a detached note. Switch it off to hear overlapped notes go soft.

context.oscA.pw: The thinness of the sound. At 1.6 the pulse is 18 % wide; towards 5 it fills out and stops sounding like a clavinet.
context.oscB.octave: An octave above Oscillator A, for the bright, stringy top.
context.filter.env: How far the filter opens on the "tk" at the front of the note.
context.fenv.decay: The length of the bright part: about 50 ms here.
context.aenv.decay: The length of the whole note. With SUSTAIN at 0 this, not the key, decides when the note ends.
context.aenv.sustain: At 0, so held keys do not ring on.
context.out.volume: Raised to make up for the very short notes. Turn it back to 7 if you lengthen them.

tweaks.hear: From a thin, almost buzzing wire to a hollow, woody knock.
At 3.5 the note is a muted tick, like a damped string. At 5.5 it rings for a quarter of a second and the part loses its tightness.
Each note gains a quacking, wah-like peak.
A little noise adds the scrape of a key mechanism to the front of each note.

sounds.name: Key-Tracked Squelch Stabs
sounds.ref: In the style of Talking Heads — "Girlfriend Is Better"
sounds.blurb: Funk stabs that are plain and thumpy low down and squelch harder the higher you play.
sounds.how: Squelch is resonance plus a fast filter sweep. Here the sweep is the same on every note, but the resonance is not: a cable from KYBD CV to RESO CV lets the keyboard set it. The keyboard voltage is zero at middle C, so there the RESONANCE knob is in charge. Above middle C the cable adds resonance and below it the cable takes resonance away. A riff that jumps between low and high stabs gets two different sounds from one patch.

steps.title: A full stab tone
steps.why:
A stab needs plenty of overtones for the filter to work on, so both oscillators go in full of buzz.
- Osc A saw + pulse, PULSE WIDTH 4 (41 %): both waves added, bright with a reedy edge. OCTAVE 2, FREQUENCY 0, SYNC off.
- Osc B sawtooth, OCTAVE 1: an octave below for weight. FREQUENCY 0.1 puts it a tenth of a semitone sharp so it beats slightly against A. Low frequency at NORMAL, keyboard on.
- OSC A 8, OSC B 6, NOISE/EXT 0: A leads and the lower saw fills in behind.
- Listen for: a thick, bright, slightly moving tone, far too buzzy for now. The filter tames it next.

steps.title: Low filter, moderate resonance
steps.why:
The 24 dB low-pass filter is set low, so each stab rests dark and gets its bite from the sweep in the next step.
- CUTOFF 3.6 (about 240 Hz): where the sweep will come to rest. Most of the buzz is gone.
- RESONANCE 3.5: a moderate peak at the cutoff. Remember this figure: it is what you will hear at middle C, and the cable in step 4 adds to it above and takes from it below.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5: ordinary cutoff tracking, separate from the cable, which will track resonance.
- Listen for: a dull, muffled thump with a faint ring.

steps.title: A fast, deep sweep
steps.why:
The filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), sweeps the cutoff up and back on every stab. Squelch is resonance plus a fast sweep.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 6: nearly five octaves of lift at the start. More is a harder hit; less a softer one.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): the sweep starts at the top, right on the beat.
- DECAY 4.9 (160 ms), SUSTAIN 1: most of the way back down in about 160 ms and held nearly closed. Shorter is a "bip", longer a "bwow". RELEASE 34 ms.
- Listen for: a firm "bow" on each note, the same at both ends of the keyboard.

steps.title: Patch KYBD CV into RESO CV
steps.why:
One cable lets the keyboard set the resonance. KYBD CV sends the keyboard pitch as a control voltage, and RESO CV adds a voltage to the RESONANCE knob.
- Cable KYBD CV → RESO CV: the voltage is zero at middle C, so there the knob is in charge. Above it the cable adds resonance, below it takes some away. One keyboard octave is worth the whole range of the knob.
- Across the riff: the G above middle C plays as if RESONANCE were at 9, just short of whistling, and the F just below that G as if it were at about 7.5. The G below middle C gets none at all.
- RESONANCE knob: now moves the point on the keyboard where the squelch starts.
- Listen for: the low stabs thump plainly and the high ones squelch.

steps.title: Short, separate notes
steps.why:
The loudness envelope keeps the stabs short and separate, and RETRIG makes sure every one gets its own sweep.
- ATTACK 0: instant, so the punch lands with the sweep.
- DECAY 5.2 (210 ms), SUSTAIN 5: a quick drop to half level, so held stabs have a punchy front and a quieter body.
- RELEASE 3 (34 ms): notes stop almost as soon as you let go, keeping the gaps clean.
- Retrigger on: every key press restarts both envelopes, even with overlapping fingers.
- Listen for: tight, choppy stabs with clear gaps between them.

context.filter.res: The resonance at middle C. The cable adds to this above middle C and subtracts below, so the knob moves the point on the keyboard where the squelch starts.
context.filter.env: The depth of the sweep on every stab.
context.fenv.decay: The length of the sweep. Shorter is a "bip", longer is a "bwow".
context.filter.cutoff: Where the sweep comes to rest.
context.filter.kbd: Ordinary cutoff tracking. It is separate from the cable, which tracks resonance.
context.mode.retrig: Gives every stab its own sweep, even with overlapping fingers.

tweaks.hear: At 1 the point where the squelch begins moves up the keyboard, and only the top notes of the riff ring. At 6 the high G goes past the whistling point and squeals, and the low G has a little resonance too.
Every stab comes to rest brighter, so the low ones lose their thump and the difference between low and high is mostly in the ring.
The sweep slows to nearly half a second, and on the high notes you can follow the resonant peak sliding down.
Without the octave below, the stabs are lighter and the resonance stands out more.

sounds.name: Rubbery Squelch Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of George Clinton — "Atomic Dog"
sounds.blurb: Fat, elastic bass that says "bwow" on each note and slurs between overlapping ones.
sounds.how: The rubbery quality comes from three settings working together. A lot of resonance turns the filter sweep into a vowel. A filter ATTACK of about 20 ms means the sweep rises before it falls, so the note says "bwow" and not "dow". AUTO glide slides the pitch only when two keys overlap, and because RETRIG is off those overlapped notes also skip the "bwow", so they sound stretched out of the note before. A saw with a square wave an octave below keeps the low end solid underneath the resonance.

steps.title: Saw on top, square an octave below
steps.why:
A saw with a square an octave below gives the bass bite on top and a solid low end underneath. Resonance thins out the bottom of a sound, and the low square puts it back.
- Osc A sawtooth, OCTAVE 1: the bright part, an octave below the starting pitch. Pulse and SYNC off, FREQUENCY 0.
- Osc B pulse, PULSE WIDTH 5, OCTAVE 0: a square wave an octave below A, hollow and round, working as a sub. Low frequency at NORMAL and keyboard on, in tune.
- OSC A 8, OSC B 6, NOISE/EXT 0: the saw leads, the square sits just under it.
- Listen for: a big, buzzy bass note. Turn OSC B to 0 and the bottom octave drops away.

steps.title: Low cutoff, plenty of resonance
steps.why:
A low cutoff with plenty of resonance sets up the vowel. The Pro-1’s filter is a 24 dB low-pass, so this low it passes little more than the fundamentals.
- CUTOFF 2.8 (about 140 Hz): a very dark resting point.
- RESONANCE 6: a strong peak at the cutoff. Below about 4 the bass would be just a bright pluck; towards 9 it starts to whistle.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5: half tracking, as the synth starts.
- Listen for: with no envelope yet, a dull hum with a nasal ring.

steps.title: A sweep that rises before it falls
steps.why:
The filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), makes the sweep rise before it falls, so the note says "bwow" and not "dow".
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 5.5: about 4.4 octaves of lift at the top of the sweep.
- ATTACK 2.8 (19 ms): short, but long enough to hear the filter open: the "b". At 0 the filter jumps open and the note has a hard front.
- DECAY 5.4 (250 ms), SUSTAIN 1.5: the "wow", closing over about a quarter of a second to a low level. RELEASE 41 ms.
- Listen for: set ATTACK to 0 and back to 2.8 to hear "dow" turn into "bwow".

steps.title: Plain bass volume
steps.why:
A plain loudness envelope. The filter does the shaping, so the volume just needs to hit and hold.
- ATTACK 0: full level at once.
- DECAY 5.5 (270 ms), SUSTAIN 7: a slight drop after the front, then held notes keep most of their weight in the low end.
- RELEASE 3 (34 ms): a quick stop when you let go, keeping the line tight.
- Listen for: even, solid notes under the squelch.

steps.title: AUTO glide, RETRIG off
steps.why:
Glide, or portamento, and the trigger mode give the rubbery slur between notes.
- RATE 2.5 (190 ms): a slide of about a fifth of a second.
- Glide mode AUTO: slides only when you press a new key while still holding the last one, what other synths call legato or fingered glide.
- Retrigger off: overlapping notes do not restart the sweep either, so they sound stretched out of the note before.
- Listen for: in the riff two pairs of notes overlap. Those bend up or down out of the one before with no new "bwow"; the detached notes each get their own.

context.filter.res: Turns the sweep into a vowel. Below about 4 the bass is just a bright pluck.
context.fenv.attack: The "b" of "bwow". At 0 the filter jumps open and the note has a hard front.
context.fenv.decay: How long the "wow" takes to close.
context.filter.env: How far the filter opens at the top of the sweep.
context.mix.oscB: The square wave an octave below. It keeps the low end full while the resonance does its work.
context.mode.retrig: Off, so overlapping notes do not restart the sweep. That is what makes them sound stretched.

tweaks.hear: "Dow", then "bwow", then at 4.5 a slower "mwow" that lags behind the beat.
From a plain plucked bass to a thin, whistling squelch. Above 7 the low end starts to empty out.
The slurs between overlapping notes take over half a second and sound lazy and slurred.
Every note now gets its own "bwow", including the slurred ones. Tighter, and less elastic.

sounds.name: Bubbling Second-LFO Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Parliament — "Flash Light"-era P-Funk synth bass
sounds.blurb: Resonant bass whose tone bubbles up and down about six times a second while each note sounds.
sounds.how: Bernie Worrell played the synth bass on "Flash Light" on Minimoogs, working the filter as he went. This patch gets a similar constantly moving filter from the Pro-1’s own trick: Oscillator B is switched to LO FREQ, which drops it far below hearing and turns it into a second LFO. Its triangle is sent to the cutoff of a resonant filter, so the tone bubbles while the note holds. The real LFO is left free, so you can still use it for wheel vibrato or REPEAT.

steps.title: One bright oscillator
steps.why:
One bright oscillator for the bass, because Oscillator B is about to become a modulator.
- Osc A saw + pulse, PULSE WIDTH 5: saw and square added together, bright with a hollow body. OCTAVE 1 puts it in bass range; FREQUENCY 0, SYNC off.
- OSC A 8, OSC B 0, NOISE/EXT 0: only Oscillator A is heard. In low frequency mode Oscillator B would only add clicks.
- Listen for: a plain, buzzy bass note with no movement.

steps.title: Resonant bass filter
steps.why:
A resonant low-pass filter for the bubble to move. The Pro-1’s is 24 dB per octave, keeping the lows and cutting the highs steeply.
- CUTOFF 4.4 (about 420 Hz): the centre of the bubble. Lower it and the bottom of each swing will close the filter almost completely.
- RESONANCE 5.5: a strong peak that will make the swing audible as a moving vowel.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 3: the filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), gives each note a bright front with ATTACK 0, DECAY 170 ms and SUSTAIN 3. KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5.
- Listen for: an ordinary resonant bass that sits still once the front has passed.

steps.title: Turn Oscillator B into a 6 Hz LFO
steps.why:
Oscillator B becomes a second LFO (low-frequency oscillator). LO FREQ drops it far below hearing, and the real LFO stays free for wheel vibrato or REPEAT.
- Osc B LO FREQ, keyboard off: below hearing, and not following the keys, so every note bubbles at the same speed.
- Osc B triangle only: moves the filter smoothly up and down. A saw would ramp and a pulse would jump.
- OCTAVE 2, FREQUENCY −0.7: at 0 it runs at about 8 Hz, and −0.7 brings it down to about 6 Hz. One panel unit is about seven semitones, so small moves change the speed a lot.
- Listen for: nothing yet. It is not routed anywhere.

steps.title: Send it to the filter
steps.why:
The modulation section sends Oscillator B to the cutoff, and the bass starts to bubble.
- AMOUNT OSC B 5.5: the cutoff swings about an octave and a half either side of where the envelope leaves it. Less is a gentle wobble; more opens and closes it fully.
- OSC B route DIRECT: onto the always-on bus, not the mod wheel bus (WHEEL).
- To FILTER DIR: the cutoff listens to the DIRECT bus.
- Listen for: hold a long note and hear "wub-wub-wub" under the pitch. Turn RESONANCE to 0 and the bubble fades to a faint change in brightness.

steps.title: Bass volume shape
steps.why:
A simple bass loudness envelope, so the bubble carries on for as long as the note is held.
- ATTACK 0: an instant start.
- DECAY 5.5 (270 ms), SUSTAIN 8: a small dip after the front, then the note holds and keeps bubbling.
- RELEASE 3.2 (41 ms): a quick stop when you let go.
- VOLUME 8: a resonant filter this low lets little of the oscillator through, so the output is raised.
- Listen for: long notes bubbling evenly from start to finish; short ones catching only one or two bubbles.

context.oscB.lo: Drops Oscillator B below hearing so that it works as an LFO.
context.oscB.freq: In LO FREQ this is the bubble speed. One panel unit is about seven semitones, so it covers a lot of ground quickly.
context.oscB.kbd: Off, so every note bubbles at the same speed.
context.oscB.tri: A triangle moves the filter smoothly up and down.
context.mod.oscBAmt: How far the cutoff swings: 5.5 is about an octave and a half each way.
context.filter.res: Makes the swing audible as a moving vowel. With no resonance the bubble is only a faint change in brightness.
context.mix.oscB: At 0. In LO FREQ Oscillator B is far too low to hear and would only add clicks.
context.filter.cutoff: The centre of the bubble. Lower it and the bottom of each swing closes the filter almost completely.

tweaks.hear: The bubble runs from about 3.5 Hz, a slow wobble, to about 10 Hz, a fast flutter.
Oscillator B now follows the keys, so the bubble halves in speed for each octave down. On the low C of the riff, two octaves below middle C, it runs at a quarter speed: about 1.5 Hz.

tweaks.try: Switch the triangle off and the pulse on
tweaks.hear: The cutoff jumps between two positions and the bubble becomes a hard "wa-wa-wa" trill.
At 0 the bass sits still. At 7.5 the swing is nearly three octaves each way and the note almost disappears at the bottom of each bubble.

sounds.name: Growling Funk Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Bernie Worrell — Parliament-Funkadelic synth leads
sounds.blurb: Nasal, rough-edged lead with a constant growl, and vibrato waiting on the mod wheel.
sounds.how: The growl is Oscillator B shaking the filter cutoff at audio rate. Oscillator B follows the keys an octave below the note, so it moves the cutoff up and down a couple of hundred times a second, in step with the pitch. You hear that as a rough, throaty edge that stays the same from note to note. It goes through the DIRECT bus, so it is always there. The LFO is set up for vibrato on the WHEEL bus, so it is silent until you push the mod wheel. One bus is fixed and the other is played by hand.

steps.title: A nasal lead tone, with Oscillator B an octave below
steps.why:
A nasal lead voice, with Oscillator B an octave below. A little of B goes into the mixer for body, but its main job comes in step 3, when it shakes the filter.
- Osc A saw + pulse, PULSE WIDTH 3.5 (36 %): both waves added. The narrowish pulse gives the saw a nasal, reedy edge. OCTAVE 2, FREQUENCY 0, SYNC off.
- Osc B sawtooth, OCTAVE 1: an octave below A, in tune, low frequency at NORMAL and keyboard on. Following the keys means the growl will keep the same character on every note.
- OSC A 8, OSC B 3, NOISE/EXT 0: A carries the lead; B adds a little weight underneath.
- Listen for: a bright, buzzy, slightly honky lead with no movement yet.

steps.title: Resonant filter, half closed
steps.why:
A resonant low-pass filter, half closed. The resonant peak is what Oscillator B will shake to make the growl.
- CUTOFF 4.8 (about 550 Hz), RESONANCE 5: a darkish tone with a strong, vocal peak. At 0 resonance the growl in the next step is much milder.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 6: a little more than half tracking, so high notes stay bright.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 3.5: the filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), brightens the front of each note. ATTACK 0, DECAY 270 ms, SUSTAIN 4, RELEASE 87 ms.
- Listen for: a "yow" at the start of each note, settling to a nasal hold.

steps.title: Oscillator B to the filter, DIRECT
steps.why:
Oscillator B now moves the cutoff at audio rate, a couple of hundred times a second, in step with the pitch. That is far too fast to hear as wobble; you hear it as a rough, throaty edge.
- AMOUNT OSC B 4.5: the cutoff is pushed an octave either way. More is a harsher, buzzier growl; less is a slight grit.
- OSC B route DIRECT: onto the always-on bus, so the growl is part of the basic sound and needs no wheel.
- To FILTER DIR: the filter listens to the DIRECT bus, which carries only Oscillator B.
- Listen for: the tone turning rough and throaty, the same on every note. Set AMOUNT OSC B to 0 and back to compare.

steps.title: Vibrato on the WHEEL bus
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) is set up for vibrato, but on the WHEEL bus, so it is silent until you push the mod wheel. One bus is fixed and the other is played by hand.
- LFO triangle only: a smooth up-and-down, the usual vibrato shape.
- LFO FREQUENCY 7 (5.07 Hz): about five wobbles a second, a fairly quick, singing vibrato.
- AMOUNT LFO 2: the most the wheel can bring in, about a semitone each way.
- LFO route WHEEL, To OSC A and B FREQ WH: both oscillators listen to the WHEEL bus, so they wobble together and stay in tune with each other.
- Listen for: nothing with the wheel down. Push it up on a held note and vibrato fades in.

steps.title: Lead volume and AUTO glide
steps.why:
Lead volume and a slide between overlapping notes.
- ATTACK 0, DECAY 170 ms, SUSTAIN 8: an immediate start with a slight dip, then held notes stay strong.
- RELEASE 4 (87 ms): a short tail so phrases do not sound chopped.
- Glide RATE 2.2 (150 ms), mode AUTO: glide (portamento) slides the pitch, and AUTO does it only when a new key is pressed while the last is still held.
- VOLUME 8.5: raised to make up for the level the resonance takes away.
- Listen for: in the riff the second note runs into the third, and that join slides; the detached notes jump.

context.mod.oscBAmt: The amount of growl. 4.5 moves the cutoff one octave each way.
context.mod.oscBRoute: DIRECT, so the growl is part of the basic sound and does not need the wheel.
context.mod.toFilter: Down at DIR, so the filter hears the DIRECT bus, which carries only Oscillator B.
context.oscB.octave: The pitch of the growl relative to the note. One octave below gives a throaty roughness.
context.oscB.kbd: On, so the growl keeps the same character on every note.
context.filter.res: The growl is the resonant peak being shaken. At 0 it is much milder.
context.mod.lfoRoute: WHEEL, so the vibrato is only heard as you push the mod wheel.
context.mod.lfoAmt: The most vibrato the wheel can bring in: about a semitone each way.

tweaks.hear: At 0 the lead is clean and nasal. At 4.5 it growls. At 6.5 the swing is two octaves each way and the tone breaks up into a rasp.

tweaks.try: Set Oscillator B to octave 2, then 0
tweaks.hear: At the same octave as the note the growl is tighter and brighter. Two octaves below, it slows to a purr you can almost count.
Oscillator B is no longer in tune with the note, so the growl turns clangy and different on every key.

tweaks.try: Flip OSC B ROUTE to WHEEL and FILTER to WH, then push the mod wheel
tweaks.hear: The growl now comes in with the wheel. The WHEEL bus is one mix, so Oscillator B also reaches both oscillators’ pitch along with the vibrato, and the result is rougher than the DIRECT version.

sounds.name: Unstable Metallic Tones
sounds.ref: In the style of Japan — "Ghosts"
sounds.blurb: Slow, clanging tones with no clear pitch, a different colour on every key and never quite still.
sounds.how: The Prophet-5 was one of the main synths on Japan’s "Tin Drum" album, and the Pro-1 has the same trick of using Oscillator B as a modulator. Here Oscillator B runs at audio rate, is taken off the keyboard so it stays at one fixed pitch, and is sent to both Oscillator A’s pitch and the filter. Modulating pitch that fast adds a cluster of new overtones that are not in tune with the note, which the ear hears as metal. Because Oscillator B does not move with the keys, the cluster is different on every key. A very slow LFO on the same bus stops anything from settling.

steps.title: One square wave to listen to
steps.why:
One square wave to listen to. Oscillator B comes out of the mixer: you will hear what it does to Oscillator A, not Oscillator B itself.
- Osc A pulse only, PULSE WIDTH 5: a plain square, hollow and simple. A clean starting point makes the metallic overtones easy to hear later. OCTAVE 2, FREQUENCY 0, SYNC off.
- OSC A 7, OSC B 0, NOISE/EXT 0: only Oscillator A is heard, slightly lower than usual to leave room for the added overtones.
- Listen for: a plain hollow tone with a clear pitch.

steps.title: Oscillator B: fixed pitch, triangle
steps.why:
Oscillator B is set up as a fixed-pitch modulator. It is still at audio rate, but no longer follows the keys.
- Osc B keyboard off: it sits near the E flat above middle C, about 315 Hz, whatever you play. That is why each key will sound different.
- Osc B triangle only: the smoothest modulator gives the clearest, most bell-like result. A saw would be harsher.
- OCTAVE 2, FREQUENCY 2.3 (+3.2 st): puts it between the notes of the scale, so it lines up with nothing. Every position gives a different set of clangs. Low frequency stays at NORMAL.
- Listen for: nothing changes yet. Oscillator B is out of the mixer and not routed.

steps.title: Oscillator B to pitch and filter
steps.why:
Oscillator B now throws Oscillator A’s pitch up and down 315 times a second. At that speed it is FM (frequency modulation): new overtones appear that are not in tune with the note, and the ear hears metal.
- AMOUNT OSC B 5.5: about seven semitones each way. More means more metal and less note.
- OSC B route DIRECT: onto the always-on bus.
- To OSC A FREQ DIR, To FILTER DIR: both take the DIRECT bus. The cutoff is shaken at 315 Hz too, which roughens the ring.
- Listen for: play a few different keys. Each has its own clang, and none has a clear pitch.

steps.title: A very slow LFO on the same bus
steps.why:
A very slow LFO (low-frequency oscillator) joins Oscillator B on the DIRECT bus, so nothing ever settles.
- LFO triangle only: a smooth drift, no jumps.
- LFO FREQUENCY 1.6 (0.21 Hz): one cycle about every five seconds.
- AMOUNT LFO 2, route DIRECT: it drifts Oscillator A about a semitone each way and nudges the cutoff, because both destinations already listen to that bus.
- Listen for: hold a note. As Oscillator A drifts against the fixed Oscillator B, the overtones slide past each other and the clang slowly changes colour.

steps.title: A ringing filter that opens slowly
steps.why:
A resonant filter picks out one band of the clang and makes it ring, and a slow envelope lets each note bloom.
- CUTOFF 5.2 (about 730 Hz), RESONANCE 6: a strong peak that rings on part of the cluster. Sweep CUTOFF to choose which part.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 2: the filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), lifts the cutoff a little on each note.
- ATTACK 5 (110 ms): the brightness arrives just after the note, a small bloom rather than a hit.
- DECAY 7 (1.0 s), SUSTAIN 4: with RELEASE 6 (570 ms), a slow settle and a slow close. KEYBOARD AMOUNT stays at 5.
- Listen for: each note opening slightly after it starts, with a ringing band on top.

steps.title: Soft start, long fade
steps.why:
The loudness envelope gives each tone a soft start and a long fade, so tones overlap like struck metal dying away.
- ATTACK 4.5 (76 ms): a soft front, no click.
- DECAY 7.5 (1.6 s), SUSTAIN 5: a slow fall to half level while the key is held.
- RELEASE 6.6 (1.0 s): about a second of tail after you let go, so each tone hangs on into the next.
- Listen for: slow notes blurring together, with the clang still shifting as each one fades.

context.oscB.kbd: Off. The modulator stays put while the note moves, so the relationship between them, and with it the tone, changes on every key.
context.oscB.freq: Tunes the fixed modulator. Every position gives a different set of clangs.
context.mod.oscBAmt: How far Oscillator B throws Oscillator A’s pitch. More means more metal and less note.
context.mod.lfoAmt: The slow drift that keeps the tone from settling.
context.lfo.rate: The speed of the drift: one cycle every five seconds.
context.mod.toFilter: The filter takes the same bus, so the cutoff is shaken at 315 Hz too, which roughens the ring.
context.filter.res: Makes one band of the clang ring out.
context.mix.oscB: At 0. Bring it up and you hear the fixed 315 Hz tone as a drone under every note.

tweaks.hear: The modulator now follows the keys, so every note has the same clang, moved up or down. It is more playable and less strange.
A plain square wave, then a growl, then bells, then at 8 a dense noise-like clang with no pitch left.

tweaks.try: Turn slowly while holding a note
tweaks.hear: The overtones fan in and out. Now and then they line up into something nearly musical, then fall apart again.

tweaks.try: Switch the triangle off and the saw on
tweaks.hear: A harsher modulator: the bell-like tone turns into a buzzing, ripping one.

sounds.name: Shifting Pulse Sequencer Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Japan — "Quiet Life"
sounds.blurb: Driving sixteenth-note bass whose tone is slightly different on every step.
sounds.how: A line of equal sixteenth notes gets dull quickly if every step sounds the same. Here the LFO moves Oscillator A’s pulse width at about 2.5 Hz. That speed is not tied to the tempo, so each step catches the pulse at a different width: one step is hollow, the next thin and nasal. A square wave from Oscillator B an octave down holds the low end steady underneath. On the hardware you would record the notes into the sequencer; here the riff player under the keyboard plays them.

steps.title: Pulse on top, square an octave below
steps.why:
A pulse on top and a square an octave below. Both are square waves for now, so the line is hollow and even.
- Osc A pulse, PULSE WIDTH 5, OCTAVE 1: a square in bass range. Its width will be moved in step 5. Saw and SYNC off, FREQUENCY 0.
- Osc B pulse, PULSE WIDTH 5, OCTAVE 0: a square an octave below. It is not modulated, so the low end stays steady. Low frequency at NORMAL, keyboard on.
- OSC A 8, OSC B 5, NOISE/EXT 0: A leads, the sub square sits underneath.
- Listen for: a round, hollow bass with a solid bottom.

steps.title: A short, resonant pluck on each step
steps.why:
A short, resonant pluck on each step. The Pro-1’s filter is a 24 dB low-pass, and the filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), snaps it open at the start of every note.
- CUTOFF 4 (about 320 Hz), RESONANCE 4: dark between notes, with a nasal peak.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 4.5: opens about three and a half octaves at the front.
- DECAY 4.2 (85 ms), SUSTAIN 1: with ATTACK 0 and RELEASE 28 ms, mostly closed again within 85 ms, so each step gets a quick bright front.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 6: extra tracking makes the higher steps a little brighter.
- Listen for: a short "dow" on each note of the riff.

steps.title: Clipped volume shape
steps.why:
A clipped loudness envelope keeps sixteenth notes separate.
- ATTACK 0: hits straight away, on the beat.
- DECAY 4.8 (140 ms), SUSTAIN 5: a quick drop to half level, so each step has a punchy front.
- RELEASE 2.6 (23 ms): each note stops before the next begins.
- Listen for: clear gaps between the sixteenths, which gives the line its drive.

steps.title: LFO at a speed unrelated to the tempo
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) is set to a speed that has nothing to do with the tempo. It will move the pulse width, so every step catches it at a different point.
- LFO triangle only: a smooth sweep back and forth.
- LFO FREQUENCY 5.8 (2.49 Hz): the sixteenths run at about 8.4 a second, so the LFO is at a different point in its cycle on every step.
- Listen for: nothing changes yet, because the LFO is not routed anywhere.

steps.title: Route it to Oscillator A’s pulse width
steps.why:
Routing the LFO to Oscillator A’s pulse width gives PWM (pulse-width modulation): the pulse keeps changing between hollow and thin.
- AMOUNT LFO 6.5: about 19 % each way, so the width swings between about 31 % and 69 %. More gives stronger changes; less, subtler ones.
- LFO route DIRECT: onto the always-on bus.
- To OSC A PW DIR: Oscillator A’s pulse width listens to that bus.
- Listen for: a run of the same note. One step is hollow, the next thin and nasal; no two sound quite the same, while the low square stays steady underneath.

context.oscA.pw: The centre of the swing. At 5 the width moves evenly either side of square.
context.mod.lfoAmt: How far the width swings: 6.5 is about 19 % each way.
context.lfo.rate: How quickly the tone changes from step to step. It is deliberately not in time with the notes.
context.mod.toAPw: Connects the DIRECT bus (carrying the LFO) to Oscillator A’s pulse width.
context.mix.oscB: The steady square an octave down. It is not modulated, so the low end does not shift with the tone.
context.fenv.decay: The length of the bright front of each step.
context.aenv.release: Very short, to keep the sixteenth notes apart.

tweaks.hear: At 0 every step has the same hollow tone. At 6.5 the tone shifts from step to step.
At about half a cycle a second the change is a slow sweep across each bar, not a step-to-step difference.
The swing now runs from about 8 % to 45 %, so some steps come out thin and buzzy and none is fully hollow.

tweaks.try: Open slowly from 3 to 6 while the riff loops
tweaks.hear: The line builds from a muted throb to a bright, buzzing sequence.

sounds.name: Octave-Stacked Riff Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Eurythmics — "Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This)"
sounds.blurb: Buzzy, sustained bass with its own octave on top, for riffs that carry a whole song.
sounds.how: Two saws tuned an octave apart play every note as a stacked pair, so one line does the work of a bass and a riff at once. The filter is left half open, which keeps the buzz of the saws, and the volume envelope holds each note at nearly full level for as long as the key is down. That sustained, even level is what separates this from a plucked bass: the rhythm comes from note lengths, not from the envelope.

steps.title: Two saws an octave apart
steps.why:
Two saws an octave apart play every note as a stacked pair, so one line does the work of a bass and a riff at once.
- Osc A sawtooth, OCTAVE 1: the bass note, bright and buzzy. Pulse and SYNC off, FREQUENCY 0.
- Osc B sawtooth, OCTAVE 2: the stacked octave above. Triangle and pulse off; low frequency at NORMAL, keyboard on.
- Osc B FREQUENCY 0.1 (+0.1 st): a very small detune. At exactly 0 the two saws can lock into one static tone.
- Listen for: only the lower saw is in the mixer so far. The octave comes in next.

steps.title: Low octave in front
steps.why:
The mixer balance decides how much of the upper octave you hear.
- OSC A 8: the low octave stays in front for weight.
- OSC B 5.5: the upper saw a little behind.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: bring OSC B up from 0 and notice the point where the bass turns into a riff. Stop there or go past it to taste.

steps.title: Half-open filter
steps.why:
A half-open low-pass filter keeps the buzz of the saws. The filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), adds a slightly brighter front.
- CUTOFF 5 (about 630 Hz), RESONANCE 2: half open with a little peak. Lower it for a rounder, more ordinary bass; raise it for more buzz.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 6: slightly more than half tracking, so higher notes stay bright.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 3 with ATTACK 0, DECAY 170 ms: a small bright front on each note.
- SUSTAIN 4, RELEASE 41 ms: keeps held notes buzzy after the front has passed.
- Listen for: a small push at the start of each note, then a steady buzzy tone.

steps.title: Held, even volume
steps.why:
Held, even volume. The rhythm comes from note lengths, not from the envelope.
- ATTACK 0: full level at once.
- DECAY 5.5 (270 ms), SUSTAIN 8: a slight dip after the front, then notes hold nearly full level for as long as the key is down.
- RELEASE 3 (34 ms): short notes stop cleanly.
- Listen for: long notes staying loud to the end. That sustained, even level is what separates this from a plucked bass.

context.oscB.octave: One octave above Oscillator A. This is the stacked octave that makes the line read as a riff.
context.mix.oscB: How much of the upper octave you hear.
context.oscB.freq: A very small detune. At exactly 0 the two saws can lock into one static tone.
context.filter.cutoff: Half open. Lower it for a rounder, more ordinary bass; raise it for more buzz.
context.fenv.sustain: Keeps held notes bright after the front has passed.
context.aenv.sustain: High, so notes hold their level for as long as the key is down.

tweaks.hear: At 0 it is a plain saw bass. At 5.5 the octave makes it a riff. At 8 the upper octave starts to lead.
From a dark, rounded bass to a fully open buzz.

tweaks.try: Switch Oscillator A’s pulse on as well
tweaks.hear: The low octave gets thicker and more hollow underneath the buzz.
Notes now fall away after the start, and the riff turns into a plucked line.

sounds.name: LFO-Swept Sync Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Thomas Dolby — "She Blinded Me with Science"
sounds.blurb: Quirky, talkative lead whose tone goes "wee-oo-wee-oo" three times a second by itself.
sounds.how: With SYNC on, Oscillator A is restarted by Oscillator B on every cycle, so Oscillator B fixes the pitch and Oscillator A’s own frequency only changes the tone. Most sync patches sweep that frequency once per note with an envelope. This one hands the job to the LFO, so the vowel-like sweep repeats for as long as a note is held. The LFO runs freely and does not restart with each key, so every note catches the sweep at a different point and no two short notes sound alike.

steps.title: Sync Oscillator A to Oscillator B
steps.why:
Hard sync ties Oscillator A to Oscillator B. On the Pro-1 it is A that gets restarted every time B completes a cycle, the reverse of most synths, so B sets the pitch and A’s frequency only changes the tone.
- Sync on: the heart of the sound.
- Osc B sawtooth, OCTAVE 2, FREQUENCY 0: sets the pitch you hear. Low frequency at NORMAL, keyboard on.
- Osc A sawtooth, OCTAVE 3: an octave above B. This is the centre of the sweep: higher is thinner and more nasal. Pulse off, FREQUENCY 0.
- Listen for: turn Oscillator A’s FREQUENCY by hand. The note stays put and the tone changes, from hollow to thin and nasal.

steps.title: Mostly the synced oscillator
steps.why:
Mostly the synced oscillator, with a little plain saw underneath.
- OSC A 8: carries the sound.
- OSC B 3: a little of Oscillator B’s plain saw for body. It steadies the pitch while the sync tone moves.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: the synced tone in front with a smooth saw behind. Turn OSC B to 0 and the lead gets thinner.

steps.title: LFO at about 3 Hz
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) will turn Oscillator A’s frequency for you, three times a second.
- LFO triangle only: a smooth up-and-down, so the sweep goes both ways evenly.
- LFO FREQUENCY 6.1 (2.97 Hz): about three cycles a second, how fast the tone opens and closes.
- Listen for: nothing changes yet, because the LFO is not routed anywhere.

steps.title: Let the LFO turn Oscillator A’s frequency for you
steps.why:
The LFO goes to Oscillator A’s frequency, so the sync sweep repeats for as long as a note is held.
- AMOUNT LFO 6: about eight and a half semitones either side of A’s setting. A always stays above B, which is what sync needs.
- LFO route DIRECT: onto the always-on bus.
- To OSC A FREQ DIR: Oscillator A’s pitch listens to the DIRECT bus.
- Listen for: hold a note and hear the tone open and close like a mouth, "wee-oo-wee-oo", with the pitch steady. The LFO runs freely, so short notes each catch it at a different point.

steps.title: Open filter, plain volume
steps.why:
The sync sweep is the tone control here, so the filter stays open and out of the way.
- CUTOFF 7 (2.5 kHz), RESONANCE 2: the low-pass filter wide open, so the sweep is not hidden.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 1.5: the filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), adds only a touch of brightness at the front. KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5; filter ATTACK 0, DECAY 170 ms, SUSTAIN 5, RELEASE 87 ms.
- Loudness ATTACK 0, SUSTAIN 8, RELEASE 72 ms: an immediate start, strong held level and a short tail.
- Retrigger on: fast repeated notes each restart the envelopes and start cleanly.
- Listen for: plain, clean notes with the sync sweep doing all the talking.

context.oscA.sync: The heart of the sound. Switch it off and the LFO just bends Oscillator A’s pitch up and down like a siren.
context.oscA.octave: An octave above Oscillator B. This is the centre of the sweep: higher is thinner and more nasal.
context.oscA.freq: With SYNC on this is a tone control. It shifts the centre of the sweep.
context.mod.lfoAmt: The width of the sweep: 6 is about eight and a half semitones each way.
context.lfo.rate: How fast the tone opens and closes.
context.mod.toAFreq: Connects the DIRECT bus (carrying the LFO) to Oscillator A’s frequency.
context.mix.oscB: A little plain saw under the synced oscillator, for body.
context.filter.cutoff: Open, so that the sync sweep is not hidden.

tweaks.try: Switch the triangle off and the saw on
tweaks.hear: The tone now climbs and snaps back, three times a second: "zip, zip, zip" in place of "wee-oo".
At 4 one slow sweep lasts more than a second. At 8.5 it is a 12 Hz flutter, like a rolled "r".
A wider sweep of about an octave each way. At the bottom of each sweep Oscillator A drops to Oscillator B’s pitch and the tone goes briefly plain.

tweaks.try: Flip LFO ROUTE to WHEEL and OSC A FREQ to WH, then move the mod wheel
tweaks.hear: The wheel now sets the width of the sweep, from none to full.

sounds.name: Abrasive Sweeping Drone
sounds.ref: In the style of Cabaret Voltaire and The Human League — "The Dignity of Labour"
sounds.blurb: A harsh, grinding drone that plays by itself and slowly opens and closes, faster while a key is held.
sounds.how: DRONE holds the gate open, so the synth sounds with no key down. The grinding comes from Oscillator B: taken off the keyboard and parked at about 50 Hz, it throws Oscillator A’s pitch ten semitones either way fifty times a second. That uses up the DIRECT bus, and anything else put on that bus would reach Oscillator A’s pitch as well. So the slow filter sweep goes round the matrix by cable: LFO OUT into CUTOFF CV. A second cable, GATE into LFO CV, turns the keyboard into a speed control for the sweep.

steps.title: Hold the gate open
steps.why:
DRONE holds the gate open, the signal that normally says a key is down, so the synth keeps sounding with no key held. Keys now only choose the pitch.
- Drone on, Repeat off: both envelopes rise to their sustain levels and stay there. Switch DRONE off to stop the sound.
- Loudness ATTACK 6 (260 ms), SUSTAIN 8: the drone fades in over about a quarter of a second and then holds just under full level. SUSTAIN is now the drone’s volume.
- Filter SUSTAIN 5: where the filter envelope parks. With no ENVELOPE AMOUNT it has no effect yet.
- Listen for: a plain saw sounding on its own. Press a key to change its pitch; letting go does not stop it.

steps.title: A thick low tone with some noise
steps.why:
A thick low tone, with Oscillator B parked at a fixed low pitch as a hum and a little noise on top.
- Osc A saw + pulse, OCTAVE 1: PULSE WIDTH 4 (41 %), both waves added for a buzzy, reedy low note. FREQUENCY 0, SYNC off.
- Osc B sawtooth, OCTAVE 0, keyboard off: it no longer follows the keys, so it stays put whichever note Oscillator A plays. Low frequency at NORMAL.
- Osc B FREQUENCY −3.3 (−4.6 st): parks it at about 50 Hz. Small moves here change the grind a lot later.
- OSC A 8, OSC B 4, NOISE/EXT 2.5: A in front, the fixed hum under it, and a little white noise hiss for the filter to sweep later.
- Listen for: a steady low drone with a hum that does not move when you change key.

steps.title: Oscillator B grinds Oscillator A’s pitch
steps.why:
Oscillator B now grinds Oscillator A’s pitch. Using one oscillator to move another’s pitch is FM (frequency modulation); at 50 Hz it sits between a rattle and a new tone.
- AMOUNT OSC B 6.5: Oscillator A is pushed about ten semitones each way, 50 times a second. More is harsher; less is a buzzing vibrato.
- OSC B route DIRECT: onto the always-on bus. That uses up the DIRECT bus: anything else put on it would reach Oscillator A’s pitch too.
- To OSC A FREQ DIR: Oscillator A’s pitch listens to the DIRECT bus.
- Listen for: the steady low tone turning into a grinding one, slow enough to hear as a rattle and fast enough to add a mass of overtones.

steps.title: Resonant filter, no envelope
steps.why:
A resonant low-pass filter with no envelope. In DRONE mode the envelope never moves, so the movement will come from a cable.
- CUTOFF 6 (about 1.3 kHz): fairly open for now. It will be the middle of the sweep.
- RESONANCE 5: a strong peak, so the sweep will have a moving point you can follow.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 0: the envelope sits still at its sustain, so any amount would only shift the cutoff by a fixed step.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 3: less tracking than the starting 5, so the key you choose changes the brightness only a little.
- Listen for: the grind losing some of its top and gaining a slight ring.

steps.title: Patch LFO OUT into CUTOFF CV
steps.why:
The slow sweep goes round the matrix by cable. The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) has an output jack, and CUTOFF CV adds a control voltage to the CUTOFF knob.
- LFO triangle, FREQUENCY 1.2 (0.16 Hz): one smooth cycle about every six seconds. Saw and pulse off.
- Cable LFO OUT → CUTOFF CV: the matrix could send the LFO to the filter only through a bus, and the DIRECT bus would hand the same sweep to Oscillator A’s pitch. The cable gives the LFO its own path.
- Depth: fixed at five octaves each way. The drone sinks to a rumble at about 40 Hz and then opens completely. The CUTOFF knob sets the middle of the sweep; lower it and the drone spends more time closed.
- Listen for: the grind and the noise closing and opening together over six seconds.

steps.title: Patch GATE into LFO CV
steps.why:
A second cable turns the keyboard into a speed control for the sweep. GATE sends a voltage while a key is down, and LFO CV adds a voltage to the LFO’s speed.
- Cable GATE → LFO CV: DRONE keeps the envelopes open, but the GATE jack still follows the keys. The jack has a fixed depth of three octaves of speed, so while a key is down the LFO runs eight times faster: about 1.3 Hz in place of one sweep every six seconds.
- Listen for: hold a key and the sweep speeds up into a churning wobble; let go and it slows back to a crawl. Play and release to stir the drone up and let it settle.

context.mode.drone: Keeps the sound going with no key held. Switch it off to stop the drone.
context.oscB.kbd: Off, so the grinding stays at 50 Hz whichever note Oscillator A is playing.
context.oscB.freq: The speed of the grind. Small moves change its character a lot.
context.mod.oscBAmt: How far Oscillator B throws Oscillator A’s pitch: 6.5 is about ten semitones each way.
context.mix.noise: A little hiss that the filter sweep opens and closes along with everything else.
context.filter.cutoff: The middle of the ten-octave sweep supplied by the LFO cable. Lower it and the drone spends more of each cycle closed down.
context.filter.res: Gives the sweep a moving peak you can follow.
context.lfo.rate: The resting speed of the sweep. The GATE cable multiplies it by eight while a key is held.
context.filter.env: At 0. In DRONE mode the envelope sits still, so it would only shift the cutoff by a fixed amount.

tweaks.hear: The grind runs from about 44 Hz, a loose rattle, up to 65 Hz, a tighter buzz. The overtones rearrange themselves as you go.
At 0 it is a steady low chord of hum and note. At 9 the swing is nearly twenty semitones each way and the pitch is lost in the grinding.

tweaks.try: Switch the triangle off and the pulse on
tweaks.hear: The filter slams between shut and open with no sweep in between. Hold a key to make it chop faster.
Oscillator A is locked to the 50 Hz of Oscillator B, so the keys stop changing the pitch and the pitch modulation turns into a snarling change of tone.

sounds.name: Key-Accented Interlocking Pluck
sounds.ref: In the style of King Crimson — "Discipline"
sounds.blurb: Short pluck that is muted on low notes and bright on high ones, for fast repeating patterns.
sounds.how: On "Discipline" the repeating patterns are played by two electric guitars, with picked notes that run from damped to ringing. This patch gives a synth pluck the same spread, and ties it to pitch. KEYBOARD AMOUNT is turned to 0 and a cable from KYBD CV to CUTOFF CV takes over, tracking five times more steeply than the knob can. Notes below middle C come out muted and notes above it bright. The riff is a five-note cell played in sixteenth notes, so it slips against the bar and the bright notes fall in a different place each time round.

steps.title: A narrow pulse with a triangle above
steps.why:
A narrow pulse with a quiet triangle above it gives a plucked-string sort of tone.
- Osc A pulse, PULSE WIDTH 3 (31 %): fairly narrow, so the tone is thin and string-like. Saw off, OCTAVE 2, FREQUENCY 0, SYNC off.
- Osc B triangle, OCTAVE 3: an octave higher and smooth, to give the top of each note a rounder ring. Saw and pulse off; low frequency at NORMAL, keyboard on, in tune.
- OSC A 8, OSC B 4, NOISE/EXT 0: the pulse leads and the triangle sits quietly above. You will hear it mostly on the bright notes.
- Listen for: a thin, hollow tone with a faint high shine.

steps.title: Pluck filter with keyboard tracking off
steps.why:
A pluck filter with its keyboard tracking turned off, so the cable in step 5 can take over. The Pro-1’s filter is a 24 dB low-pass, and the filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), flicks it open on each note.
- CUTOFF 4.2 (about 360 Hz), RESONANCE 3: dark at rest, with a small peak for a bit of bite.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 4: opens just over three octaves at the front: the size of the pluck.
- DECAY 4.4 (100 ms), SUSTAIN 0.5: with ATTACK 0 and RELEASE 34 ms, closed again within 100 ms.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 0: every note has the same cutoff, so the cable will be the only key tracking.
- Listen for: the high notes of the riff sounding duller than the low ones.

steps.title: Notes that die away by themselves
steps.why:
Notes that die away by themselves, like a picked string.
- ATTACK 0: instant, so the pluck lands on the beat.
- DECAY 5.2 (210 ms), SUSTAIN 0: the whole note is over in about a fifth of a second, however long the key is held.
- RELEASE 3.5 (54 ms): a short tail after the key comes up.
- VOLUME 8.5: raised because plucked notes sound quieter than held ones.
- Listen for: short, separate plucks with a clear gap between them.

steps.title: Retrigger every note
steps.why:
A fast pattern is played with overlapping fingers, and RETRIG makes sure each key still gets a pluck.
- Retrigger on (RETRIG): every key press restarts both envelopes. In NORMAL an overlapped note would change pitch without a new pluck, and with SUSTAIN at 0 it might hardly sound.
- Listen for: every note of the riff clicking evenly, however the notes overlap.

steps.title: Patch KYBD CV into CUTOFF CV
steps.why:
The cable ties brightness to pitch. KYBD CV sends the keyboard pitch as a control voltage, and CUTOFF CV adds a voltage to the CUTOFF knob.
- Cable KYBD CV → CUTOFF CV: the voltage is zero at middle C, and the jack moves the cutoff five octaves for each octave played. KEYBOARD AMOUNT at 10 would give only one. Each semitone now moves the cutoff nearly half an octave.
- Across the riff: the A below middle C rests at about 150 Hz and sounds damped; the G above middle C rests at about 2.7 kHz and rings.
- CUTOFF knob: now sets the cutoff at middle C, so it moves the whole muted-to-bright spread up or down.
- Listen for: the five-note cell slipping against the bar, with the bright notes landing in a different place each time round.

context.filter.kbd: At 0, so the cable is the only key tracking and its effect is easy to hear.
context.filter.cutoff: The cutoff at middle C. The cable pivots around that note, so this knob moves the whole muted-to-bright spread up or down.
context.filter.env: The size of the pluck on every note.
context.fenv.decay: The length of the bright front of each note.
context.aenv.decay: The length of the whole note.
context.oscA.pw: A fairly narrow pulse, for a string-like tone.
context.mix.oscB: The triangle an octave up. You hear it mostly on the bright notes.
context.out.volume: Raised to make up for the short notes.

tweaks.hear: At 3 only the top notes of the cell ring and the rest are thuds. At 5.5 everything is bright except the lowest note.
Knob and cable add up to six octaves of cutoff per octave played. The spread from muted to bright gets a little steeper still.
The bright notes gain a hard, wiry ping and the muted ones a rounded knock.
Every note becomes a dry tick and the pattern sounds more like tuned percussion.

sounds.name: Mellow Horn Line
sounds.ref: In the style of Soft Cell — "Say Hello, Wave Goodbye"
sounds.blurb: Soft, rounded horn-like lead for slow melodies, with a light vibrato.
sounds.how: This is synth brass with the blare taken out. The tone is mostly Oscillator B’s triangle with a quieter saw from Oscillator A for a little buzz. The filter starts nearly closed and the envelope opens it over about 115 ms, which is slow enough to hear as the note swelling, the way a softly blown horn does.
