It never opens far, so the sound stays round. A shallow 5 Hz vibrato on both oscillators and AUTO glide on overlapping notes make a slow line sing.

steps.title: Triangle with a little saw
steps.why:
Synth brass with the blare taken out starts from a soft wave: mostly Oscillator B’s triangle, with a quieter saw from Oscillator A for a little buzz.
- Osc B triangle only: few overtones, which keeps the sound soft. Saw and pulse off.
- Osc A sawtooth: the buzz that makes it read as brass. Pulse and SYNC off.
- Both OCTAVE 2, FREQUENCY 0: same octave and tuning, so the two fuse into one tone. Oscillator B at low frequency NORMAL, keyboard on.
- Listen for: only the saw is in the mixer so far. The triangle comes in next.

steps.title: Triangle in front
steps.why:
The triangle goes in front, with the saw behind it.
- OSC B 8: most of the tone, round and soft.
- OSC A 6: the saw supplies the buzz that the filter will let through as the note swells. At 0 the sound is closer to a flute.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: turn OSC A down and up to hear the sound move between flute and horn.

steps.title: A filter that swells open
steps.why:
A filter that swells open gives the horn its breath. The filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), opens the low-pass filter slowly enough to hear, like a softly blown note.
- CUTOFF 3.4 (about 210 Hz), RESONANCE 0.5: nearly closed, with almost no peak, so it stays round.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 4.5: about three and a half octaves at the top of the swell. Keep it moderate or the sound starts to blare.
- ATTACK 5 (110 ms): the swell. Shorter is harder and more trumpet-like.
- DECAY 6 (420 ms), SUSTAIN 6, RELEASE 140 ms: eases back to a fairly bright held tone.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 6: slightly more than half tracking.
- Listen for: "hwaa" at the start of each note, then the tone easing back.

steps.title: Gentle volume shape
steps.why:
A gentle loudness shape, so notes arrive softly and end without a thud.
- ATTACK 3.5 (34 ms): slightly softened, so notes do not click. The volume arrives before the brightness does.
- DECAY 170 ms, SUSTAIN 9: held notes stay nearly full.
- RELEASE 4.8 (190 ms): a short fade after you let go, which joins slow phrases.
- Listen for: a soft front followed by the filter swell, the way a horn player’s breath builds.

steps.title: Shallow vibrato
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) adds a shallow vibrato to both oscillators, which makes a slow line sing.
- LFO triangle only: a smooth wobble. Saw and pulse off.
- LFO FREQUENCY 7 (5.07 Hz): about five cycles a second, a natural vibrato speed.
- AMOUNT LFO 1: about a quarter of a semitone each way. You feel it more than you hear it.
- LFO route DIRECT, To OSC A and B FREQ DIR: both oscillators take the always-on bus, so they move together and stay fused.
- Listen for: a faint shimmer on held notes. Turn AMOUNT LFO to 3 to hear the vibrato clearly, then bring it back.

steps.title: AUTO glide, RETRIG off
steps.why:
Glide, or portamento, slurs overlapping notes, and RETRIG off stops them swelling again.
- RATE 2 (120 ms): a quick slide.
- Glide mode AUTO: slides only when a new key goes down while the last is still held.
- Retrigger off: overlapping notes change pitch without restarting the envelopes, so they carry on from the last note’s level.
- Listen for: in the riff the second note runs into the third. That join is slurred, and every detached note gets its own swell.

context.oscB.tri: Most of the tone. The triangle is what keeps this soft.
context.mix.oscA: The saw. It adds the buzz that makes the sound read as brass; at 0 it is closer to a flute.
context.fenv.attack: The swell at the start of each note. Shorter is harder and more trumpet-like.
context.filter.env: How far the filter opens at the top of the swell. Keep it moderate or the sound starts to blare.
context.fenv.sustain: How bright a held note stays.
context.mod.lfoAmt: The depth of the vibrato: about a quarter of a semitone each way.
context.aenv.attack: Slightly softened, so notes do not click.

tweaks.hear: At 2 the note starts with a firm "da". At 5 it swells. At 6.5 the swell takes nearly 400 ms, like a player easing into a long note.
From a flute-like hoot to a buzzier, more trumpet-like tone.
The filter opens over five octaves and the mellow horn turns into bright synth brass.
The vibrato widens to a semitone each way and becomes an obvious, singer-like wobble.

sounds.name: Soft Rounded Electric-Piano Keys
sounds.ref: In the style of Radiohead — "Everything In Its Right Place"
sounds.blurb: Soft, rounded keyboard tone with a gentle knock at the front and a slow fade while the key is held.
sounds.how: An electric piano note is a soft thud followed by a nearly pure tone that fades. Oscillator B’s triangle gives the pure tone, and a quiet square wave from Oscillator A gives it a slightly hollow outline. The filter sits low and a small envelope opens it for about a third of a second, which is the thud. The volume envelope is set like a struck instrument: it falls slowly while the key is down instead of holding. The record used a Prophet-5 playing chords. The Pro-1 is one voice of that design, so it plays the same kind of tone one note at a time.

steps.title: Triangle with a square outline
steps.why:
An electric piano note is a soft thud followed by a nearly pure tone. Oscillator B’s triangle gives the pure tone, and a square wave from Oscillator A a hollow outline.
- Osc B triangle only: the softest shape on the panel. Saw and pulse off.
- Osc A pulse only, PULSE WIDTH 5: a square wave, hollow. Saw and SYNC off.
- Both OCTAVE 2, FREQUENCY 0: same octave, same tuning, so they fuse into one tone. Oscillator B at low frequency NORMAL, keyboard on.
- Listen for: only the square is in the mixer so far. The triangle comes in next.

steps.title: Mostly triangle
steps.why:
Mostly triangle, with the square as outline.
- OSC B 9: the body of the note.
- OSC A 4: the square that outlines it. More makes it sound more like an organ and less like an electric piano.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: turn OSC A to 0 and back. Without it the tone is close to a plain hum; with it the note has a hollow edge you can pick out.

steps.title: Low, plain filter
steps.why:
A low, plain low-pass filter sets the resting tone once the knock has passed.
- CUTOFF 4.4 (about 420 Hz): dark and round. Higher is brighter and thinner.
- RESONANCE 0.5: almost no peak, so nothing rings or squelches.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 7: the cutoff rises with the notes more than the default, so the top of the keyboard does not go dull.
- Listen for: a soft, muted tone with no edge at all.

steps.title: A soft knock on each note
steps.why:
The filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), adds the knock: a short lift of brightness at the start of each note.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 3: opens the filter about two and a half octaves. The size of the knock.
- ATTACK 0: the brightness is there at once, like a hammer.
- DECAY 5.8 (350 ms), SUSTAIN 2: closes over about a third of a second to a low level. Shorter makes a tighter tick.
- RELEASE 4.5 (140 ms): closes smoothly after you let go.
- Listen for: each note starting a little brighter and rounding off, like a hammer hitting a metal bar.

steps.title: Volume that fades under your finger
steps.why:
The volume envelope is set like a struck instrument: it falls while the key is down instead of holding.
- ATTACK 1 (4 ms): just enough to take the click off.
- DECAY 7.2 (1.2 s), SUSTAIN 4: the level falls over about a second to under half, so a held note fades. At SUSTAIN 10 it would hold like an organ.
- RELEASE 5 (220 ms): notes ring on briefly after you let go.
- Listen for: hold a chord shape note by note: each one fades under your finger.

steps.title: Retrigger every note
steps.why:
With RETRIG on, every key press gets its own knock and fade, even if the last key is still down.
- Retrigger on (RETRIG): restarts both envelopes on each key press. In NORMAL, an overlapped note would carry on from the faded level with no knock.
- Listen for: repeated and overlapping notes each starting with the same soft thud.

context.oscB.tri: Most of the tone. The triangle is the softest shape on the panel.
context.mix.oscA: The square wave that outlines the note. More of it makes the sound more like an organ and less like an electric piano.
context.filter.cutoff: The resting tone once the knock has passed. Higher is brighter and thinner.
context.filter.env: The size of the knock at the start of each note.
context.fenv.decay: How long the knock takes to round off.
context.aenv.decay: How quickly a held note fades.
context.aenv.sustain: Where a held note settles. At 10 the note would hold like an organ.
context.mode.retrig: Gives every key press a fresh start.

tweaks.hear: The knock gets harder and brighter, like playing the keys with more force.
From a plain hum, to a soft electric piano, to a hollow organ-like tone.
Held notes stop fading. The sound turns from a struck instrument into a blown or bowed one.

tweaks.try: Set LFO AMOUNT to 5, LFO FREQUENCY to 4 and OSC A PW to DIR
tweaks.hear: The width of the square wave drifts slowly, which adds a slight movement inside held notes.

sounds.name: Dark Riff Lead with a Self-Made Rasp
sounds.ref: In the style of Daft Punk — "Da Funk"
sounds.blurb: Low, filtered riff sound with a gritty edge that gets rougher the louder the note is.
sounds.how: The riff tone is two saws behind a filter that is mostly closed, with enough resonance to give each note a "wow". Closing the filter normally makes a sound smooth. Here a cable takes the synth’s own output and sends it to CUTOFF CV, so the filter is pushed open and shut by the wave it has just produced, once for every cycle of the note. That bends the shape of the wave and puts back a rough set of high overtones without opening the filter. AUTO glide slides the pitch between overlapping notes.

steps.title: Two low saws, run hot
steps.why:
Two low saws, run hot into the filter. Mixer levels this high are more than the filter input takes cleanly, which thickens the tone a little before anything else happens.
- Osc A and B sawtooth, OCTAVE 1: both an octave below the starting pitch, bright and buzzy. Pulse, triangle and SYNC off.
- Osc B FREQUENCY 0.1 (+0.1 st): a hair sharp, so the saws beat slowly and the rasp added later keeps shifting. Low frequency at NORMAL, keyboard on.
- OSC A 9, OSC B 7, NOISE/EXT 0: a hot level to push the filter input. Lower levels give a cleaner, smaller tone.
- Listen for: a thick, buzzy low saw with slow beating.

steps.title: Mostly closed, resonant filter
steps.why:
A mostly closed, resonant low-pass filter. The filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), gives each note its "wow".
- CUTOFF 4.4 (about 420 Hz): kept low. The rasp from the cable is strongest when the filter is mostly closed.
- RESONANCE 5: the peak that makes the "wow" vocal, and the peak the cable will shake.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 4: opens just over three octaves at the front. KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5.
- DECAY 5.4 (250 ms), SUSTAIN 2.5: with ATTACK 0 and RELEASE 54 ms, the filter falls back in about a quarter of a second to a low held level.
- Listen for: a "wow" at the start of each note, then a dark, smooth held tone.

steps.title: Full, short-tailed volume
steps.why:
Full, short-tailed volume. The level matters in this patch, because the cable in the last step takes its signal from after the amplifier.
- ATTACK 0: full level at once.
- DECAY 170 ms, SUSTAIN 10: no drop; held notes keep full level, which is also the strength of the rasp later.
- RELEASE 3.2 (41 ms): a quick stop when you let go.
- Listen for: even, solid notes with no dip after the front.

steps.title: AUTO glide
steps.why:
Glide, or portamento, slurs the riff where notes overlap.
- RATE 2.2 (150 ms): a quick slide.
- Glide mode AUTO: slides only when a new key goes down before the last is released.
- Retrigger off: those overlapped notes also skip the "wow", because the envelopes do not restart.
- Listen for: in the riff two pairs of notes overlap. Those slur with no new "wow"; the rest each get their own.

steps.title: Patch AUDIO OUT into CUTOFF CV
steps.why:
The cable makes the filter rough itself up. AUDIO OUT is the finished sound, and CUTOFF CV adds a control voltage to the CUTOFF knob.
- Cable AUDIO OUT → CUTOFF CV: a fixed depth of five octaves each way for a full signal. The output is an audio wave, so the cutoff is thrown up and down on every cycle of the note, which bends the wave and puts back rough high overtones.
- Measured effect: above 1.2 kHz the held note gains 10 dB or more while the filter setting has not changed. With the filter wide open the cable changes very little.
- Level: the rasp follows the volume envelope, so it fades as the note fades. On the hardware you would listen through PHONES while this cable is in.
- Listen for: the held part of each note, smooth before, now with a dry rasp on top.

context.filter.cutoff: Kept low. The rasp from the cable is strongest when the filter is mostly closed; with the filter wide open the cable changes very little.
context.filter.res: Gives the "wow" at the start of each note and a peak for the cable to shake.
context.fenv.sustain: How far the filter stays open on a held note. Lower settings leave more room for the rasp to be heard.
context.fenv.decay: The length of the "wow".
context.aenv.sustain: Full. The cable takes its signal after the amplifier, so this is also the strength of the rasp on held notes.
context.mix.oscA: High, to push the filter input. Lower levels give a cleaner, smaller tone.
context.oscB.freq: A small detune, so the two saws beat slowly and the rasp keeps shifting.

tweaks.try: Lower to 4, then bring it back to 10
tweaks.hear: At 4 the held note is quieter and nearly clean. At 10 the output is stronger, it shakes the filter harder, and the rasp is at its roughest.
Low down the note is a dark tone with grit on top. From about 5.5 upwards the filter lets the saws’ own brightness through, and the cable adds very little.
The "wow" turns into a squelch and the rasp gathers around the resonant peak.
One saw alone: the rasp stops shifting and becomes a fixed, buzzing edge.

sounds.name: Soft Lead with an Uneven Warble
sounds.ref: In the style of Air — "Kelly Watch the Stars"
sounds.blurb: Rounded, gliding lead whose pitch sags and flicks back up a few times a second.
sounds.how: The tone is a high saw rounded off by a resonant filter, with a triangle an octave below for warmth and a long glide on every note. The warble starts as ordinary vibrato from the LFO. A cable from LFO OUT to LFO CV then makes the LFO control its own speed: it crawls through the low part of its cycle and rushes through the high part. The pitch spends most of its time just under the note and flicks up about three times a second, which sounds less like a player’s vibrato and more like an old tape machine that cannot hold its speed.

steps.title: High saw, triangle below
steps.why:
A high saw carries the tune and a triangle an octave below adds warmth underneath.
- Osc A sawtooth, OCTAVE 3: the top octave, bright and thin. Pulse and SYNC off, FREQUENCY 0.
- Osc B triangle, OCTAVE 2: a soft lower octave, few overtones. Saw and pulse off; low frequency at NORMAL, keyboard on, in tune.
- OSC A 7, OSC B 7, NOISE/EXT 0: an even balance. Turn OSC B down for a thinner, more whistling lead.
- Listen for: a bright, slightly buzzy lead with a round body underneath.

steps.title: Round the saw off
steps.why:
A resonant low-pass filter rounds the saw into an "oo". The filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), lets each note ease open.
- CUTOFF 5.2 (about 730 Hz), RESONANCE 4.5: a soft peak just above each note, which gives the saw a vocal, flute-like quality.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 8: strong tracking, so the peak stays near each note across the keyboard.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 1.5, ATTACK 4 (51 ms): a small lift that arrives just after the note starts, so the front is soft.
- DECAY 420 ms, SUSTAIN 6, RELEASE 220 ms: settles back slightly and closes smoothly.
- Listen for: the buzz turning to a rounder "oo" tone.

steps.title: Soft edges and a long glide
steps.why:
Soft edges and a long glide, so notes flow into each other.
- ATTACK 3.5 (34 ms): the volume eases in without a click.
- DECAY 170 ms, SUSTAIN 9: held notes stay nearly full.
- RELEASE 5.2 (270 ms): a soft tail after each note.
- Glide RATE 3.5 (370 ms), mode NORMAL: glide, or portamento, slides into every note over about a third of a second, overlapped or not.
- Listen for: each note of the riff swooping in from the last.

steps.title: Plain vibrato first
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) starts as plain vibrato on both oscillators. The next step bends it out of shape.
- LFO triangle only: a smooth, even wobble.
- LFO FREQUENCY 7.4 (6.42 Hz): fairly quick. With the cable in, the warble will run at roughly half this.
- AMOUNT LFO 1.4: about half a semitone each way.
- LFO route DIRECT, To OSC A and B FREQ DIR: both oscillators take the always-on bus and move together.
- Listen for: an even, rather nervous flutter.

steps.title: Patch LFO OUT into LFO CV
steps.why:
The cable makes the LFO control its own speed. LFO OUT is the LFO’s wave, and LFO CV adds a voltage to the LFO FREQUENCY knob.
- Cable LFO OUT → LFO CV: a fixed depth of three octaves of speed each way. The LFO runs eight times faster at the top of its cycle and eight times slower at the bottom, so it lingers low and hurries through the high part. The whole cycle slows to about 3.4 a second.
- FREQUENCY 0.2 on Osc A and B (+0.3 st): the pitch now sits under the note about nine tenths of the time, averaging about a quarter of a semitone flat, so both oscillators go up by the same amount to put the tune back. Return them to 0 if you remove the cable.
- Listen for: the pitch sagging and flicking up about three times a second, like an old tape machine that cannot hold its speed.

context.lfo.rate: The LFO speed before the cable bends it. With the cable in, the warble you hear runs at roughly half this rate.
context.mod.lfoAmt: The depth of the warble: about half a semitone each way at 1.4.
context.oscA.freq: Raised slightly to make up for the warble spending most of its time below the note. Put it back to 0 if you remove the cable.
context.oscB.freq: Raised by the same amount as Oscillator A, so the two stay in tune with each other.
context.filter.res: The soft peak that rounds the saw into an "oo".
context.glide.rate: How long each slide takes. In NORMAL mode every note slides, overlapped or not.
context.mix.oscB: The triangle an octave down. Turn it down for a thinner, more whistling lead.

tweaks.hear: From a slow sag every half second to a quick, hiccuping flutter. The lopsided shape stays the same.
The flick grows to a semitone and a half and the lead sounds properly seasick.

tweaks.try: Switch the triangle off and the saw on
tweaks.hear: The pitch creeps upward, speeds up as it goes and drops back, over and over.
At 0 the notes step cleanly. At 5 each slide takes three quarters of a second and short notes never reach their pitch.

sounds.name: Wide-Leaping Computer Bleeps
sounds.ref: In the style of Kraftwerk — "Pocket Calculator"
sounds.blurb: Short, clean bleeps that jump across three octaves from a handful of neighbouring keys.
sounds.how: The bleep is a square wave with a triangle an octave above it, through an open filter, with a volume envelope that dies away in about a tenth of a second. There is no filter movement and no vibrato, which is what keeps it clean. The wide leaps come from a cable: KYBD CV into OSC CV sends the keyboard to the oscillators a second time, so each semitone you play moves the pitch by three. Middle C stays where it is, and every other key lands on C, E flat, F sharp or A in some octave.

steps.title: Square wave with a triangle on top
steps.why:
A square wave with a triangle an octave above gives a clean, computer-like bleep.
- Osc A pulse only, PULSE WIDTH 5: a square, with a hollow, clear pitch. Saw and SYNC off, OCTAVE 2, FREQUENCY 0.
- Osc B triangle only, OCTAVE 3: one octave higher, adding a soft ping on top. Low frequency at NORMAL, keyboard on.
- OSC A 7, OSC B 6, NOISE/EXT 0: the square leads and the triangle sits just under it. More OSC B makes the ping stronger.
- Listen for: a plain, hollow tone with a slight glassy shine on top.

steps.title: Open filter, no envelope
steps.why:
The low-pass filter is left open and still, which keeps every bleep clean.
- CUTOFF 7.5 (about 3.6 kHz): high, so the square comes through almost unchanged.
- RESONANCE 0: no peak, no ring.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 0: no filter movement at all, so every bleep has the same plain tone. KEYBOARD AMOUNT stays at 5.
- Listen for: very little change from the last step. That is the point: the tone should not move.

steps.title: A tenth of a second of sound
steps.why:
A tenth of a second of sound per key press. The loudness envelope has no sustain, so the note dies on its own.
- ATTACK 0: instant start.
- DECAY 4.4 (100 ms), SUSTAIN 0: one short bleep however long you hold the key. DECAY is the length of each bleep.
- RELEASE 3.2 (41 ms): a clean stop if you let go early.
- VOLUME 9: raised because short sounds seem quieter than held ones.
- Listen for: short, dry bleeps. Raise DECAY to hear them turn into tones.

steps.title: Retrigger every note
steps.why:
RETRIG gives every key press its own bleep, even when the last key has not quite come up.
- Retrigger on (RETRIG): restarts the envelopes on each key press. In NORMAL, an overlapped key would change pitch but, with SUSTAIN at 0, could be almost silent.
- Listen for: quick runs where every note bleeps equally.

steps.title: Patch KYBD CV into OSC CV
steps.why:
The cable stretches the keyboard. KYBD CV sends the keyboard pitch as a control voltage, and OSC CV adds it to both oscillators’ pitch a second time.
- Cable KYBD CV → OSC CV: the voltage is zero at middle C, and the jack adds 24 semitones for each octave played. That adds two semitones to every semitone the keyboard already gives, so each key is now a step of three.
- Resulting notes: middle C stays where it is, and every other key lands on C, E flat, F sharp or A in some octave. Osc A FREQUENCY would shift that set of four.
- Listen for: play C, D, B, E around middle C and hear C, the F sharp above, the A below and the C an octave up. The riff uses nine neighbouring keys and covers two octaves.

context.aenv.decay: The length of each bleep.
context.aenv.sustain: At 0, so a held key still gives a single short bleep.
context.oscB.octave: One octave above Oscillator A. It adds the ping on top of the square wave.
context.mix.oscB: How much of the upper triangle you hear.
context.filter.cutoff: High, so the square wave comes through unchanged.
context.oscA.freq: With the cable in, every key lands on one of four notes. This knob shifts Oscillator A’s set of four up or down.
context.out.volume: Raised to make up for the short notes.

tweaks.hear: From a dry tick of 45 ms to a quarter-second "boop".
The triangle now sits a fifth above the octave, and each bleep becomes a small two-note chord.
Glide works on the keyboard voltage, and the cable carries that voltage too, so each bleep swoops in from the last one over three times the distance.
The square wave alone: a plainer, more hollow bleep.

sounds.name: Nasal Reed-Style Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Depeche Mode — "Everything Counts"
sounds.blurb: Thin, nasal lead with a fixed honk in its tone, like a double-reed instrument.
sounds.how: Two things make a reed instrument sound nasal. The reed gives a buzz with many strong overtones, and the tube of the instrument boosts the same band of frequencies whatever note is played. A very narrow pulse wave supplies the buzz. For the fixed band, the filter is given a resonant peak at about 1.4 kHz and KEYBOARD AMOUNT is turned almost off, so the peak stays where it is while the notes move under it. A filter attack of about 35 ms gives each note a blown start.

steps.title: A very narrow pulse
steps.why:
A very narrow pulse supplies the buzz of a reed. The narrower the pulse, the thinner and buzzier it gets.
- Osc A pulse, PULSE WIDTH 1.2 (14 %): thin and buzzy. At 5 it would be a hollow square, closer to a clarinet. Saw and SYNC off, OCTAVE 2, FREQUENCY 0.
- Listen for: sweep PULSE WIDTH from 5 down to 1.2 and hear the hollow square thin out into a buzz.

steps.title: Oscillator A alone
steps.why:
Oscillator A alone. A second oscillator would fatten the tone, and this sound should stay thin.
- OSC A 9: a narrow pulse is quieter than a square, so its level goes up.
- OSC B 0: kept out on purpose.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: a thin, reedy buzz with no beating or movement.

steps.title: A resonant peak that stays put
steps.why:
A resonant peak that stays put gives the fixed honk. A reed instrument’s tube boosts the same band of frequencies whatever note is played, and the low-pass filter copies that.
- CUTOFF 6.2 (about 1.4 kHz): the position of the honk. Around 6 is nasal; lower sounds more like a muted horn.
- RESONANCE 5: how strongly that band is boosted.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 2: nearly off, so the boosted band stays in one place while the notes change under it.
- Listen for: play a low note, then a high one. The same honking band sounds in both. At KEYBOARD AMOUNT 10 the peak would follow the notes and the nasal quality would go.

steps.title: A blown start
steps.why:
The filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), gives each note a blown start.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 1.5: a small lift, so the peak rises into place rather than sweeping.
- ATTACK 3.5 (34 ms): the breath. At 0 the note begins with a hard edge.
- DECAY 170 ms, SUSTAIN 6, RELEASE 54 ms: settles slightly and stays fairly open while held.
- Listen for: a soft "h" at the start of each note, like breath reaching a reed.

steps.title: Even, slightly softened volume
steps.why:
Even, slightly softened volume, so the lead is steady while held and stops cleanly.
- ATTACK 2.5 (15 ms): takes the click off without blurring the front.
- DECAY 170 ms, SUSTAIN 8: a small dip after the start, then a steady level.
- RELEASE 3.8 (72 ms): a short, clean stop.
- Listen for: an even line with clear note ends.

context.oscA.pw: The reed. Narrower is thinner and buzzier; at 5 it is a hollow square wave, closer to a clarinet.
context.filter.cutoff: The position of the honk. Around 6 is nasal; lower settings sound more like a muted horn.
context.filter.res: How strongly the band is boosted.
context.filter.kbd: Nearly off, so the boosted band stays in one place while the notes change.
context.fenv.attack: The blown start of each note. At 0 the note begins with a hard edge.
context.mix.oscA: High, to make up for the low level of a narrow pulse.

tweaks.hear: At 10 the peak follows the keys and every note has the same synthetic tone. At 2 the instrument keeps its own honk.
From a thin buzz, through an oboe-like tone, to a hollow clarinet.
The honk moves from a covered "aw" to a bright, pinched "ee".

tweaks.try: Set LFO AMOUNT to 1, LFO FREQUENCY to 7 and OSC A FREQ to DIR
tweaks.hear: A shallow 5 Hz vibrato of about a quarter of a semitone, as a player would add to long notes.

sounds.name: Wavering Twin-Saw Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Duran Duran — "Save a Prayer"
sounds.blurb: Bright two-oscillator lead that drifts in and out of tune with itself three times a second.
sounds.how: Both oscillators play a saw at the same octave, but only Oscillator B gets the LFO. Its pitch swings about 60 cents either way while Oscillator A holds still. When the two pitches cross, the pair sound like one clean note. As they pull apart the beating between them speeds up and the note sours and widens. You hear a waver in pitch and a change in thickness at the same time, which one LFO on both oscillators cannot give. A medium filter envelope gives each note a soft pluck.

steps.title: Two saws at the same pitch
steps.why:
Two saws at the same pitch, a hair apart, are the start of a thick, bright lead.
- Osc A and B sawtooth, OCTAVE 2: both bright and buzzy at the usual pitch. Pulse, triangle and SYNC off.
- Osc B FREQUENCY 0.1 (+0.1 st): a tiny fixed detune. It decides where in the LFO swing the two will meet later. Low frequency at NORMAL, keyboard on.
- OSC A 8, OSC B 7, NOISE/EXT 0: nearly level, so the beating between them is strong.
- Listen for: a fat saw with very slow beating.

steps.title: Send the LFO to Oscillator B only
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) goes to Oscillator B only. Oscillator A holds still, so the two drift in and out of tune with each other.
- LFO triangle only: a smooth swing.
- LFO FREQUENCY 6.2 (3.15 Hz): about three wavers a second.
- AMOUNT LFO 1.6: Oscillator B swings about 60 cents either way. Much more and the note sounds out of tune rather than wavering.
- To OSC B FREQ DIR, OSC A FREQ OFF: with LFO route DIRECT, only Oscillator B listens to the always-on bus.
- Listen for: hold a note. Three times a second it tightens into one pitch and then spreads and sours, a change in pitch and thickness at once.

steps.title: Half-open filter with a soft pluck
steps.why:
A half-open low-pass filter with a soft pluck. The filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), brightens the front of each note.
- CUTOFF 5.6 (just under 1 kHz), RESONANCE 2: half open with a small peak.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 3.5: opens nearly three octaves at the start.
- DECAY 5.5 (270 ms), SUSTAIN 4: with ATTACK 0 and RELEASE 140 ms, at once, then settling back over about a quarter of a second.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 6: slightly more than half tracking.
- Listen for: each note starting bright and settling, with the waver carrying on underneath.

steps.title: Notes that ring on a little
steps.why:
Notes that ring on a little after the key comes up.
- ATTACK 0: an instant start.
- DECAY 6 (420 ms), SUSTAIN 7: a gentle drop to a solid held level.
- RELEASE 5 (220 ms): the waver carries on briefly after each key is let go.
- Listen for: short notes with a soft, wavering tail.

context.mod.toBFreq: The only destination switched on. Oscillator A is left alone as the fixed pitch that Oscillator B moves against.
context.mod.lfoAmt: How far Oscillator B swings: 1.6 is about 60 cents each way. Much more and the note sounds out of tune instead of wavering.
context.lfo.rate: The speed of the waver.
context.oscB.freq: The small fixed detune. It decides where in the LFO’s swing the two oscillators meet.
context.mix.oscB: Nearly level with Oscillator A, so the beating between them is strong.
context.fenv.decay: The length of the bright start of each note.

tweaks.try: Switch OSC A FREQ to DIR as well
tweaks.hear: Both oscillators now move together. The pitch still wobbles, but the thickening and souring have gone: ordinary vibrato.
From a faint shimmer to a swing of a semitone and a half that sounds like a warped record.
One slow swell of detune about every second, closer to a chorus effect than a waver.
The moving oscillator drops behind the fixed one and the waver becomes a light shimmer.

sounds.name: Dry One-Oscillator Punch Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Soft Cell (Marc Almond and Dave Ball) — "Bedsitter"
sounds.blurb: Plain, punchy bass from a single oscillator, with a hard start and a dead stop.
sounds.how: There is only one oscillator in this sound, which keeps it dry: two oscillators always beat against each other a little, and one cannot. To give that one oscillator more body, its saw and pulse switches are both on, which the Pro-1 allows and most synths do not. A short filter envelope puts a punch on the front of each note and then holds the filter part open, so the note keeps its weight for as long as the key is down. A very short release stops it dead.

steps.title: Saw and pulse from one oscillator
steps.why:
One oscillator keeps the bass dry, because two oscillators always beat against each other a little. To give it more body, both waveform switches are on, which the Pro-1 allows and most synths do not.
- Osc A saw + pulse, PULSE WIDTH 4 (41 %): the saw is buzzy and light, and the pulse fills in a hollow body under it. Lower PULSE WIDTH is more nasal.
- OCTAVE 1: bass range. FREQUENCY 0, SYNC off.
- Listen for: switch the pulse off and on to hear the body come and go.

steps.title: Oscillator B stays out
steps.why:
Oscillator B stays out of the mixer.
- OSC A 9: the single oscillator, near full.
- OSC B 0: at 0 on purpose. One oscillator gives a steady tone with no beating.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: bring OSC B up for a moment and hear the slow swirl two oscillators make. This bass is meant to be without it.

steps.title: Low filter with a short punch
steps.why:
A low filter with a short punch. The filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), opens the low-pass filter hard at the start and then holds it part open.
- CUTOFF 4 (about 320 Hz), RESONANCE 2: dark and solid, with a small peak.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 4.5: opens three and a half octaves at the front: the size of the punch.
- ATTACK 0, DECAY 4.6 (120 ms): the punch is over in about an eighth of a second.
- SUSTAIN 3, RELEASE 34 ms: keeps the filter part open, which is the weight of the bass after the punch.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 4: a little less tracking than usual, so high notes stay round.
- Listen for: a bright "d" at the front of each note and a solid, darker tone behind it.

steps.title: Hold, then stop dead
steps.why:
Hold, then stop dead. The gaps between notes matter as much as the notes.
- ATTACK 0: instant, so the punch lines up with the filter.
- DECAY 170 ms, SUSTAIN 7: a steady level while the key is down.
- RELEASE 2.8 (28 ms): notes stop the moment the key comes up.
- Listen for: tight, clearly separated notes. Lengthen RELEASE to hear the line get looser.

context.oscA.pulse: On together with the saw. It is the body of the bass.
context.oscA.pw: The tone of the pulse layer. At 5 it is hollow; lower settings are more nasal.
context.mix.oscB: At 0 on purpose. One oscillator gives a dry, steady tone with no beating.
context.filter.env: The size of the punch at the front of each note.
context.fenv.decay: The length of the punch.
context.fenv.sustain: How open the filter stays on a held note. This is the weight of the bass after the punch.
context.aenv.release: Very short, so notes stop the moment the key comes up.

tweaks.hear: The layer under the saw goes from thin and nasal to round and hollow.
At 0 every note closes to a dull thud after the punch. At 5 it stays buzzy for as long as you hold it.
A second saw joins in and the tone starts to swirl slowly. Fatter, and less dry.
Notes now tail off over about 140 ms and the line loses its clipped feel.

sounds.name: Deep Round Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Pet Shop Boys — "West End Girls"
sounds.blurb: Deep, smooth bass whose notes open gently and close slowly, for slow, spacious lines.
sounds.how: Two saws an octave apart go through a filter set so low that almost none of their buzz gets through. The lower saw is the louder of the two, so the weight sits an octave under the note you play. A filter envelope with a half-second decay opens the tone a little at the start of each note and lets it close slowly, so long notes go "doom" instead of "dit". Both envelopes have releases long enough for the notes to run softly into one another.

steps.title: Two saws, an octave apart
steps.why:
Two saws an octave apart, tuned dead on, lock into one tone with a strong bottom octave.
- Osc A sawtooth, OCTAVE 2: the upper saw, so the note can be heard on small speakers. Pulse and SYNC off, FREQUENCY 0.
- Osc B sawtooth, OCTAVE 1: one octave under Oscillator A. This is where the depth comes from. Low frequency at NORMAL, keyboard on.
- Osc B FREQUENCY 0: no detune, so the pair do not swirl.
- Listen for: only Oscillator A is in the mixer so far. The lower octave comes in next.

steps.title: Lower octave in front
steps.why:
The lower octave goes in front.
- OSC B 8: the depth, the louder of the two. Turn it down and the bass gets lighter and easier to hear on small speakers.
- OSC A 6: the upper saw, for definition.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: the weight dropping an octave under the note you play.

steps.title: Filter almost shut
steps.why:
The low-pass filter is almost shut, so almost none of the saws’ buzz gets through.
- CUTOFF 2.9 (about 150 Hz): at this setting you mostly hear the first two or three overtones of each saw, which is why the bass sounds round. Small moves change a lot: up for more buzz, down for a pure thud.
- RESONANCE 0.5: next to no peak.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5: half tracking, as the synth starts.
- Listen for: a deep, muffled tone with no edge.

steps.title: A slow-closing envelope
steps.why:
The filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), opens the tone at the start of each note and lets it close slowly, so long notes go "doom" rather than "dit".
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 3.8: opens about three octaves.
- ATTACK 0: the opening starts at once.
- DECAY 6.2 (510 ms), SUSTAIN 2: about half a second to darken to a low level. Half a second suits slow lines.
- RELEASE 5 (220 ms): closes gently after you let go.
- Listen for: hold a long note and hear it darken gradually.

steps.title: Smooth volume
steps.why:
Smooth volume, so notes run softly into one another.
- ATTACK 1 (4 ms): takes the click off the front.
- DECAY 6.5 (660 ms), SUSTAIN 7: a slow, slight drop to a solid held level.
- RELEASE 4.8 (190 ms): each note fades under the start of the next. Shorten it for a tighter line.
- Listen for: a spacious line with no hard edges between notes.

context.oscB.octave: One octave under Oscillator A. This is where the depth comes from.
context.mix.oscB: The louder of the two. Turn it down and the bass gets lighter and easier to hear on small speakers.
context.filter.cutoff: Very low. Small moves here change the character a lot: up for more buzz, down for a pure thud.
context.filter.env: How far each note opens before it starts to close.
context.fenv.decay: How long the note takes to darken. Half a second suits slow lines.
context.aenv.release: Lets notes overlap softly. Shorten it for a tighter line.

tweaks.hear: At 4.5 each note has a quick "dum". At 7 it takes a full second to close and long notes seem to sink.
From a soft thud that is mostly felt, to a bass with a clear buzzy edge.
The two saws drift against each other and the bass starts to swell and thin slowly.

tweaks.try: Set RATE to 2.5 and the glide switch to AUTO
tweaks.hear: Notes played with overlapping fingers slide into each other over about 190 ms.

sounds.name: Tight Funk Bass with an Envelope Thump
sounds.ref: In the style of Yazoo — "Situation"
sounds.blurb: Short, snappy bass with a knock at the front of every note, as if a kick drum were layered under it.
sounds.how: The bass is a saw and a square wave through a resonant filter with a very short envelope, and RETRIG makes sure every note in a fast line gets that snap. The knock is a patch trick. The filter envelope is a control signal, not a sound, but it jumps from nothing to full in two thousandths of a second at the start of each note. A cable sends it into EXT, the mixer’s audio input, and that sudden jump goes through the filter and amplifier as a thump. The same envelope is opening the filter at that moment, so the thump and the snap always land together.

steps.title: Saw plus square
steps.why:
A saw and a square at the same pitch: the saw gives the bite and the square a hollow body.
- Osc A sawtooth, OCTAVE 1: bright and buzzy in bass range. Pulse and SYNC off, FREQUENCY 0.
- Osc B pulse, PULSE WIDTH 5, OCTAVE 1: a square wave at the same octave, tuned the same, so the two lock together. Low frequency at NORMAL, keyboard on.
- OSC A 7, OSC B 6: the saw slightly in front.
- Listen for: a thick, buzzy bass with a hollow middle and no beating.

steps.title: A very short snap
steps.why:
A very short snap from the filter. The filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), flicks the 24 dB low-pass filter open and shut on each note.
- CUTOFF 3.6 (about 240 Hz), RESONANCE 3.5: dark at rest, with a peak that adds a "quack" to the snap.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 5: opens the filter four octaves at the front.
- ATTACK 0 (2 ms): instant. This matters again in step 5.
- DECAY 4 (71 ms), SUSTAIN 1.5, RELEASE 34 ms: shut again in about 70 ms, down to a low level. Longer DECAY makes a looser "bow".
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5: half tracking.
- Listen for: each note a quick "bip" with a dull tail.

steps.title: Short notes
steps.why:
Short notes keep the line tight at any speed.
- ATTACK 0: instant, lined up with the snap.
- DECAY 4.8 (140 ms), SUSTAIN 5: the volume falls to half quickly, so each note has a punchy front and a quieter body.
- RELEASE 2.8 (28 ms): notes stop almost as soon as you let go, keeping clean gaps.
- Listen for: tight, bouncy notes with clear space between them.

steps.title: Retrigger every note
steps.why:
Some notes in the riff start before the one before has ended. RETRIG gives them their own snap.
- Retrigger on (RETRIG): every key press restarts both envelopes. In NORMAL those overlapped notes would get no snap.
- Listen for: every note in a fast run snapping the same, however the fingers overlap.

steps.title: Patch FILTER ENV into EXT
steps.why:
The knock is a patch trick. The filter envelope is a control signal, but it jumps from nothing to full in two thousandths of a second, and fed into an audio input that jump is heard as a thump.
- Cable FILTER ENV → EXT: EXT is the mixer’s external audio input. With a cable in it the noise generator is switched out.
- NOISE/EXT 8: now the level of the thump, not of noise. At 0 the cable does nothing.
- Timing: the same envelope is opening the filter at that moment, so the thump and the snap always land together. Its DECAY sets the thump’s tail too.
- Listen for: a knock under the snap at the front of each note, as if a kick drum were layered under it. Pull the cable out and the fronts go soft again.

context.mix.noise: With the cable in EXT this is the level of the thump, not of noise. At 0 the cable does nothing.
context.fenv.attack: At 0, which is what makes the thump. The thump is the envelope’s sudden rise; slow the attack and there is no sudden rise to hear.
context.fenv.decay: The length of the snap, and of the thump’s tail, because one envelope makes both.
context.filter.env: How far the filter opens for the snap. It also decides how much of the thump gets through the filter.
context.filter.res: Adds a "quack" to the snap.
context.mode.retrig: Every key press gets its own snap and thump, even when notes overlap.
context.aenv.release: Very short, to keep the notes apart.

tweaks.hear: At 0 there is no thump. At 5 it is a light tap. At 10 it is a heavy knock, nearly as loud as the note itself.
The envelope now takes 50 ms to rise. The thump disappears and the snap turns into a soft "bwip".
From a dry tick to a rounder "bow", with the knock getting longer and lower as you go.
The saw alone: thinner and buzzier, and the thump stands out more.

sounds.name: Slow-Blooming Organ Drone
sounds.ref: In the style of Brian Eno — "The Big Ship"
sounds.blurb: A calm, organ-like tone that plays by itself while a ringing overtone slowly grows out of it and sinks back.
sounds.how: DRONE holds the gate open, so the synth sounds with no key down and the keys only choose the pitch. The tone is a square wave with a triangle an octave above it, which is close to two stops of a small organ. One very slow LFO does two jobs. Through the modulation matrix it opens and closes the filter by most of an octave. Through a cable into RESO CV it also raises the resonance as the filter opens. The result is a bloom: every seven seconds the tone brightens, one overtone near the cutoff starts to ring, and then it all settles back.

steps.title: Hold the gate open
steps.why:
DRONE holds the gate open, the signal that normally says a key is down, so the synth sounds with no key held. From here on a key press only changes the pitch.
- Drone on, Repeat off: both envelopes rise to their sustain levels and stay there. Switch DRONE off to stop the drone.
- Loudness ATTACK 6.5 (380 ms): the drone fades in over about 400 ms rather than switching on.
- Loudness SUSTAIN 8: the level the drone holds at. It is now the drone’s volume.
- Listen for: a plain saw sounding by itself. Press keys to move its pitch.

steps.title: Square wave and an octave triangle
steps.why:
A square wave with a triangle an octave above, close to two stops of a small organ.
- Osc A pulse, PULSE WIDTH 5, OCTAVE 1: a square, hollow and woody, an octave below the starting pitch. Saw and SYNC off.
- Osc B triangle, OCTAVE 2: a soft, flute-like octave on top. Saw and pulse off; low frequency at NORMAL, keyboard on.
- Osc B FREQUENCY 0.1 (+0.1 st): a hair sharp. It sets the speed of a slow beat between the two.
- OSC A 7, OSC B 7, NOISE/EXT 0: an even blend.
- Listen for: a slow, gentle beat between the two, which keeps the held tone from sounding frozen.

steps.title: A low filter that follows the keys
steps.why:
A low filter that follows the keys. The Pro-1’s filter is a 24 dB low-pass: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs.
- CUTOFF 4.3 (about 390 Hz): fairly dark. It is the middle of the drift to come, and decides which overtone rings at the top of each bloom.
- RESONANCE 0: the cable in step 5 will supply all the resonance.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 0: in DRONE mode the envelope sits still, so it could only shift the cutoff by a fixed amount.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 10: full tracking keeps the cutoff the same distance above whichever note you choose, so the bloom sounds the same on every key.
- Listen for: a soft, muted organ tone.

steps.title: A very slow LFO on the filter
steps.why:
A very slow LFO (low-frequency oscillator) opens and closes the filter, like an organ’s swell pedal.
- LFO triangle only: a smooth rise and fall.
- LFO FREQUENCY 1 (0.14 Hz): one cycle about every seven seconds: the time between blooms.
- AMOUNT LFO 4: the cutoff drifts 0.8 of an octave each way.
- LFO route DIRECT, To FILTER DIR: the always-on bus, and the filter listens to it.
- Listen for: the tone slowly brightening and dulling over seven seconds.

steps.title: Patch LFO OUT into RESO CV
steps.why:
The same LFO also raises the resonance as the filter opens. LFO OUT sends the LFO’s wave, and RESO CV adds a voltage to the RESONANCE knob.
- Cable LFO OUT → RESO CV: a fixed depth of the full resonance range each way. With the knob at 0 the lower half of the swing has nothing to take away; the upper half takes resonance up to the edge of whistling and back.
- Timing: because it is the same LFO, that happens while the filter is at its most open. Any RESONANCE on the knob is added to the cable and pushes the peak into a whistle.
- Listen for: every seven seconds one overtone, a little over two octaves above the note, steps forward and rings, then fades as the tone darkens. The body drops back slightly while it rings, because resonance takes level from everything below the cutoff.

context.mode.drone: Keeps the sound going with no key held. Switch it off to stop the drone.
context.lfo.rate: The time between blooms: about seven seconds at 1.
context.mod.lfoAmt: How far the filter opens and closes with each bloom.
context.filter.cutoff: The middle of the filter’s drift, and so the overtone that rings at the top of each bloom. Move it a little and a different overtone is picked out.
context.filter.res: At 0, so the cable supplies all the resonance. Anything you add here is added to the cable and takes the peak of the bloom into a whistle.
context.filter.kbd: At 10, so the bloom sits in the same place against every note.
context.oscB.freq: A very small detune. It sets the speed of the slow beat between the two oscillators.
context.filter.env: At 0. In DRONE mode the envelope sits still, so it could only shift the cutoff by a fixed amount.

tweaks.try: Move in small steps between 3.8 and 5
tweaks.hear: A different overtone rings at the top of each bloom: low settings pick a hollow one near the note, higher settings a thin, glassy one.
The triangle moves to a fifth above the octave and the drone takes on the sound of a fuller organ registration.
A bloom every two seconds, about the pace of slow breathing.

tweaks.try: Switch the triangle off and the saw on
tweaks.hear: The bloom builds slowly to its ringing peak and then cuts off at once.

sounds.name: Punchy Synth Brass Stab
sounds.ref: In the style of Prince — "1999"
sounds.blurb: Short, bright brass stab that starts wide and slightly sharp and pulls into tune.
sounds.how: Synth brass stabs took the place of a horn section on early-80s funk records. On those records they were chords from Oberheim polysynths; the Pro-1 gives you one note of the chord. Two saws supply the buzz, and the filter envelope has a 15 ms attack, so the brightness arrives just after the note starts, as it does when air hits a horn. The same envelope is also sent, very lightly, to Oscillator A’s pitch. At the front of each stab Oscillator A is pushed a third of a semitone sharp and away from Oscillator B, then falls back beside it. That brief spread is what makes it sound like several players hitting a note together.

steps.title: Two saws
steps.why:
Two saws supply the buzz of a brass section. The Pro-1 gives you one note of the chord the records played on polysynths.
- Osc A and B sawtooth, OCTAVE 2: bright, buzzy and full of harmonics for the filter to work on. Pulse, triangle and SYNC off.
- Osc B FREQUENCY 0.1 (+0.1 st): about a tenth of a semitone sharp, close to where Oscillator A will settle in step 4. Low frequency at NORMAL, keyboard on.
- OSC A 8, OSC B 8, NOISE/EXT 0: equal levels for a wide, even tone.
- Listen for: a big, buzzy saw with slow beating.

steps.title: A filter that blares open
steps.why:
A filter that blares open on each stab. The filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), sweeps the 24 dB low-pass filter.
- CUTOFF 3.6 (about 240 Hz), RESONANCE 1: dark at rest, with very little peak.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 6: nearly five octaves at the top: how bright the peak of each stab gets.
- ATTACK 2.5 (15 ms): the brightness arrives just after the note starts, as it does when air hits a horn. At 0 it is a hard click; by 4 it is a slow swell.
- DECAY 5 (170 ms), SUSTAIN 4.5, RELEASE 54 ms: a quick fall to a medium tone. KEYBOARD AMOUNT 6.
- Listen for: "bap": a very short rise, a bright peak, then a quick fall.

steps.title: Short, firm volume
steps.why:
Short, firm volume so stabs end cleanly.
- ATTACK 1 (4 ms): just enough to take off the click.
- DECAY 170 ms, SUSTAIN 8: a small dip, then a firm held level.
- RELEASE 3.6 (60 ms): stabs stop cleanly but not with a click.
- Listen for: short stabs with tidy gaps between them.

steps.title: A touch of the envelope on Oscillator A’s pitch
steps.why:
A touch of the filter envelope goes to Oscillator A’s pitch. At the front of each stab A is pushed sharp and away from B, then falls back beside it, which sounds like several players hitting a note together.
- AMOUNT FIL ENV 1.2: about a third of a semitone at the peak. The scale is not even: 2 is nearly a whole semitone.
- FIL ENV route DIRECT: the filter envelope onto the always-on bus.
- To OSC A FREQ DIR: only Oscillator A listens.
- Listen for: the front of each stab sounding wide and a little sour, then pulling into tune. On a held note A settles about 16 cents sharp, close beside B, and the two beat slowly.

steps.title: Retrigger every note
steps.why:
Stabs are often played in quick repeats, and RETRIG gives each one its full attack.
- Retrigger on (RETRIG): every key press restarts both envelopes, so each stab gets its own swell and pitch spread even if the fingers overlap.
- Listen for: fast repeated stabs all with the same "bap". Switch it off to hear overlapped stabs lose their front.

context.fenv.attack: The short rise that makes this brass and not a plain synth stab. At 0 it is a hard click; by 4 it is a slow swell.
context.filter.env: How bright the peak of each stab gets.
context.fenv.sustain: The tone a held note settles to. It also sets how sharp Oscillator A stays, because the same envelope reaches its pitch.
context.mod.envAmt: How far Oscillator A is pushed sharp at the front of the stab. The scale is not even: 1.2 is a third of a semitone, 2 is nearly a whole one.
context.oscB.freq: Set so that Oscillator B sits close to where Oscillator A settles on a held note.
context.aenv.release: Short, so stabs stay separate.

tweaks.hear: At 0 the stab is clean and narrow. At 1.2 the front is wide. At 2.5 each stab scoops down by a semitone and a half, like a section falling on to the note.
From a hard pluck, through a brass "bap", to a slow "bwaah".
The peak is less bright and the stab sounds like muted horns.
An octave underneath, like trombones doubling the trumpets.

sounds.name: Bouncy Bass with a Pulse-Width Snap
sounds.ref: In the style of Howard Jones — "New Song"
sounds.blurb: Bright, bouncy bass whose tone changes from nasal to hollow inside every note.
sounds.how: Most bass sounds get their movement from the filter alone. Here the filter envelope is also sent to Oscillator A’s pulse width through the modulation matrix. At the start of each note the pulse is pushed out to about 79 %, which is thin and nasal, and as the envelope falls it comes back to a square wave, which is hollow and round. The filter is closing over the same 170 ms, so each note goes from bright and pinched to soft and open. A quiet saw from Oscillator B adds some buzz. Howard Jones played a Sequential Pro-One, the synth the Pro-1 copies, in his early live set-up.

steps.title: Square wave, quiet saw beside it
steps.why:
A square wave with a quiet saw beside it. Oscillator A’s pulse width will move inside every note in step 3.
- Osc A pulse, PULSE WIDTH 5, OCTAVE 1: a square in bass range, hollow and round. At 5 every note will end as a square. Saw and SYNC off.
- Osc B sawtooth, OCTAVE 1: the same octave, FREQUENCY 0.1 (a tenth of a semitone sharp). Low frequency at NORMAL, keyboard on.
- OSC A 8, OSC B 4, NOISE/EXT 0: the square leads and a little saw adds buzz. The saw is not affected by the pulse-width movement.
- Listen for: a hollow bass with a faint buzzy edge and slow beating.

steps.title: A bounce from the filter
steps.why:
A bounce from the filter. The filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), opens the 24 dB low-pass filter at the front of each note.
- CUTOFF 4.5 (about 450 Hz), RESONANCE 1.5: fairly dark, with a small peak.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 3.5: opens nearly three octaves.
- ATTACK 0, DECAY 5 (170 ms), SUSTAIN 0: closes fully again in about 170 ms. With sustain at 0 the movement always runs to the end.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 6: slightly more than half tracking, so higher notes bounce a little brighter. RELEASE 34 ms.
- Listen for: an ordinary bouncy bass so far.

steps.title: Send the same envelope to the pulse width
steps.why:
The same envelope now moves Oscillator A’s pulse width as well. Moving pulse width is PWM (pulse-width modulation); here it happens once per note rather than as a wobble.
- AMOUNT FIL ENV 8: at the top the width is pushed from 50 % to about 79 %, thin and nasal. The scale is not even: 5 is only 11 %.
- FIL ENV route DIRECT: the filter envelope onto the always-on bus.
- To OSC A PW DIR: Oscillator A’s pulse width listens to it.
- DECAY now sets two movements: the filter closing and the pulse returning to square.
- Listen for: inside each note it starts pinched and ends hollow.

steps.title: Volume a little longer than the bounce
steps.why:
The volume lasts a little longer than the bounce, so the hollow end of each note is still heard after the filter has closed.
- ATTACK 0: instant start.
- DECAY 5.2 (210 ms), SUSTAIN 5: falls to half level a bit after the filter has shut.
- RELEASE 3 (34 ms): short, so notes stay separate.
- Listen for: each note going from bright and pinched to soft and open.

context.mod.envAmt: How far the envelope pushes the pulse width. The scale is not even: 8 is 29 %, 5 is only 11 %.
context.mod.toAPw: Connects the DIRECT bus, which carries the filter envelope, to Oscillator A’s pulse width.
context.oscA.pw: Where the width comes to rest. At 5 every note ends as a square wave.
context.fenv.decay: One knob for two movements: the filter closing and the pulse returning to square.
context.fenv.sustain: At 0, so both movements always run to the end.
context.mix.oscB: A little saw for buzz. It is not affected by the pulse-width movement.

tweaks.hear: At 0 the notes bounce but the tone inside them is fixed. At 8 each note has a "nyow" in it.
Now the width rests at 22 % and the envelope pushes it to 51 %. The movement runs the other way: notes start hollow and end thin.
From a quick blip of tone change to a slow slide that you can follow through the whole note.
The pulse alone, so the change of tone is completely exposed.

sounds.name: Hard, Flat Riff Lead with Glide
sounds.ref: In the style of Gary Numan — "We Are Glass"
sounds.blurb: Hard, bright lead that switches on and off like a machine and slides into every note.
sounds.how: This lead is hard because nothing in it moves. Oscillator A has its saw and pulse on together, Oscillator B adds a saw an octave below, and the filter is left well open with a little resonance to sharpen the top. ENVELOPE AMOUNT is at 0 and there is no vibrato, so a note sounds exactly the same from start to finish. The volume goes straight to full and stops almost at once. The one expressive thing is glide, in NORMAL mode, so every note slides in from the one before whether or not the keys overlap.

steps.title: Saw and pulse, with a saw below
steps.why:
This lead is hard because nothing in it moves. The raw tone is thick and buzzy from the start.
- Osc A saw + pulse, PULSE WIDTH 5: both waves added. The square thickens the middle of the saw. OCTAVE 2, FREQUENCY 0, SYNC off.
- Osc B sawtooth, OCTAVE 1: an octave below for weight under the riff, a hair sharp (FREQUENCY 0.1). Low frequency at NORMAL, keyboard on.
- OSC A 8, OSC B 6, NOISE/EXT 0: A in front, the lower saw behind.
- Listen for: a thick, buzzy tone straight away.

steps.title: Open filter, no envelope
steps.why:
An open low-pass filter with no envelope, so a note sounds the same from start to finish.
- CUTOFF 6.7 (about 2 kHz): well open. This is the brightness of the whole sound, because nothing else moves it.
- RESONANCE 3: a small peak near 2 kHz that gives the tone a hard edge.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 0: on purpose. Any envelope movement would soften the flat, mechanical quality.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 7: keeps high notes as bright as low ones.
- Listen for: hold a note and notice how little it changes.

steps.title: On and off
steps.why:
On and off, like a machine.
- ATTACK 0: straight to full level.
- DECAY 170 ms, SUSTAIN 10: no drop at all; held notes do not fade.
- RELEASE 3.5 (54 ms): stops almost at once.
- Listen for: each note at full level for exactly as long as the key is down.

steps.title: Glide on every note
steps.why:
Glide, or portamento, is the one expressive thing in this sound.
- RATE 2 (120 ms): a quick slide into each note.
- Glide mode NORMAL: every note slides from the one before, whether or not the keys overlap. AUTO would only slide overlapping notes.
- Listen for: the start of each note in the riff arriving from the pitch of the last one.

context.oscA.pulse: On together with the saw. It thickens the middle of the tone.
context.oscB.octave: An octave below Oscillator A, for weight under the riff.
context.filter.cutoff: Well open. This is the brightness of the whole sound, because nothing else moves it.
context.filter.env: At 0 on purpose. Any envelope movement would soften the flat, mechanical quality.
context.filter.res: A small peak near 2 kHz that gives the tone a hard edge.
context.aenv.sustain: Full, so held notes do not fade at all.
context.glide.rate: The length of the slide into each note.
context.glide.mode: NORMAL: every note slides. AUTO would only slide overlapping notes.

tweaks.hear: At 0 the riff is stepped and rigid. At 4 each slide takes half a second and the notes smear into one another.
The edge becomes a thin, whining peak on top of the notes.
The pulse layer goes nasal and the lead gets a more pinched, aggressive tone.

tweaks.try: Raise to 3 with the filter envelope as it is
tweaks.hear: Each note now starts brighter and settles. It is a more ordinary lead, and less severe.

sounds.name: Mellow Slow-Attack Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Zero 7 — "In the Waiting Line"
sounds.blurb: Warm, soft bass whose notes swell open instead of hitting, for slow, unhurried lines.
sounds.how: A square wave has a hollow, woody tone because it is missing every other overtone. A quiet triangle from Oscillator B, one octave up, fills in the first of the missing ones and warms the sound. The filter starts almost shut and its envelope takes about 80 ms to open it, so each note swells into place. There is no resonance and no sharp edge anywhere. AUTO glide slides overlapping notes into each other.

steps.title: Square wave, triangle an octave up
steps.why:
A square wave has a hollow, woody tone because it is missing every other overtone. A triangle an octave up fills in the first missing one and warms it.
- Osc A pulse, PULSE WIDTH 5, OCTAVE 1: a square in bass range. Away from 5 the bass gets buzzier. Saw and SYNC off.
- Osc B triangle, OCTAVE 2: an octave up, tuned the same. Saw and pulse off; low frequency at NORMAL, keyboard on.
- Listen for: only the square is in the mixer so far, hollow and woody.

steps.title: Square in front
steps.why:
The square goes in front, the triangle colours it.
- OSC A 8: the body of the bass.
- OSC B 5: the triangle should colour the note, not be heard as a second one. At 0 the bass is more hollow.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: turn OSC B up and down to hear it warm the square.

steps.title: A filter that swells open
steps.why:
A filter that swells open. The filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), opens the 24 dB low-pass filter slowly enough to hear.
- CUTOFF 2.8 (about 140 Hz), RESONANCE 0: very low, no edge; the resting tone is mostly the bottom of the note.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 3: opens about two and a half octaves.
- ATTACK 4.6 (83 ms): the swell, the main character of the sound.
- DECAY 6 (420 ms), SUSTAIN 5, RELEASE 220 ms: eases back and stays half open while held.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 6: a little more than half tracking, so high notes are not duller than low ones.
- Listen for: "bwum" at the start of each note where a normal bass would go "dum".

steps.title: Soft volume edges
steps.why:
Soft volume edges, so notes arrive without a click and leave without a gap.
- ATTACK 3 (23 ms): a soft front.
- DECAY 6 (420 ms), SUSTAIN 8: a gentle drop to a strong held level.
- RELEASE 5.2 (270 ms): each note fades under the next.
- Listen for: an unhurried, joined-up line.

steps.title: AUTO glide
steps.why:
Glide, or portamento, slides overlapping notes into each other.
- RATE 3 (270 ms): a slow, easy slide.
- Glide mode AUTO: only when a new key goes down while the last is held.
- Retrigger off: those overlapped notes skip the swell as well.
- Listen for: in the riff the second note runs into the third and slides; separate notes swell in on pitch.

context.oscA.pw: At 5 this is a square wave: hollow and woody. Away from 5 the bass gets buzzier.
context.mix.oscB: The triangle that warms the square. At 0 the bass is more hollow.
context.filter.cutoff: Very low, so the resting tone is mostly the bottom of the note.
context.fenv.attack: The swell at the front of each note. This is the main character of the sound.
context.filter.env: How far the swell opens the tone.
context.fenv.sustain: How open a held note stays after the swell.
context.aenv.release: Long enough for each note to fade under the next.

tweaks.hear: At 0 each note has a plain, plucked front. At 4.6 it swells. At 6 the swell takes a quarter of a second and the bass sounds bowed.
From hollow and woody to rounder and fuller, as the octave above fills in.
The swell opens further and you start to hear the edge of the square wave at the top of it.
Overlapped notes take 600 ms to arrive, a long lazy slide.

sounds.name: Scratch-Style Noise Sweep
sounds.ref: In the style of Herbie Hancock — "Rockit"
sounds.blurb: A short burst of noise and low tone that sweeps up and straight back down, like a record being pushed and pulled.
sounds.how: On the record the scratching is a DJ, GrandMixer D.ST, moving a record by hand under the needle. This patch copies the shape of that sound and not the method. A record scratch is a smear of noise and pitch that speeds up and slows down again within a fraction of a second. Here noise and a low saw go through a resonant filter, and the filter envelope is given an attack and a decay of about the same length, 70 and 85 ms, so the filter sweeps up and then down. The same envelope bends Oscillator A’s pitch up and back by about nine semitones. Short keys give "wick"; slightly longer ones give "wicka".

steps.title: Noise in front, a low saw behind
steps.why:
Noise in front and a low saw behind. The noise is the hiss of the scratch; the saw gives it a pitch that can be bent.
- Osc A sawtooth, OCTAVE 1: a low saw. Pulse and SYNC off, FREQUENCY 0.
- NOISE/EXT 10: white noise at full, the hiss.
- OSC A 6, OSC B 0: the saw behind the noise, Oscillator B off. Less noise and more saw sounds more like a bent note.
- Listen for: a hissy tone with a low buzz underneath.

steps.title: A resonant filter, low
steps.why:
A low, resonant filter gives the noise a rough pitch you can hear moving.
- CUTOFF 4 (about 320 Hz): dark at rest. The Pro-1’s filter is a 24 dB low-pass.
- RESONANCE 6: turns the noise from a plain hiss into a band of sound with a rough pitch of its own.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 3: low, so every key gives nearly the same scratch.
- Listen for: a dull, whooshing hum.

steps.title: An envelope that goes up and comes back
steps.why:
The filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), is set to go up and come straight back, the shape of a record pushed and pulled.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 5.5: a sweep of more than four octaves: the width of the scratch.
- ATTACK 4.4 (70 ms): the upward half. A key released before this gives only the rise.
- DECAY 4.2 (85 ms), SUSTAIN 0: the downward half, back to closed. RELEASE 34 ms.
- Listen for: hold a key: "wee-oo", once.

steps.title: Bend the pitch with the same envelope
steps.why:
The same envelope bends the saw’s pitch, as a record’s pitch rises when it is pushed faster.
- AMOUNT FIL ENV 6: the saw goes up about nine semitones as the filter opens and falls back as it closes.
- FIL ENV route DIRECT: the filter envelope onto the always-on bus.
- To OSC A FREQ DIR: Oscillator A’s pitch listens to it.
- Listen for: the low buzz now whooping up and down with the hiss.

steps.title: Gate-length volume, retriggered
steps.why:
The volume is simply on while the key is down, so the length of the key press decides how much of the sweep is heard.
- ATTACK 1 (4 ms), DECAY 170 ms, SUSTAIN 9: on almost at once and held.
- RELEASE 3.2 (41 ms): a quick cut when you let go.
- Retrigger on: every key press restarts the sweep.
- VOLUME 9.5: raised because short bursts sound quiet.
- Listen for: short keys give "wick"; slightly longer ones give "wicka".

context.mix.noise: The hiss of the scratch. With less noise and more oscillator it sounds more like a bent note.
context.mix.oscA: The pitched part of the scratch.
context.fenv.attack: How long the upward half of the sweep takes. A key released before this time is up gives only the rising half.
context.fenv.decay: How long the downward half takes.
context.filter.env: The width of the sweep.
context.filter.res: Gives the noise a rough pitch that you can hear moving.
context.mod.envAmt: How far the saw’s pitch is bent: 6 is about nine semitones.
context.out.volume: Raised to make up for the short bursts.

tweaks.hear: At 3 the rise is a 20 ms flick and the scratch is mostly the fall. At 5.5 the rise takes 170 ms, like a slow push of the record.
At 10 it is a scratch. At 3 the saw takes over and it becomes a rubbery "woop".
The band of noise narrows to a whistle that swoops up and down: more laser than record.
The pitch bend grows to two octaves and the scratch squeals at the top.

sounds.name: Smooth Layering Line
sounds.ref: In the style of Gary Numan — Telekon
sounds.blurb: Even, slow-moving tone with a soft start, for sustained lines stacked one on another.
sounds.how: On that album the Prophet-5 supplied smooth, sustained parts under and around the harder Moog sounds. The Pro-1 is one voice of a Prophet-5, so build the part a line at a time. A sawtooth and a pulse sit at the same octave, a touch out of tune. A very slow LFO moves the width of the pulse, which keeps the tone shifting gently without any vibrato. Both envelopes have soft attacks and the release is long enough for each note to overlap the next.

steps.title: Sawtooth and pulse at the same octave
steps.why:
A sawtooth and a pulse at the same octave, a touch out of tune. The two waves fill in each other’s gaps and the detune makes them drift slowly.
- Osc A sawtooth, OCTAVE 2: bright and full. Pulse and SYNC off, FREQUENCY 0.
- Osc B pulse, PULSE WIDTH 5, OCTAVE 2: a square wave, hollow. Its width will move in step 3.
- Osc B FREQUENCY 0.1 (+0.1 st): a tenth of a semitone sharp, for slow drift. Low frequency at NORMAL, keyboard on.
- Listen for: only the saw is in the mixer so far. The pulse comes in next.

steps.title: Equal levels
steps.why:
Equal levels, so neither wave leads.
- OSC A 7, OSC B 7: saw and pulse blended evenly.
- NOISE/EXT 0: no noise.
- Listen for: a full, slowly swirling tone.

steps.title: Slow pulse-width movement
steps.why:
A very slow LFO (low-frequency oscillator) moves the pulse width of Oscillator B. Moving pulse width is PWM (pulse-width modulation), and it keeps the tone shifting without any vibrato.
- LFO triangle only, FREQUENCY 2.5 (0.35 Hz): about one cycle every three seconds. Keep it slow or it turns into a wobble.
- AMOUNT LFO 5: how far the width moves.
- LFO route DIRECT, To OSC B PW DIR: the always-on bus, and Oscillator B’s pulse width listens to it.
- Listen for: the pulse slowly thinning and fattening, like a gentle chorus.

steps.title: Half-open filter, very little envelope
steps.why:
A half-open low-pass filter with very little envelope.
- CUTOFF 5.2 (about 730 Hz), RESONANCE 0.5: takes the fizz off both waves. Smooth, but not dark.
- ENVELOPE AMOUNT 1.5: the filter envelope, an ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release), adds only a small lift.
- ATTACK 6 (260 ms): with DECAY 420 ms, SUSTAIN 7 and RELEASE 360 ms, notes brighten only slightly after they start.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 6: slightly more than half tracking, so higher notes keep their brightness.
- Listen for: a smooth tone that opens a touch as each note settles in.

steps.title: Soft start, long tail
steps.why:
Soft start, long tail, for sustained lines stacked one on another.
- ATTACK 5.5 (170 ms): removes the front edge.
- DECAY 170 ms, SUSTAIN 10: full level held.
- RELEASE 6 (570 ms): each note hangs over the next and covers the gap.
- Listen for: notes fading in and overlapping, with no hard edges.

steps.title: Slide only when notes overlap
steps.why:
Glide, or portamento, only where notes overlap.
- RATE 2.5 (190 ms): a gentle slide.
- Glide mode AUTO: separate notes start on pitch; overlapped notes slide into each other.
- Listen for: play legato for a slide, detached for clean starts.

context.oscB.freq: Slight detune against Oscillator A. It gives the slow drift.
context.mod.lfoAmt: How far the pulse width moves.
context.lfo.rate: The speed of the movement. Keep it slow or it turns into a wobble.
context.filter.cutoff: Half open: smooth, but not dark.
context.aenv.release: The tail that covers the gap to the next note.

tweaks.hear: At 4 it is a dark background hum. At 6.5 it comes forward as a bright string line.

tweaks.try: Switch Oscillator A’s sawtooth off and its pulse on, then flip OSC A PW to DIR
tweaks.hear: Both oscillators now move together, for a deeper, more obvious chorus effect.
An octave layer: the second part of a stacked arrangement, played with the same hand.

sounds.name: Hazy Pad with Drifting Tuning
sounds.ref: In the style of Boards of Canada — "Olson"
sounds.blurb: Soft, dark pad over a faint bed of hiss, with two oscillators that slide slowly in and out of tune with each other.
sounds.how: Two sawtooth waves at the same octave go through a filter that is mostly closed. Normally the detune between two oscillators is fixed, so they beat against each other at one steady speed. Here the LFO runs at its slowest, one cycle every twelve seconds, and moves Oscillator B’s pitch by a few cents. The beating slows almost to a stop, speeds up and slows again, like a tape machine that cannot quite hold its speed. A little noise in the mixer comes through the filter as a low hush under the notes.

steps.title: Two saws at the same octave
steps.why:
Two oscillators on the same waveform and octave, tuned very slightly apart. The small gap makes them beat against each other, which turns one plain note into something wider and slowly moving.
- Osc A and B sawtooth on, the rest off: a saw carries every harmonic, so it is the fullest raw tone on the panel. With both on the same shape the two match closely, and only the tuning separates them.
- OCTAVE 2 on both: the two sit in the same register, so they blend into one note rather than an octave pair.
- Osc B FREQUENCY +0.1: Oscillator B about eight cents sharp (a cent is a hundredth of a semitone). Too small to sound out of tune, big enough to beat. Turn it further and the beating speeds up into a sour wobble.
- OSC A 7, OSC B 7: equal mixer levels, which makes the beating as deep as it can be. SYNC off, LO FREQ on NORMAL and KYBD on keep B an ordinary oscillator that follows the keys.
- Listen for: hold a note. The filter is still open, so it is bright and buzzy, with a slow, even pulse in the tone. Turn OSC B to 0 and the pulse stops.

steps.title: Let the detune drift
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator, a wave too slow to hear as a pitch) is set up to move Oscillator B’s tuning, so the detune is no longer fixed.
- LFO triangle on, FREQUENCY 0 (0.08 Hz): a smooth up-and-down shape at the slowest speed, one cycle every twelve seconds. Far too slow to hear as vibrato.
- AMOUNT LFO 0.6: moves Oscillator B about eight cents each way, about the same size as the fixed detune. The detune now swings between nothing and about seventeen cents. More amount and it starts to sound out of tune.
- LFO route DIRECT: the LFO goes onto the always-on bus rather than waiting for the mod wheel.
- To OSC B FREQ DIR: Oscillator B’s pitch listens to the DIRECT bus. Oscillator A stays put, so the two drift apart and together.
- Listen for: a long held note. The beating slows almost to a stop, comes back faster, and dies away again, like a tape machine that cannot hold its speed.

steps.title: A faint bed of noise
steps.why:
A faint bed of noise under the notes, the kind of hush you hear on an old recording.
- NOISE/EXT 4.5: white noise into the filter, well below the two oscillators. White noise has equal energy at all frequencies, so on its own it is a bright hiss.
- Listen for: with the filter still open you may hear it as hiss for now; once the next step closes the filter it turns into a low hush. Turn NOISE/EXT to 0 and back to check it is there.

steps.title: Mostly closed filter
steps.why:
The filter takes the buzz off the saws and turns the sound into a dark pad. The Pro-1’s is a 24 dB low-pass: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs steeply.
- CUTOFF 4.4 (about 420 Hz): mostly closed. The saws lose their edge and the noise turns into a soft hush. Raise it and the pad gets brighter and the hiss comes back.
- RESONANCE 1: a slight boost at the cutoff, just enough to give a little shape.
- KEYBOARD AMOUNT 5: higher notes open the filter by half as much as they rise, so chords at the top do not go dull.
- Filter envelope, ENV AMOUNT 2: the filter envelope (ADSR: attack, decay, sustain, release) lifts the cutoff a little on each note. ATTACK 570 ms, DECAY 1.0 s, SUSTAIN 6 and RELEASE 1.5 s: the slow attack means each note opens a little after it starts, then settles back.
- Listen for: hold a chord of notes one after another. Each one starts dull and warms slightly over half a second.

steps.title: Fade in, long fade out
steps.why:
The loudness envelope shapes the volume of each note. Here it removes the front edge and lets notes overlap.
- ATTACK 380 ms: each note fades in over about 0.4 s instead of arriving at once. Shorter and the notes start to click in; longer and fast changes blur.
- DECAY 170 ms, SUSTAIN 10: the sustain is full, so the decay has nothing to do and held notes stay at full level.
- RELEASE 1.8 s: after you let go the note takes nearly two seconds to fade. Each note is still sounding when the next arrives, which fills the gaps.
- Listen for: play slow changes and let go early. The old note tails off under the new one. Turn RELEASE down to 3 to hear how bare the gaps sound without it.

context.oscB.freq: The fixed part of the detune, about eight cents. The LFO adds to it and takes away from it.
context.mod.lfoAmt: How far the tuning drifts. At 0.6 the drift is about as large as the fixed detune, so at one end of the swing the two oscillators are almost in tune.
context.mod.toBFreq: Connects the DIRECT bus (carrying the LFO) to Oscillator B’s pitch only. Oscillator A stays where it is, so the two move apart and together.
context.lfo.rate: At 0: one cycle every twelve seconds. The drift should be too slow to hear as vibrato.
context.mix.noise: The bed of noise. The filter turns it into a low hush.
context.filter.cutoff: Low, which keeps the pad dark and keeps the noise soft. This is the first knob to reach for.
context.aenv.release: The long fade-out that covers the gap between notes.

tweaks.hear: At 0 the beating is steady. At 0.6 it comes and goes. At 1.5 the pad goes noticeably out of tune at each end of the swing.
The hush becomes a clear layer of wind under the notes.
The saws and the noise both brighten, and the beating becomes easier to hear.
The drift takes two seconds instead of twelve, and you start to hear it as a slow vibrato that goes out of tune.

sounds.name: Fixed Pedal Note under a Gliding Voice
sounds.ref: In the style of Vangelis — "Blade Runner Blues"
sounds.blurb: A low note that never moves, with a second voice above it that slides slowly from one pitch to the next.
sounds.how: That piece was played on a Yamaha CS-80, a far larger synth. This patch borrows its layout: a long held low note with a slow line above it. DRONE holds the gate open, so the sound never stops. Oscillator B is taken off the keyboard with its KYBD switch, so it stays on a low C whatever you play. Oscillator A still follows the keys, and a long glide makes it take over a second to travel to each new note. Each key you press changes the interval between the moving voice and the fixed one.

steps.title: Hold the gate open
steps.why:
DRONE holds the gate open, so the synth sounds all the time and a key only sets the pitch. The gate is the on signal that starts the envelopes when you press a key.
- Drone on: the envelopes run to their sustain level and stay there. Switch it off to stop the drone.
- Repeat off: the LFO does not re-fire the envelopes, so the drone is one continuous note.
